00136 [PDF p.8]                                                            Abstract


00137 [PDF p.8] 


00138 [PDF p.8] 


00139 [PDF p.8]                  AI-based Model Updating for


00140 [PDF p.8]                  Nonlinear Dynamical Systems


00141 [PDF p.8] 


00142 [PDF p.8] To predict the behavior of complex engineering systems, models for their dynamics


00143 [PDF p.8] are typically constructed using first principles. Such models are commonly used by


00144 [PDF p.8] engineers to aid the system design process. In a digital twin context, these models


00145 [PDF p.8] may also be used in the operational life of the physical system to enable, among


00146 [PDF p.8] others, structural health monitoring and (control) performance enhancement. In


00147 [PDF p.8] this case, it is of vital importance that the digital twin is and remains an accurate


00148 [PDF p.8] representation of the physical system. Warranting such model accuracy is chal-


00149 [PDF p.8] lenged, firstly, by the fact that machine-to-machine variations may not allow to


00150 [PDF p.8] construct one model to represent all variations and, secondly, by hard-to-model


00151 [PDF p.8] (nonlinear) dynamical phenomena. Moreover, machine parts may deteriorate un-


00152 [PDF p.8] der the influence of wear, thereby changing the dynamical behavior of the system


00153 [PDF p.8] throughout its operational life. To address these challenges, this thesis develops


00154 [PDF p.8] artificial intelligence-based model updating techniques to update parameter values


00155 [PDF p.8] of a model and to augment and extend the governing dynamical model equations


00156 [PDF p.8] using measured response data.


00157 [PDF p.8]     In Part I of this thesis, a novel model parameter updating method is introduced.


00158 [PDF p.8] The proposed method enables values of physically interpretable parameters of


00159 [PDF p.8] nonlinear (dynamical) models to be updated in (near) real-time. Hereto, the use


00160 [PDF p.8] of artificial neural networks is proposed to construct an inverse mapping model


00161 [PDF p.8] that maps features, obtained from measured time response data, to parameter


00162 [PDF p.8] values. This complex, highly nonlinear mapping is learned, in an offline phase,


00163 [PDF p.8] by training a direct feedforward neural network using simulated response data.


00164 [PDF p.8] In the online phase, updated parameter values are inferred, within microseconds,


00165 [PDF p.8] using features that are extracted from measured response data. Different types


00166 [PDF p.8] 


00167 [PDF p.9] viii                                                                        Abstract


00168 [PDF p.9] 


00169 [PDF p.9] 


00170 [PDF p.9] of features are defined, where engineering knowledge, such as, e.g., the frequency


00171 [PDF p.9] ranges of interest for a particular system, are exploited to improve the accuracy


00172 [PDF p.9] of the inferred parameter values. Moreover, the generalizability of the model that


00173 [PDF p.9] is updated using the inferred parameter values is demonstrated. Additionally, the


00174 [PDF p.9] potential to use the inverse mapping model beyond the training space is illustrated.


00175 [PDF p.9]     In this scope, attention is also devoted to the automated selection of features


00176 [PDF p.9] based on several mutual information-based techniques to improve inference accu-


00177 [PDF p.9] racy and reduce training and inference times. Here, the aim is to maximize the


00178 [PDF p.9] information about the model parameter values contained within a small set of


00179 [PDF p.9] selected features. Additionally, hyperparameters of the neural network are tuned


00180 [PDF p.9] using Bayesian optimization. Furthermore, the proposed method is applied to


00181 [PDF p.9] a real-world high-precision wire bonder (with feedback and feedforward control)


00182 [PDF p.9] resulting in improved simulation accuracy compared to a model with manually


00183 [PDF p.9] tuned parameter values.


00184 [PDF p.9]     Since decisions that are based on updated parameter values or models may


00185 [PDF p.9] have great impact, an engineer benefits from knowing to which extent the updated


00186 [PDF p.9] model can be trusted. To this end, quantifying the uncertainty in the inferred pa-


00187 [PDF p.9] rameter values is enabled by employing probabilistic Bayesian neural networks as


00188 [PDF p.9] the inverse mapping model. This type of neural network captures both aleatoric


00189 [PDF p.9] (data) and epistemic (model) uncertainty by inferring both parameter values and


00190 [PDF p.9] their corresponding variances while using non-deterministic weights to parameter-


00191 [PDF p.9] ize the neural network. Results for a medical mechanical ventilation use case show


00192 [PDF p.9] that parameter values are inferred with (more than) sufficiently high accuracy.


00193 [PDF p.9] Although the inferred uncertainties give an indication of the relative (un)certainty


00194 [PDF p.9] in the inferred parameter values, the validation of the magnitudes of these inferred


00195 [PDF p.9] uncertainties is complicated due to the uncertainty in the true parameter values


00196 [PDF p.9] of the physical system.


00197 [PDF p.9]     In Part II of this thesis, a methodology is proposed to update the existing


00198 [PDF p.9] dynamical equations of a first principles model using measured data. This method


00199 [PDF p.9] augments the existing equations to incorporate unmodeled and/or incorrectly mod-


00200 [PDF p.9] eled dynamical terms. Simultaneously, an encoder network extends the number of


00201 [PDF p.9] states, and their governing dynamical equations are identified. The extended and


00202 [PDF p.9] augmented dynamics are captured by recurrent neural networks that are trained


00203 [PDF p.9] by minimizing an output prediction error. The resulting grey-box model retains


00204 [PDF p.9] physical interpretability of its first principles part, while demonstrating improved


00205 [PDF p.9] predictive capacity with respect to the existing first principles model. To illustrate


00206 [PDF p.9] this, the proposed method is employed to update a first principles model of a wire


00207 [PDF p.9] bonder using data measured on a physical system. Moreover, by using the first


00208 [PDF p.9] principles model as a basis, the training process and extrapolation beyond the


00209 [PDF p.9] training space are improved.


00210 [PDF p.9]     Summarizing, this PhD thesis presents techniques to update, using measure-


00211 [PDF p.9] 


00212 [PDF p.10] Abstract                                                                        ix


00213 [PDF p.10] 


00214 [PDF p.10] 


00215 [PDF p.10] ment data, parameter values of dynamical models and their governing equations


00216 [PDF p.10] while preserving the original model’s physical interpretability, thereby enhancing


00217 [PDF p.10] their use in digital twins.


00218 [PDF p.10] 


00219 [PDF p.10] Keywords:       Model updating, Nonlinear dynamical systems, Artificial intelli-


00220 [PDF p.10] gence, Feature selection, Uncertainty quantification, Grey-box system identifica-


00221 [PDF p.10] tion, Digital twins

00226 [PDF p.12] Om het dynamische gedrag van complexe technologische systemen te voorspellen


00227 [PDF p.12] worden wiskundige modellen die dit gedrag (in benadering) beschrijven meestal


00228 [PDF p.12] geconstrueerd op basis van bestaande natuurkundige wetten. Dergelijke modellen


00229 [PDF p.12] worden vaak door ingenieurs gebruikt ter ondersteuning van het ontwerpproces


00230 [PDF p.12] van systemen. In een digitale tweeling context kunnen deze modellen ook wor-


00231 [PDF p.12] den gebruikt tijdens het operationele leven van het fysieke systeem om, onder


00232 [PDF p.12] andere, de conditie van het systeem te monitoren en de (regel)prestaties te ver-


00233 [PDF p.12] beteren. In dit geval is het van vitaal belang dat de digitale tweeling een accurate


00234 [PDF p.12] beschrijving van het fysieke systeem is en blijft. Het waarborgen van deze mod-


00235 [PDF p.12] elnauwkeurigheid is een uitdaging, ten eerste, door het feit dat (kleine) variaties


00236 [PDF p.12] tussen machines (bijvoorbeeld veroorzaakt door maattoleranties) het niet toelaten


00237 [PDF p.12] om één model te construeren, en ten tweede, door mogelijke aanwezigheid van


00238 [PDF p.12] moeilijk te modelleren (niet-lineaire) dynamische verschijnselen in het fysieke sys-


00239 [PDF p.12] teem. Bovendien kunnen machineonderdelen slijten, waardoor het dynamische


00240 [PDF p.12] gedrag gedurende de operationele levensduur van het systeem verandert. Om deze


00241 [PDF p.12] uitdagingen aan te pakken, worden in dit proefschrift op Kunstmatige Intelligentie


00242 [PDF p.12] (KI) gebaseerde model update technieken ontwikkeld die: 1) parameterwaarden


00243 [PDF p.12] van een model online updaten, en die 2) de dynamische vergelijkingen van een


00244 [PDF p.12] model met behulp van gemeten responsiedata aanvullen en uitbreiden.


00245 [PDF p.12]     In deel I van dit proefschrift wordt een nieuwe methode voor het updaten


00246 [PDF p.12] van modelparameterwaarden geïntroduceerd. De voorgestelde methode maakt het


00247 [PDF p.12] mogelijk om waarden van fysisch interpreteerbare parameters van niet-lineaire


00248 [PDF p.12] (dynamische) modellen online, d.w.z., in real-time, te updaten. Hiertoe wordt


00249 [PDF p.12] het gebruik van neurale netwerken voorgesteld om een inverse-projectiemodel te


00250 [PDF p.12] construeren dat signaalkenmerken, verkregen uit gemeten responsiedata, vertaalt


00251 [PDF p.12] naar parameterwaarden. Deze zeer complexe, sterk niet-lineaire projectie wordt


00252 [PDF p.12] in een offline fase geleerd door een neuraal netwerk te trainen met gesimuleerde


00253 [PDF p.12] responsiedata. In de online fase worden geüpdatete parameterwaarden vervolgens


00254 [PDF p.12] binnen microseconden afgeleid met behulp van signaalkenmerken die zijn geëxtra-


00255 [PDF p.12] heerd uit gemeten responsiedata. Verschillende soorten signaalkenmerken worden

00260 [PDF p.13] gedefinieerd, waarbij inzicht in het systeem, zoals bijvoorbeeld zijn relevante fre-


00261 [PDF p.13] quentiegebied(en), wordt benut om de nauwkeurigheid van de afgeleide parame-


00262 [PDF p.13] terwaarden te verbeteren. Bovendien wordt de generalisatie van het gebruik van


00263 [PDF p.13] het dynamische model, geüpdatet met de afgeleide parameterwaarden, en het po-


00264 [PDF p.13] tentieel om het inverse-projectiemodel te gebruiken buiten de ruimte waarin het


00265 [PDF p.13] getraind is, geïllustreerd.


00266 [PDF p.13]     In dit kader wordt ook aandacht besteed aan de automatische selectie van


00267 [PDF p.13] signaalkenmerken op basis van verschillende technieken gebaseerd op wederzijdse


00268 [PDF p.13] informatie om de nauwkeurigheid van de te updaten parameterwaarden te ver-


00269 [PDF p.13] beteren en de trainingstijd van het neuraal netwerk en de benodigde afleidingstijd


00270 [PDF p.13] voor het inverse-projectiemodel te reduceren. Het doel hierbij is om de informatie


00271 [PDF p.13] over de modelparameterwaarden binnen een klein aantal geselecteerde signaalken-


00272 [PDF p.13] merken te maximaliseren. Daarnaast worden hyperparameters van het neuraal


00273 [PDF p.13] netwerk geoptimaliseerd met behulp van Bayesiaanse optimalisatie. Verder wordt


00274 [PDF p.13] de voorgestelde methode toegepast op een zeer precieze draadverbindermachine


00275 [PDF p.13] (met terugkoppelende en voorwaartse regeling) uit de halfgeleiderindustrie, het-


00276 [PDF p.13] geen resulteert in een verbeterde simulatienauwkeurigheid ten opzichte van een


00277 [PDF p.13] model met handmatig ingestelde parameterwaarden.


00278 [PDF p.13]     Aangezien beslissingen op basis van geüpdatete parameterwaarden of modellen


00279 [PDF p.13] grote impact kunnen hebben, heeft een ingenieur baat bij inzicht in de mate


00280 [PDF p.13] waarin het geüpdatete model kan worden vertrouwd. Om deze reden wordt


00281 [PDF p.13] het kwantificeren van de onzekerheid in de afgeleide parameterwaarden mogelijk


00282 [PDF p.13] gemaakt door het gebruik van een probabilistisch Bayesiaans neuraal netwerk


00283 [PDF p.13] voor het inverse-projectiemodel. Dit type neuraal netwerk legt zowel aleatorische


00284 [PDF p.13] (data) als epistemische (model) onzekerheid vast door zowel de parameterwaar-


00285 [PDF p.13] den als hun bijbehorende varianties af te leiden, waarbij niet-deterministische


00286 [PDF p.13] gewichten worden gebruikt om het neuraal netwerk te parametriseren. Resul-


00287 [PDF p.13] taten voor een medische mechanische ventilatie casus tonen aan dat parameter-


00288 [PDF p.13] waarden met (ruim) voldoende hoge nauwkeurigheid worden afgeleid. Hoewel de


00289 [PDF p.13] afgeleide onzekerheden een indicatie geven van de relatieve (on)zekerheid in de


00290 [PDF p.13] afgeleide parameterwaarden, wordt de validatie van deze afgeleide onzekerheden


00291 [PDF p.13] gecompliceerd door de onzekerheid in de daadwerkelijke parameterwaarden van


00292 [PDF p.13] het fysieke systeem.


00293 [PDF p.13]     In deel II van dit proefschrift wordt een methodologie voorgesteld om op een


00294 [PDF p.13] andere manier de dynamische vergelijkingen van een op fysische wetten gebaseerd


00295 [PDF p.13] bestaand model te updaten naar een grey-box model met behulp van gemeten


00296 [PDF p.13] data. Deze methode vult de bestaande dynamische vergelijkingen aan met neu-


00297 [PDF p.13] rale netwerken om zodoende niet-gemodelleerde en/of verkeerd gemodelleerde dy-


00298 [PDF p.13] namische termen op te nemen in het geüpdatete model. Tegelijkertijd breidt een


00299 [PDF p.13] additioneel neuraal netwerk het aantal dynamische toestanden uit, en worden hun


00300 [PDF p.13] dynamische vergelijkingen geïdentificeerd en gekoppeld met de toestanden van de

00304 [PDF p.14] 


00305 [PDF p.14] oorspronkelijke vergelijkingen. De uitgebreide en aangevulde dynamica wordt vast-


00306 [PDF p.14] gelegd door de (recursieve) neurale netwerken zo te trainen dat de voorspellings-


00307 [PDF p.14] fout van de uitgangssignalen geminimaliseerd wordt. Het resulterende grey-box


00308 [PDF p.14] model verbetert de nauwkeurigheid, terwijl de fysische interpreteerbaarheid van


00309 [PDF p.14] het deel van het model dat is gebaseerd op fysische wetten behouden blijft. Om dit


00310 [PDF p.14] te illustreren wordt de voorgestelde methode gebruikt om een op fysische wetten


00311 [PDF p.14] gebaseerd model van de draadverbindermachine te updaten op basis van signalen


00312 [PDF p.14] die zijn gemeten op de fysieke machine. Bovendien worden het trainingsproces en


00313 [PDF p.14] de extrapolatie buiten de trainingsruimte verbeterd door het fysische model als


00314 [PDF p.14] basis voor het grey-box model te gebruiken.


00315 [PDF p.14]     Samenvattend presenteert dit proefschrift technieken om, met behulp van ge-


00316 [PDF p.14] meten data, de parameterwaarden van een dynamisch model en zijn dynamische


00317 [PDF p.14] vergelijkingen te updaten, terwijl de fysische interpreteerbaarheid van het oor-


00318 [PDF p.14] spronkelijke model behouden blijft, wat de bruikbaarheid in digitale tweelingen


00319 [PDF p.14] verbetert.

00321 [PDF p.15] 


00322 [PDF p.16]                                 Societal summary


00323 [PDF p.16] 


00324 [PDF p.16] Digital twins play a crucial role in the fourth industrial revolution. A digital twin


00325 [PDF p.16] is a digital replica of a physical system, which may be used to optimize the system’s


00326 [PDF p.16] performance, monitor its condition, and predict its dynamical behavior. Due to


00327 [PDF p.16] the digital nature, these advantages are realized with minimal (operational) costs


00328 [PDF p.16] and without risk of damaging the physical system. Conventionally, digital twins


00329 [PDF p.16] are constituted by mathematical models that are derived from existing physical


00330 [PDF p.16] laws, which give the users valuable (physical) insight in the relations between the


00331 [PDF p.16] system’s variables such as the positions and accelerations of system components.


00332 [PDF p.16]     In practice, however, it is very challenging to accurately model the dynamical


00333 [PDF p.16] behavior of physical systems using these physical laws. Moreover, tolerances in


00334 [PDF p.16] production processes may lead to variations in the dynamic characteristics of dis-


00335 [PDF p.16] tinct physical systems that are based on the same design, and wear may lead to


00336 [PDF p.16] changes in the dynamics over time, which decreases the accuracy of these models.


00337 [PDF p.16] To overcome these problems, in this thesis, methods are developed that update


00338 [PDF p.16] these physics-based models by using data measured on the physical system in


00339 [PDF p.16] combination with artificial intelligence.


00340 [PDF p.16]     The first method developed in this thesis updates a physics-based mathematical


00341 [PDF p.16] model by adapting the parameter values of the model. These parameter values de-


00342 [PDF p.16] scribe physical characteristics of the system, such as, for example, mass, damping,


00343 [PDF p.16] or stiffness properties. This method is referred to as the Inverse Mapping Param-


00344 [PDF p.16] eter Updating (IMPU) method. The IMPU method specifically aims at updating


00345 [PDF p.16] these physically interpretable parameter values using data that is measured during


00346 [PDF p.16] operation of the system. Moreover, these parameter values are updated in real-


00347 [PDF p.16] time, such that changes in the condition of the system are identified instantly. The


00348 [PDF p.16] accurate, real-time knowledge on the system’s condition can then be immediately


00349 [PDF p.16] used, for instance, to optimize the system’s performance related to operational


00350 [PDF p.16] throughput and precision. This knowledge may also be used to monitor the phys-


00351 [PDF p.16] ical system for predictive maintenance. Moreover, an extended version of this


00352 [PDF p.16] method provides estimates of the uncertainty in the updated parameter values,


00353 [PDF p.16] which quantifies the trust to be placed in the updated model by the user, and


00354 [PDF p.16] 


00355 [PDF p.17] xvi                                                             Societal summary


00356 [PDF p.17] 


00357 [PDF p.17] 


00358 [PDF p.17] supports the decision-making process.


00359 [PDF p.17]     The second method developed in this thesis updates a physics-based model by


00360 [PDF p.17] augmenting the existing mathematical equations in the model with extra terms.


00361 [PDF p.17] Simultaneously, the number of equations is extended. Consequently, this method


00362 [PDF p.17] is referred to as the Extension and Augmentation-based (EA) model updating


00363 [PDF p.17] method. Using this method, we can correct the model for incorrectly and/or


00364 [PDF p.17] unmodelled dynamics. The extended and augmented mathematical terms are de-


00365 [PDF p.17] scribed using artificial intelligence (neural networks) based on measured data. By


00366 [PDF p.17] combining the physics-based model and the terms based on artificial intelligence,


00367 [PDF p.17] in the resulting EA model, the advantages of both approaches are combined. More


00368 [PDF p.17] specifically, the EA model retains the physical insight of the original model and


00369 [PDF p.17] significantly improves the predictive accuracy of the model due to the added, data-


00370 [PDF p.17] based neural networks. Moreover, the EA model may be used to design controllers


00371 [PDF p.17] to improve the performance of the physical system.


00372 [PDF p.17]     To conclude, this thesis presents methods to update traditional physics-based


00373 [PDF p.17] models using artificial intelligence, such that a more accurate digital twin is ob-


00374 [PDF p.17] tained that can continuously monitor the physical system’s condition and improve


00375 [PDF p.17] its performance.

00640 [PDF p.28]                                                 Introduction


00641 [PDF p.28]                                                                         1


00642 [PDF p.28] In science and engineering, mathematical models are abundantly used to describe


00643 [PDF p.28] the dynamic behavior of real-world systems, processes, and phenomena. These


00644 [PDF p.28] models are governed by mathematical relationships between model variables, that


00645 [PDF p.28] allow experts to describe, understand, analyze, and predict the dynamic behav-


00646 [PDF p.28] ior of complex systems in various fields, such as engineering, biology, economics,


00647 [PDF p.28] environmental sciences, meteorology, and psychology. The characteristics of such


00648 [PDF p.28] systems are represented by so-called model parameters. Traditionally, fundamen-


00649 [PDF p.28] tal (physical or empirical) laws, more generally referred to as first principles, are


00650 [PDF p.28] used to construct such models. Principles such as Newton’s laws of motion, Kir-


00651 [PDF p.28] choff’s law, Maxwell’s equations, Bernoulli’s principle, and conservation laws of


00652 [PDF p.28] energy, mass, and momentum allow the modeling of a wide range of engineering


00653 [PDF p.28] systems, such as high-tech systems, roller coasters, wind turbines, and medical


00654 [PDF p.28] equipment. Models of such engineering systems are extremely valuable for model-


00655 [PDF p.28] based system design, as they can be used to simulate and optimize the behavior


00656 [PDF p.28] of a system in a fast and cheap manner, lessening the need for time-consuming


00657 [PDF p.28] experiments on expensive prototypes. Besides applications in the design phase,


00658 [PDF p.28] nowadays, models are used more and more in an online context as well. For ex-


00659 [PDF p.28] ample, model-based control [32, 150, 209] is used to position motion stages with


00660 [PDF p.28] high accuracy and precision. Models can also be used to simulate various scenarios


00661 [PDF p.28] to aid in the decision-making process without the risk of damaging an expensive


00662 [PDF p.28] physical system [11, 45, 94]. If such a model is used throughout the system’s entire


00663 [PDF p.28] lifecycle (design, manufacturing, operation, and end of life), we may refer to this


00664 [PDF p.28] model as a digital twin of the physical system [64, 224].


00665 [PDF p.28] 


00666 [PDF p.29]     2                                                         Chapter 1. Introduction


00667 [PDF p.29] 


00668 [PDF p.29] 


00669 [PDF p.29] 1         Physical system


00670 [PDF p.29]                                                      Model-based decisions


00671 [PDF p.29] 


00672 [PDF p.29] 


00673 [PDF p.29]                                              Data     Updated model


00674 [PDF p.29] 


00675 [PDF p.29] 


00676 [PDF p.29]           First principles model


00677 [PDF p.29] 


00678 [PDF p.29] 


00679 [PDF p.29]                                              Model


00680 [PDF p.29] 


00681 [PDF p.29] 


00682 [PDF p.29] 


00683 [PDF p.29]     Figure 1.1. Schematic representation of updating a first principles model using


00684 [PDF p.29]     measured data. In the picture at the top left, the Z-stage of the XYZ-motion stage


00685 [PDF p.29]     of an industrial wirebonder is highlighted.


00686 [PDF p.29] 


00687 [PDF p.29] 


00688 [PDF p.29]         For a digital twin to fulfill its full potential in the operation phase, the model


00689 [PDF p.29]     (that constitutes the digital twin) should be an accurate representation of the phys-


00690 [PDF p.29]     ical system. Due to the complexity of real-world systems and the typically limited


00691 [PDF p.29]     descriptive power of models that are based on first principles, mismatches between


00692 [PDF p.29]     the model and the physical system often exist, leading to insufficiently accurate


00693 [PDF p.29]     model predictions, resulting in poor design decisions or sub-optimal operational


00694 [PDF p.29]     decisions [151]. Moreover, due to, among others, wear, aging, and environmental


00695 [PDF p.29]     factors, the condition of the physical system may change over time, altering the


00696 [PDF p.29]     system’s behavior. Consequently, the digital twin should be adjusted accordingly


00697 [PDF p.29]     during operation of the system [225, 232]. Additionally, such online adjustments


00698 [PDF p.29]     enable, among others, online predictive maintenance through model-based (struc-


00699 [PDF p.29]     tural) health monitoring [60]. It is essential to use data measured on the physical


00700 [PDF p.29]     system that captures its current condition to enhance and enrich the digital twin


00701 [PDF p.29]     [119]. The process of adjusting an existing model, i.e., its governing mathemati-


00702 [PDF p.29]     cal relations and/or parameter values, using data measured on its corresponding


00703 [PDF p.29]     physical system, is referred to as model updating and is illustrated in Figure 1.1.


00704 [PDF p.29]         This thesis will discuss the development of techniques that may be used to


00705 [PDF p.29]     update models of dynamical engineering systems. Here, we aim at unlocking the


00706 [PDF p.29]     full potential of the updated model as a digital twin during the operation phase


00707 [PDF p.29]     of its physical counterpart. Special attention will be devoted to updating models


00708 [PDF p.29]     that are based on first principles, as these principles provide valuable insight into


00709 [PDF p.29]     the underlying physics of the system.


00710 [PDF p.29] 


00711 [PDF p.30] 1.1. Physics-based dynamical system modeling                                        3


00712 [PDF p.30] 


00713 [PDF p.30] 


00714 [PDF p.30]                                                                                          1


00715 [PDF p.30] 1.1     Physics-based dynamical system modeling


00716 [PDF p.30] As already mentioned, for many complex (mechanical) engineering systems, dy-


00717 [PDF p.30] namical models are used to predict and understand how a system behaves, e.g.,


00718 [PDF p.30] moves or vibrates, under the influence of external excitations and/or disturbances.


00719 [PDF p.30] As a result, the dynamical model can be used to control the system towards a de-


00720 [PDF p.30] sired position or time-dependent trajectory, or to avoid unwanted behavior such as


00721 [PDF p.30] destructive resonances. The mathematical relationships that describe the dynam-


00722 [PDF p.30] ical behavior of the (time-dependent) variables of the model consist of differen-


00723 [PDF p.30] tial equations, i.e., equations in which the relationships between various variables


00724 [PDF p.30] and their (higher-order) time-derivatives are expressed [30]. For models where


00725 [PDF p.30] the variables vary over more than one dimension (e.g., spatial and/or temporal),


00726 [PDF p.30] these differential equations are referred to as Partial Differential Equations (PDEs)


00727 [PDF p.30] [195]. These relatively involved PDEs can be simplified to Ordinary Differential


00728 [PDF p.30] Equations (ODEs) that only vary over one dimension (time), by discretizing the


00729 [PDF p.30] other dimensions. During simulation, an ODE for dynamical (mechanical) systems


00730 [PDF p.30] typically has user-defined time-varying input signals (e.g., applied forces and/or


00731 [PDF p.30] prescribed displacements) and output signals. Here, the output signals represent


00732 [PDF p.30] the resulting response of the system in terms of output variables that are mea-


00733 [PDF p.30] sured on the physical system using sensors, and are of interest to the engineer


00734 [PDF p.30] (e.g., positions, velocities, accelerations, and/or pressures).


00735 [PDF p.30]     Besides the dynamical input-output behavior, the physical system will contain


00736 [PDF p.30] internal dynamics (which are often too costly or practically infeasible to measure on


00737 [PDF p.30] the physical system) that underlie this input-output behavior. When using First


00738 [PDF p.30] Principles (FPs) to construct a (dynamical) model, the most relevant internal


00739 [PDF p.30] dynamics are usually included in the model. Therefore, the expert that uses


00740 [PDF p.30] the model has direct access to these internal dynamics which provide (physical)


00741 [PDF p.30] insight. For mechanical systems, models are typically constructed in the form


00742 [PDF p.30] of second-order ODEs, where the time-dependent variables are called Degrees of


00743 [PDF p.30] Freedom (DoFs). These second-order ODEs are, however, often converted to first-


00744 [PDF p.30] order ODEs. In this case, the time-dependent variables are referred to as states,


00745 [PDF p.30] where each state typically represents a DoF or the first time-derivative of a DoF


00746 [PDF p.30] (a velocity variable). The use of states to describe the dynamical model is referred


00747 [PDF p.30] to as State-Space (SS) modeling [230]. Having the ODEs in SS form is, among


00748 [PDF p.30] others, attractive for the use of well-established techniques for controller design.


00749 [PDF p.30]     A relevant distinction to be made for dynamical (state-space) models is the


00750 [PDF p.30] existence of linear and nonlinear models. The theory for linear ODEs is well-


00751 [PDF p.30] developed. For a linear model, the relationships between the variables (or states)


00752 [PDF p.30] are proportional [160, 163]. Consequently, if the input to a system (e.g., a force) is


00753 [PDF p.30] increased with a certain factor, the magnitude of the output of the system (e.g., a


00754 [PDF p.30] displacement) will increase with that same factor. Furthermore, a useful property

00757 [PDF p.31] 


00758 [PDF p.31] 


00759 [PDF p.31] 1   of linear ODEs is the superposition property [160]. Superposition dictates that


00760 [PDF p.31]     the sum of the responses to individual excitations is identical to the response to


00761 [PDF p.31]     the sum of those individual excitations. The behavior of many dynamical systems


00762 [PDF p.31]     is approximated by linear ODEs, although, in practice, most engineering systems


00763 [PDF p.31]     do not behave linearly. Some of the many examples of nonlinearities are friction


00764 [PDF p.31]     effects, spring stiffening, position-dependent dynamics, non-symmetric (bolted)


00765 [PDF p.31]     connections between system components, large rotations, and impacts. Especially


00766 [PDF p.31]     given the increasing performance demands on modern engineering systems, e.g.,


00767 [PDF p.31]     the accuracy and throughput of high-performance motion stages, it has become


00768 [PDF p.31]     increasingly relevant to employ accurate nonlinear models instead of using approx-


00769 [PDF p.31]     imate linear(ized) models [158]. Due to the non-proportional relations between


00770 [PDF p.31]     variables/states in the nonlinear case, useful tools for (and properties of) linear


00771 [PDF p.31]     systems, such as the superposition property, cannot be used anymore, however.


00772 [PDF p.31]     Additionally, the analysis of nonlinear models is generally more challenging than


00773 [PDF p.31]     for linear models.


00774 [PDF p.31]         An advantage of both linear and nonlinear FP models is that the entire model


00775 [PDF p.31]     structure is mathematically interpretable, i.e., mathematical relations between


00776 [PDF p.31]     variables are clear and facilitate the analytical understanding of the model. Con-


00777 [PDF p.31]     sequently, constructing models using FPs is also referred to as white-box modeling


00778 [PDF p.31]     [174]. In addition to mathematical interpretability, the FP model also benefits from


00779 [PDF p.31]     physical interpretability, i.e., the physical meaning of the mathematical relation-


00780 [PDF p.31]     ships, the system state variables, and the involved model parameters is understood.


00781 [PDF p.31]     Physical interpretability is highly valuable to engineers when designing and opti-


00782 [PDF p.31]     mizing (properties of) a dynamical system and when monitoring the condition of a


00783 [PDF p.31]     physical system. Note, however, that, in the end, any model is a simplification of


00784 [PDF p.31]     reality, where the modeler’s skill and time, and the availability of tools (e.g., knowl-


00785 [PDF p.31]     edge of first principles, availability of modeling software, and computing power)


00786 [PDF p.31]     dictate and limit the complexity and accuracy of a model. Consequently, in prac-


00787 [PDF p.31]     tice, it is infeasible to capture all real-world dynamics of a system. Moreover, the


00788 [PDF p.31]     true model parameter values, which aim to capture the true characteristics of the


00789 [PDF p.31]     physical system, may be challenging to derive or tune with sufficient accuracy and,


00790 [PDF p.31]     in addition, may suffer from machine-to-machine variations due to manufacturing


00791 [PDF p.31]     tolerances, and wear and tear.


00792 [PDF p.31]         To address the relatively limited descriptive capacity of FP models and the chal-


00793 [PDF p.31]     lenges in deriving/tuning their parameter values, alternative, data-driven modeling


00794 [PDF p.31]     methods have been developed. A highly popular data-driven modeling method is,


00795 [PDF p.31]     for example, System Identification (SI) [95, 134, 165]. In SI, a generic (linear


00796 [PDF p.31]     or nonlinear) model structure is defined by the user, such as is the case in the


00797 [PDF p.31]     Nonlinear Autoregressive (Moving Average) with Exogenous Inputs (NAR(MA)X)


00798 [PDF p.31]     method [20] and in methods using (nonlinear) state-space model structures [161,


00799 [PDF p.31]     186]. Then, the output response of this model is fitted to the physical system’s

00823 [PDF p.32] 1.2.1     Introduction to artificial intelligence


00824 [PDF p.32] In recent years, the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has gained a lot of attention.


00825 [PDF p.32] This field aspires to create smart machines (or systems and computers) that can


00826 [PDF p.32] think and act independently and intelligently. Using AI, these smart machines


00827 [PDF p.32] learn to perform tasks that were traditionally only performed by humans, e.g.,


00828 [PDF p.32] understanding language, image recognition, and decision making. As a subset of


00829 [PDF p.32] the vast field of AI, Machine Learning (ML) methods learn from experience (or


00830 [PDF p.32] data). Consequently, instead of letting humans program a machine to perform


00831 [PDF p.32] one specific task, machine learning feeds a machine with data, allowing it to learn


00832 [PDF p.32] patterns in this data and improve its behavior by training itself on this data.


00833 [PDF p.32] Then, when new data is provided to the machine, the learned patterns are used


00834 [PDF p.32] to predict or infer outcomes, make decisions, or provide other types of insights.


00835 [PDF p.32]     A widely used form of ML involves Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), which


00836 [PDF p.32] are inspired by the functioning of the human brain and schematically shown in


00837 [PDF p.32] Figure 1.2. Hence, an ANN consists of artificial neurons that mimic biological


00838 [PDF p.32] neurons by processing the inputs to this neuron using so-called (nonlinear) ac-


00839 [PDF p.32] tivation functions. These artificial neurons are interconnected by various edges,


00840 [PDF p.32] representing the synapses in the human brain. To each edge, a single weight is


00841 [PDF p.32] assigned, such that these edges control how information is transmitted through


00842 [PDF p.32] the ANN. By tuning the weights of all edges using data, the ANN learns how

00859 [PDF p.33]     A popular approach to tune (or train) these weights is by employing supervised


00860 [PDF p.33]     learning, in which labeled training data, i.e., consisting of known pairs of input


00861 [PDF p.33]     and output values, is used to learn which output values should be inferred based


00862 [PDF p.33]     on specific input values. Once trained, the ANN typically also generalizes to other


00863 [PDF p.33]     data that is similar yet distinct from the training data. As such, a (trained) ANN


00864 [PDF p.33]     can thus be considered as a mathematical function. The most traditional type of


00865 [PDF p.33]     ANN, the feedforward multilayer perceptron, is constructed such that it consists


00866 [PDF p.33]     of multiple consecutive layers, where the neurons in each layer are connected only


00867 [PDF p.33]     to the neurons in the adjacent layers. The first layer (or the input layer) is used


00868 [PDF p.33]     to provide the ANN with the to-be-processed information. Then, this informa-


00869 [PDF p.33]     tion is processed through one or multiple hidden layers to an output layer, which


00870 [PDF p.33]     contains the output of the ANN. By increasing the number of hidden layers, the


00871 [PDF p.33]     descriptive power of the ANN is enhanced, allowing it to capture more complex


00872 [PDF p.33]     phenomena. If ANNs with multiple hidden layers are employed, this is referred


00873 [PDF p.33]     to as deep learning. For a detailed introduction to ANNs and deep learning, the


00874 [PDF p.33]     reader is referred to [23].


00875 [PDF p.33]         The use of most ANNs (or ML-methods in general) can be divided in two


00876 [PDF p.33]     phases: an offline phase and an online phase. In the offline phase, learning algo-


00877 [PDF p.33]     rithms are employed to train the ANN weights (see Section 2.2.2.2 or [23] for a


00878 [PDF p.33]     more detailed discussion), which typically demands significant computational ef-

00890 [PDF p.34] 1.2.2    Modeling dynamical systems using AI


00891 [PDF p.34] Due to the high descriptive power and flexibility of (deep) ANNs and AI-based


00892 [PDF p.34] methods in general, their popularity in the (mechanical) engineering community


00893 [PDF p.34] has increased significantly. For example, AI has been applied on engineering sys-


00894 [PDF p.34] tems for a variety of applications, such as, control [57, 70, 155], fault detection


00895 [PDF p.34] and classification [74, 76, 86, 130, 213], path planning [196], surrogate modeling


00896 [PDF p.34] [43, 121, 175, 203, 212], and system identification [164, 197, 198]. As mentioned,


00897 [PDF p.34] (the weights of) an ANN are trained on data, similar to how parameter values of


00898 [PDF p.34] generic model structures are tuned in SI (as discussed in Section 1.1). Due to their


00899 [PDF p.34] universal function approximation characteristic, ANNs can replace the relatively


00900 [PDF p.34] simple model structures used in traditional SI, resulting in machine learning-based


00901 [PDF p.34] SI. ML-based SI methods can be categorized in black-box and grey-box techniques


00902 [PDF p.34] [174], see Figure 1.3.


00903 [PDF p.34]     Black-box SI methods are purely data-driven approaches for which the model


00904 [PDF p.34] structure (e.g., an ANN) is typically considered too complex for direct mathemat-


00905 [PDF p.34] ical interpretation. Specifically, the complexity of the model structure makes it


00906 [PDF p.34] difficult to analytically reason about the relationships between the model’s vari-


00907 [PDF p.34] ables. An advantage of black-box SI methods, however, is that they typically


00908 [PDF p.34] yield relatively accurate models of a physical system due to their high versatil-


00909 [PDF p.34] ity. Some examples of black-box SI methods are: deep kernel-based methods [47],


00910 [PDF p.34] Volterra/Wiener neural networks [31], deep NARX models [137], and (nonlinear)


00911 [PDF p.34] state-space identification using deep learning-based autoencoders [14, 140]. A


00912 [PDF p.34] disadvantage of such black-box SI methods is that valuable physics-related knowl-


00913 [PDF p.34] edge, which has been gathered in the past centuries, remains entirely unused.


00914 [PDF p.34] Consequently, the mathematical and physical interpretability of black-box models


00915 [PDF p.34] is virtually negligible, which is unfavorable for practical use [200], especially in


00916 [PDF p.34] the context of digital twins. Moreover, in (white-box) FP models, physics-related


00917 [PDF p.34] knowledge is leveraged, enabling them to achieve robust and reliable extrapola-


00918 [PDF p.34] tion capabilities beyond the conditions for which they were initially constructed.


00919 [PDF p.34] In contrast, black-box models tend to perform poorly beyond the scenarios covered


00920 [PDF p.34] by the data that was used to train them.


00921 [PDF p.34]     Recent research has therefore been involved with incorporating mathematical


00922 [PDF p.34] and physical knowledge in ML techniques [70]. This is achieved by combining

00938 [PDF p.35]     white-box and black-box methods, they are often referred to as grey-box methods,


00939 [PDF p.35]     see Figure 1.3. Other popular terms for grey-box modeling are ‘hybrid (physics-


00940 [PDF p.35]     data) modeling’ or ‘physics-enhanced ML’1.1 [44]. A major advantage of physics-


00941 [PDF p.35]     enhanced ML methods is that these methods can improve the accuracy of an


00942 [PDF p.35]     original FP model, and improve the robustness of a data-based model even beyond


00943 [PDF p.35]     the training data. Additionally, it allows to more easily train a (grey-box) model


00944 [PDF p.35]     in scenarios where limited data is available. As already indicated in Figure 1.3, in


00945 [PDF p.35]     physics-enhanced ML, we distinguish between three different types, emphasizing


00946 [PDF p.35]     that such grey-box techniques exist on a spectrum where some methods use a


00947 [PDF p.35]     relatively larger amount of black-box methods compared to white-box methods,


00948 [PDF p.35]     and vice-versa [44]:


00949 [PDF p.35] 


00950 [PDF p.35]         • Physics-informed ML enhances purely data-driven machine learning meth-


00951 [PDF p.35]           ods by including insights or constraints derived from physics. For example,


00952 [PDF p.35]           the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDY) method [17, 34,


00953 [PDF p.35]           39, 51, 201] identifies a model by finding a sparse set of terms and their


00954 [PDF p.35]           coefficients to identify a system. Here, these terms are selected from a large


00955 [PDF p.35]           collection of relatively simple functions that are defined by the user using


00956 [PDF p.35]           physical knowledge. A second popular example of physics-informed ML is


00957 [PDF p.35]           the Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) [75, 176, 216, 233], which in-


00958 [PDF p.35]           corporates physical knowledge in the form of PDEs that describe the under-


00959 [PDF p.35]           lying physical system. These PDEs are used to enforce constraints on the


00960 [PDF p.35]           neural network’s predictions by incorporating these constraints into the loss


00961 [PDF p.35]           function.

00969 [PDF p.36]   • Physics-guided ML assumes, in contrast to physics-informed ML, that a             1


00970 [PDF p.36]     high-fidelity physics-based (e.g., FP) model (structure) is available. Using


00971 [PDF p.36]     (physics-guided) ML, these FP models are enhanced by, for example, iden-


00972 [PDF p.36]     tifying or tuning (latent) parameter values of (dynamic) FP models using


00973 [PDF p.36]     ANNs [9, 125, 159] and Bayesian optimization [100, 113, 138].


00974 [PDF p.36]   • Physics-encoded ML strikes a balance between physics-informed ML and


00975 [PDF p.36]     physics-guided ML, as it assumes a decently accurate FP model to be avail-


00976 [PDF p.36]     able of which the model structure needs to be enhanced using ML techniques


00977 [PDF p.36]     to fully capture the (highly complex) underlying physics. Consequently,


00978 [PDF p.36]     their (physical) interpretability falls somewhere between physics-guided and


00979 [PDF p.36]     physics-informed ML techniques. An example of physics-encoded ML tech-


00980 [PDF p.36]     niques is the PhI-SINDy method [122], which builds upon the original SINDy


00981 [PDF p.36]     method by incorporating known terms that describe the known FP model.


00982 [PDF p.36]     Other examples are Gaussian Process-based [239] and neural network-based


00983 [PDF p.36]     [231] latent force models, where ML techniques that model specific unknown


00984 [PDF p.36]     physical phenomena, such as damping characteristics, are integrated into an


00985 [PDF p.36]     existing FP model.


00986 [PDF p.36]     When the differential equations that govern an FP model of a system are fully


00987 [PDF p.36] retained, as may be the case in physics-guided and physics-encoded ML, we refer to


00988 [PDF p.36] this as a form of model updating. In this case, both the FP model and the physical


00989 [PDF p.36] knowledge inherently embedded within the FP model are preserved. This proves


00990 [PDF p.36] valuable for the generalizability of the updated model and for the engineers that


00991 [PDF p.36] employ the (updated) model as a Digital Twin (as it warrants interpretability).


00992 [PDF p.36] In this thesis, we will specifically explore model parameter updating (a form of


00993 [PDF p.36] physics-guided ML) and model structure updating (a form of physics-encoded ML).


00994 [PDF p.36] Open challenges for these types of model updating are discussed in Section 1.3.

00997 [PDF p.36] 1.3     Challenges in model updating


00998 [PDF p.36] As discussed earlier, typically, mismatches exist between a physical system and the


00999 [PDF p.36] FP model of that system. These mismatches may originate from (a combination


01000 [PDF p.36] of) different sources as illustrated in Figure 1.4:


01001 [PDF p.36]   • Parameter values of a physical system (e.g., stiffness values or center of


01002 [PDF p.36]     mass locations) may be challenging to accurately measure or determine, be


01003 [PDF p.36]     variable due to machine-to-machine variations, or change over time due to


01004 [PDF p.36]     wear. Using such incorrect parameter values in the FP model results in a


01005 [PDF p.36]     suboptimal model that does not exactly represent the physical model.


01006 [PDF p.36]   • Dynamical effects may sometimes be too complex to be (accurately) mod-


01007 [PDF p.36]     eled using FPs. Consequently, they may be simplified, e.g., by using a linear


01008 [PDF p.36]

01010 [PDF p.37] 


01011 [PDF p.37] 


01012 [PDF p.37] 1           stiffness instead of a cubic stiffness, or, if this is not possible or the modeler


01013 [PDF p.37]             is not aware of certain effects, they may not be included in the FP model at


01014 [PDF p.37]             all.


01015 [PDF p.37]          • States can significantly increase the FP model’s complexity, or it may be


01016 [PDF p.37]            difficult to recognize which states play a significant role in the dynamical be-


01017 [PDF p.37]            havior of the physical system. Therefore, some states that can be relevant to


01018 [PDF p.37]            the behavior of the physical system, e.g., states related to flexible dynamics,


01019 [PDF p.37]            parasitic degrees of freedom, or complex friction effects, may not be included


01020 [PDF p.37]            in the FP model.


01021 [PDF p.37]          • Discretization may be related to how finely or coarsely both spatial and


01022 [PDF p.37]            temporal variables of the model, e.g., the size of finite elements and the size


01023 [PDF p.37]            of the time step in discrete time simulations, are discretized. Typically, a


01024 [PDF p.37]            finely discretized variable demands greater computational effort, whereas a


01025 [PDF p.37]            coarsely discretized one reduces the accuracy of the model.


01026 [PDF p.37]          • Measurements performed on the physical system can be erroneous, e.g.,


01027 [PDF p.37]            due to sampling-induced errors or faulty sensors, resulting in missing and


01028 [PDF p.37]            noisy measurement data, as well as outliers in the measurement data. Such


01029 [PDF p.37]            measurement errors may give a false impression of the physical system, but


01030 [PDF p.37]            also complicate the model updating or system identification process.


01031 [PDF p.37]         This thesis will focus on the first three mismatch sources. Hence, it is as-


01032 [PDF p.37]     sumed that the employed FP models are discretized such that they accurately


01033 [PDF p.37]     represent/simulate their associated non-discretized variants. Furthermore, it is


01034 [PDF p.37]     assumed that major measurement errors such as outliers and missing samples on


01035 [PDF p.37]     the physical system are negligible. The presence of noise in the measurement


01036 [PDF p.37]     data is, however, taken into consideration in this thesis, as it is typically unavoid-


01037 [PDF p.37]     able in practice. Part II of this thesis will focus on solely updating parameter


01038 [PDF p.37]     values of FP models. Specifically, the online updating of these parameter values


01039 [PDF p.37]     will be addressed. Open research challenges for online model parameter updating


01040 [PDF p.37]     are discussed in Section 1.3.1. In Part III of this thesis, a broader perspective


01041 [PDF p.37]     will be adopted in which we aim at simultaneously correcting for incorrect pa-


01042 [PDF p.37]     rameter values, incorrect or unmodeled dynamical effects, and missing states and


01043 [PDF p.37]     their governing (differential) equations. Since such model updating strategies in-


01044 [PDF p.37]     volve updating the model structure (i.e., the governing differential equations), this


01045 [PDF p.37]     updating strategy is referred to as model structure updating, for which research


01046 [PDF p.37]     challenges are discussed in Section 1.3.2.

01078 [PDF p.38] (initial) values of these physically-interpretable parameters can be difficult to pre-

01080 [PDF p.38] during operation of the system, parameter values may change due to wear and


01081 [PDF p.38] tear. Therefore, these parameter values need to be updated (online), such that


01082 [PDF p.38] some cost function, describing the mismatch between the (updated) FP model


01083 [PDF p.38] and a physical system, is minimized. For example, for linear mechanical systems,


01084 [PDF p.38] this cost can be a function of the mismatches between modal characteristics (e.g.,


01085 [PDF p.38] eigenfrequencies and eigenmodes) of the (FP) model and similar measured char-


01086 [PDF p.38] acteristics of the physical system.


01087 [PDF p.38]     To minimize such cost functions, classical methods employ gradient-based


01088 [PDF p.38] methods, e.g., methods that exploit the sensitivity of these modal characteristics


01089 [PDF p.38] of the model with respect to the parameter values [152]. Alternatively, in recent


01090 [PDF p.38] years, gradient-free parameter updating methods such as genetic algorithms, dif-


01091 [PDF p.38] ferential evolutionary methods, and particle swarm optimization have been devel-


01092 [PDF p.38] oped for nonlinear systems [38, 174]. In general, these traditional sensitivity-based


01093 [PDF p.38] methods and gradient-free methods are, however, iterative in nature and therefore


01094 [PDF p.38] may require significant (online) computation time to find the correct parameter


01095 [PDF p.38] values. Consequently, such methods are also referred to as parametric identifica-


01096 [PDF p.38] tion methods [174], as they do not necessarily aim at updating parameter values


01097 [PDF p.38] online, but offline. In a digital twin context, extensive online computation times


01098 [PDF p.38] are undesirable because latency in the updating of parameter values causes la-

01103 [PDF p.39] 1   tency in, for example, (machine/structural) health monitoring, which can lead to


01104 [PDF p.39]     overdue decisions.


01105 [PDF p.39]         Therefore, online parameter updating methods have been developed, such as


01106 [PDF p.39]     the (extended) Kalman filter [24, 132, 222]. However, typically, such filtering


01107 [PDF p.39]     methods require the dynamical model to be explicitly available. As a result, these


01108 [PDF p.39]     methods do not allow updating parameter values of models that are embedded in


01109 [PDF p.39]     complex simulation software without (direct) access to the mathematical model


01110 [PDF p.39]     (as is often encountered in industry). Moreover, for models with a large number


01111 [PDF p.39]     of states, such filter-based methods may still require significant online computa-


01112 [PDF p.39]     tion effort [5]. These limitations can be overcome by exploiting physics-guided


01113 [PDF p.39]     ML approaches. For example, as an alternative to computationally expensive for-


01114 [PDF p.39]     ward dynamics models, i.e., models that obtain outputs given some set of inputs


01115 [PDF p.39]     and model parameter values, ML-based surrogate models (already mentioned in


01116 [PDF p.39]     Section 1.2.2) can be used. These surrogate models are trained offline, requir-


01117 [PDF p.39]     ing significant computational effort. After training, however, in the online phase,


01118 [PDF p.39]     surrogate models can predict output behavior with little computational effort.


01119 [PDF p.39]     To constitute a surrogate model, ANNs may be employed due to their universal


01120 [PDF p.39]     function approximation capabilities. Similarly, ANNs may be employed as inverse


01121 [PDF p.39]     (mapping) models to solve inverse problems, e.g., obtain model parameter values


01122 [PDF p.39]     given some set of (measured) outputs and inputs. Such approaches are, for exam-


01123 [PDF p.39]     ple, employed to update parameter values of models with linear(ized) dynamics


01124 [PDF p.39]     with negligible online computation time [9, 125, 159]. Here, it is noted that the


01125 [PDF p.39]     (online) computation time scales minimally with respect to the model complexity


01126 [PDF p.39]     (e.g., number of states and parameters). The applicability of such methods to


01127 [PDF p.39]     nonlinear dynamical models is, however, left unexplored.

01129 [PDF p.39]          Challenge I. How to update physically interpretable parameter values of


01130 [PDF p.39]          models of nonlinear dynamical systems online with minimal computational


01131 [PDF p.39]          effort, based on measurement data?

01134 [PDF p.39]         As already discussed, (online) model parameter updating has significant ad-


01135 [PDF p.39]     vantages for digital twins. However, carelessly basing decisions on incorrectly es-


01136 [PDF p.39]     timated parameter values (without knowing that these values are incorrect) may


01137 [PDF p.39]     have severe negative consequences for, e.g., safety and cost, especially in critical


01138 [PDF p.39]     applications found in, e.g., the medical field. Therefore, Uncertainty Quantifi-


01139 [PDF p.39]     cation (UQ) is regarded as a valuable property of model (parameter) updating


01140 [PDF p.39]     methods. UQ involves estimating the uncertainty in the updated parameter val-


01141 [PDF p.39]     ues to quantify the confidence or trust an engineer should place in these updated


01142 [PDF p.39]     parameter values, such that they can use this knowledge in the decision-making


01143 [PDF p.39]     process. Some state-of-the-art model parameter updating methods that enable

01148 [PDF p.40] UQ are, among others, (extended) Kalman filters [24, 132, 222], Bayesian infer-       1


01149 [PDF p.40] ence [154, 162], and Markov chain Monte Carlo-based methods [18, 190]. Such


01150 [PDF p.40] methods, however, typically suffer from relatively high online computational costs


01151 [PDF p.40] for, e.g., models with a high number of states, and/or require direct access to


01152 [PDF p.40] the (differential) equations of the model. Solving inverse problems using ANNs


01153 [PDF p.40] to update parameter values, as discussed for Challenge I, does satisfy the above


01154 [PDF p.40] requirements. However, traditional (deterministic) ANNs do not provide UQ in


01155 [PDF p.40] their outputs (e.g., the updated parameter values). Therefore, alternative (ML-


01156 [PDF p.40] based) approaches that do include (estimates of) the uncertainty in their outputs


01157 [PDF p.40] are required. Preferably, these (ML-based) UQ methods allow the quantification


01158 [PDF p.40] of both the uncertainty in the trained ML-based (inverse) model (referred to as


01159 [PDF p.40] epistemic uncertainty), and the uncertainty in the data (referred to as aleatoric


01160 [PDF p.40] uncertainty), due to, e.g., measurement noise [78]. Here, it is noted that, because


01161 [PDF p.40] the inner workings of (black-box) ML techniques are typically not well under-


01162 [PDF p.40] stood, UQ is, in general, widely recognized as a critical area of focus for ML


01163 [PDF p.40] [1, 48, 78, 123, 194, 219].

01165 [PDF p.40]    Challenge II. How to include a quantification of the uncertainty in the


01166 [PDF p.40]    parameter values updated using ML-based inverse mapping models with lim-


01167 [PDF p.40]    ited additional computational cost?

01169 [PDF p.40] 


01170 [PDF p.40]     To use ANN-based inverse mapping models online to update parameter values,


01171 [PDF p.40] first, these ANNs have to be trained offline. Training the ANN is achieved using


01172 [PDF p.40] supervised learning based on training data, i.e., parameter values and their cor-


01173 [PDF p.40] responding response features, that are simulated using the FP model (as will be


01174 [PDF p.40] explained in detail in Chapter 2). This approach is based on the assumption that


01175 [PDF p.40] mismatches between the model and the physical system are exclusively caused by


01176 [PDF p.40] incorrect parameter values and that errors in the model structure are negligible.


01177 [PDF p.40] In a real-world scenario, such as industrial semiconductor production equipment


01178 [PDF p.40] and medical mechanical ventilators (both studied in this thesis), model structure


01179 [PDF p.40] errors likely do exist (to a hopefully limited extent), however. As a consequence,


01180 [PDF p.40] features extracted from measurements performed on a physical system may behave


01181 [PDF p.40] (slightly) differently from features obtained by simulating a model, when both are


01182 [PDF p.40] under the influence of (varying) parameter values. This may affect the efficacy of


01183 [PDF p.40] the parameter updating method.

01189 [PDF p.41]          Challenge III. How to employ the proposed online parameter updating


01190 [PDF p.41]          method to real-world (semiconductor and medical) systems, in which the


01191 [PDF p.41]          mismatch between the model and the physical system can not solely be at-


01192 [PDF p.41]          tributed to incorrect parameter values?


01193 [PDF p.41] 


01194 [PDF p.41] 


01195 [PDF p.41]         To summarize, for optimal use of a model as a digital twin, the model requires


01196 [PDF p.41]     to be an accurate representation of the physical system throughout the system’s


01197 [PDF p.41]     operational life. The predictive quality of nonlinear dynamical FP models is en-


01198 [PDF p.41]     hanced by online updating parameter values using measured data with negligible


01199 [PDF p.41]     online computational effort. The parameters that are updated may represent phys-


01200 [PDF p.41]     ical quantities of the system, providing insight in the condition of the system for,


01201 [PDF p.41]     e.g., (machine) health monitoring. Especially when ML is employed to update


01202 [PDF p.41]     parameter values, UQ is valuable to create trust in the updated parameter values.


01203 [PDF p.41]     If the FP model’s structure (i.e., differential equations) is, however, not an accu-


01204 [PDF p.41]     rate representation of the dynamics of the real-world system, the efficacy of the


01205 [PDF p.41]     parameter updating method may be undermined.

01207 [PDF p.41]     1.3.2     Model structure updating


01208 [PDF p.41]     In practice, multiple different sources of mismatches between an FP model and the


01209 [PDF p.41]     physical system it represents are present, as was already illustrated in Figure 1.4.


01210 [PDF p.41]     Based on output response data alone, however, it is challenging to identify the


01211 [PDF p.41]     exact source of errors between the simulated and measured signals. Therefore,


01212 [PDF p.41]     (updating) methods are required that account for multiple mismatch sources si-


01213 [PDF p.41]     multaneously. As already discussed, the scope of this thesis is limited to mis-


01214 [PDF p.41]     matches resulting from incorrect parameter values, incorrect or unmodeled dy-


01215 [PDF p.41]     namical effects, and missing states (and their governing equations), as illustrated


01216 [PDF p.41]     in Figures 1.4a-1.4c. Due to the potential complexity of (the combination of)


01217 [PDF p.41]     these mismatches, the use of versatile ML-based methods that train a (black-


01218 [PDF p.41]     box) model based on output response data measured on the physical system is


01219 [PDF p.41]     advised. As already mentioned, fully black-box models lack, however, (physi-


01220 [PDF p.41]     cal) interpretability which is regarded as an important property for digital twins.


01221 [PDF p.41]     Hence, physics-enhanced ML methods may be employed. In the current problem


01222 [PDF p.41]     setting (in which the correctness of the model structure is not guaranteed), we


01223 [PDF p.41]     can not assume a high-fidelity FP model to be available, ruling out physics-guided


01224 [PDF p.41]     ML. By starting from a decently accurate FP model, physics-encoded ML offers


01225 [PDF p.41]     a higher degree of interpretability compared to physics-informed ML, resulting in


01226 [PDF p.41]     a relatively ‘more white’ model as illustrated in Figure 1.3. Therefore, physics-


01227 [PDF p.41]     encoded ML is recognized as a promising approach to update the model structure


01228 [PDF p.41]     of existing FP models for application in a digital twin context. For example, in

01265 [PDF p.42] noted that the model class of the updated model will always remain (somewhat)


01266 [PDF p.42] restricted compared to a physical system. For example, the updated model can


01267 [PDF p.42] typically only take a limited number of states into account, e.g., for computational


01268 [PDF p.42] reasons, whereas a physical system has, in theory, an infinite number of states.


01269 [PDF p.42] Moreover, the approximative nature of ML-techniques, such as ANNs, employed


01270 [PDF p.42] as function approximators limits the fidelity of the updated model. Hence, the

01309 [PDF p.43]     1.4      General objective, contributions, and outline


01310 [PDF p.43]     Updating FP models based on measurement data is a crucial way to have an accu-


01311 [PDF p.43]     rate, up-to-date, and (physically) interpretable digital twin of a physical system.


01312 [PDF p.43]     Such digital twins are useful for a variety of applications, ranging from (design


01313 [PDF p.43]     and/or model-based control) performance enhancement to predictive maintenance.


01314 [PDF p.43]     Although much research has already been conducted on model updating, many


01315 [PDF p.43]     challenges remain to make these techniques applicable in the context of digital


01316 [PDF p.43]     twins. Some of these challenges, related to online parameter updating and updat-


01317 [PDF p.43]     ing model structures are addressed in this thesis. Based on these challenges, the


01318 [PDF p.43]     general objective addressed in this thesis is:

01321 [PDF p.44]

01324 [PDF p.44]    Develop model updating techniques for digital twins of (nonlinear) dynami-


01325 [PDF p.44]    cal systems that maintain physical interpretability of the original first prin-

01331 [PDF p.44] 1.4.1    Contributions to online model parameter updating


01332 [PDF p.44] As mentioned earlier, updating parameter values of models online, i.e., during


01333 [PDF p.44] operation of the system, ensures that the updated model, which may represent a


01334 [PDF p.44] digital twin of a physical system, is and remains an accurate representation of that


01335 [PDF p.44] system throughout the system’s operational life. In this section, the contributions


01336 [PDF p.44] of this thesis related to online model parameter updating will be introduced.


01337 [PDF p.44] 


01338 [PDF p.44] Online parameter value updating for nonlinear dynamical systems


01339 [PDF p.44] For FP models with incorrect or changing (over time) physically interpretable


01340 [PDF p.44] parameter values, it is crucial to develop (physics-guided ML) methodologies to


01341 [PDF p.44] accurately update these values online, e.g., with negligible computational cost.


01342 [PDF p.44] Here, the aim is to reduce the mismatch between the model and the physical


01343 [PDF p.44] system it represents. To cover a wide range of systems, such methodologies need


01344 [PDF p.44] to be (in theory) applicable to multi-physical nonlinear dynamical models. To


01345 [PDF p.44] capture the momentary condition of the physical system, so-called features need


01346 [PDF p.44] to be extracted from dynamical (output) responses that are measured on the


01347 [PDF p.44] physical system. To this end, physical knowledge of the system, such as known


01348 [PDF p.44] relevant frequency ranges, may be employed to enhance effectiveness. Additionally,


01349 [PDF p.44] selecting sets of relatively informative features from those extracted features can


01350 [PDF p.44] further improve the accuracy of the predicted parameter values [129], as well as


01351 [PDF p.44] improve the computational efficiency of the parameter updating method. The


01352 [PDF p.44] responses from which features are extracted may, however, be subject to change


01353 [PDF p.44] as a result of adjustments to system settings by the operator. To represent such


01354 [PDF p.44] variable system settings, so-called input parameters are used. Consequently, to


01355 [PDF p.44] ensure general applicability in an online context, parameter updating methods


01356 [PDF p.44] should allow for adjustable input parameters. The first contribution, related to


01357 [PDF p.44] Challenge I, addresses these topics and will primarily be covered in Chapter 2,


01358 [PDF p.44] with the extension on feature selection and the inclusion of input parameters in


01359 [PDF p.44] Chapters 3 and 4, respectively.

01373 [PDF p.45]     Uncertainty quantification


01374 [PDF p.45]     When parameter values of a model are updated online, it is beneficial for engineers


01375 [PDF p.45]     to have insight in how much they can trust the updated parameter values to make


01376 [PDF p.45]     optimal decisions. Therefore, model parameter updating methods should include a


01377 [PDF p.45]     quantification of the uncertainty in the updated parameter values. Extending the


01378 [PDF p.45]     ML-based parameter updating framework proposed in Contribution I, probabilistic


01379 [PDF p.45]     ML approaches may be used to estimate both parameter values and the uncertainty


01380 [PDF p.45]     in these parameter value estimates. Enabling UQ for the so-called Inverse Mapping


01381 [PDF p.45]     Parameter Updating (IMPU) method (as proposed in Contribution I), which is


01382 [PDF p.45]     related to Challenge II, is the second contribution of this thesis and will be covered


01383 [PDF p.45]     in Chapter 4.

01386 [PDF p.45]          based inverse mapping model to infer both parameter values and estimates


01387 [PDF p.45]          of the uncertainty in the inferred parameter values from measured features.

01391 [PDF p.45]     Application to real-world use cases


01392 [PDF p.45]     Model parameter updating is intended to update parameter values of models us-


01393 [PDF p.45]     ing measurement data obtained from real-world physical systems, such as high-


01394 [PDF p.45]     precision and medical systems. Benefits of online model parameter updating for


01395 [PDF p.45]     such system include: machine health monitoring for predictive maintenance, per-


01396 [PDF p.45]     formance enhancement through model-based control, and improved patient treat-


01397 [PDF p.45]     ment. Although models are updated based on measurement data that is obtained


01398 [PDF p.45]     using some user-chosen excitation of the system, the updated model must also


01399 [PDF p.45]     be generalizable to other excitations (or input signals) that may be encountered


01400 [PDF p.45]     during the system’s operational life. Furthermore, for real-world systems, we may


01401 [PDF p.45]     not assume that the mismatch between the FP model and the physical system is


01402 [PDF p.45]     solely caused by incorrect parameter values. The application of ML-based inverse


01403 [PDF p.45]     mapping models to update parameter values in two real-world use cases, as re-


01404 [PDF p.45]     lated to Challenge III, is the third contribution of this thesis and will be covered

01422 [PDF p.46] In practice, mismatches between a model and a physical system are not limited


01423 [PDF p.46] to parameter values. Therefore, besides updating model parameter values, the


01424 [PDF p.46] model structure, i.e., the model’s governing dynamical equations, may need to be


01425 [PDF p.46] updated as well. In this section, the contributions of this thesis related to model


01426 [PDF p.46] structure updating are listed.


01427 [PDF p.46] 


01428 [PDF p.46] Model structure updating methodology


01429 [PDF p.46] To alleviate various sources of mismatches between an FP model and a physical


01430 [PDF p.46] system, updating methods are required that simultaneously account for incorrect


01431 [PDF p.46] parameter values, incorrect or unmodeled dynamical effects, and unmodeled states


01432 [PDF p.46] and their governing equations. Using physics-encoded ML to achieve this goal,


01433 [PDF p.46] (physical) interpretability of the updated model is maintained. Specifically a rea-


01434 [PDF p.46] sonably accurate (white-box) FP model is retained and enhanced with (black-box)


01435 [PDF p.46] ML, resulting in a grey-box updated model. Such a grey-box model can be used


01436 [PDF p.46] for more accurate predictions for, e.g., monitoring, planning, and control purposes.


01437 [PDF p.46] As state-space models are a popular and interpretable representation of dynamical


01438 [PDF p.46] models, this thesis will focus on updating FP models of this form. In order to mit-


01439 [PDF p.46] igate the aforementioned mismatches, the existing state-space equations need to


01440 [PDF p.46] be augmented. Furthermore, the number of states needs to be extended to capture


01441 [PDF p.46] states that are related to dynamical modes/time scales which are missing in the


01442 [PDF p.46] FP model. A methodology that achieves the above, and is related to Challenge IV,


01443 [PDF p.46] is the fourth contribution of this thesis and will be discussed in Chapter 5.


01444 [PDF p.46] 


01445 [PDF p.46]    Contribution IV. A grey-box model structure updating technique that re-


01446 [PDF p.46]    tains and updates a first principles model by simultaneously extending and


01447 [PDF p.46]    augmenting its existing dynamic equations to minimize the error between


01448 [PDF p.46]    simulated and measured output responses.

01453 [PDF p.47] 1   Application to (real-world) use cases


01454 [PDF p.47]     As discussed, the combination of an FP model with ML techniques enhances the


01455 [PDF p.47]     predictive capacity of an interpretable FP model, and, at the same time, improves


01456 [PDF p.47]     the resulting model’s robustness compared to black-box models. This allows the


01457 [PDF p.47]     use of the updated model for high-fidelity prediction of the system’s behavior


01458 [PDF p.47]     and for performance enhancement through, e.g., model-based control. To vali-


01459 [PDF p.47]     date the enhanced and robust predictive capacity, the proposed (extension- and


01460 [PDF p.47]     augmentation-based) model structure updating method needs to be applied to


01461 [PDF p.47]     a (closed-loop) real-world system. Note that, although the model structure of


01462 [PDF p.47]     the updated model is an improvement over the FP model’s structure, the updated


01463 [PDF p.47]     model’s structure will not be able to exactly capture all dynamics of the real-world


01464 [PDF p.47]     system. The application of the proposed extension and augmentation-based model


01465 [PDF p.47]     structure updating methodology to an industrial use case, related to Challenge V,


01466 [PDF p.47]     is the fifth and final contribution of this thesis and will be covered in Chapter 5.


01467 [PDF p.47] 


01468 [PDF p.47]          Contribution V. Application of the grey-box (extension- and


01469 [PDF p.47]          augmentation-based) model structure updating method to a real-world


01470 [PDF p.47]          closed-loop back-end semiconductor production machine, showing high


01471 [PDF p.47]          predictive capacity and good extrapolation capabilities of the updated model,


01472 [PDF p.47]          and more robust applicability compared to a similar black-box approach,


01473 [PDF p.47]          allowing the updated model to be used for performance enhancement


01474 [PDF p.47]          through model-based control.

01479 [PDF p.47]     As previously outlined, the contributions of this thesis are organized in two parts:

01492 [PDF p.47]     the methodology is applied to a real-world medical mechanical ventilator, where

01530 [PDF p.52] Abstract - In the context of digital twins, it is essential that a model gives an accu-


01531 [PDF p.52] rate description of the (controlled) dynamical behavior of a physical system during the


01532 [PDF p.52] system’s entire operational life. Therefore, model updating techniques are required that


01533 [PDF p.52] enable real-time updating of physically interpretable parameter values and are applicable


01534 [PDF p.52] to a wide range of (nonlinear) dynamical systems. As traditional, iterative, parameter


01535 [PDF p.52] updating methods may be computationally too expensive for real-time updating, the In-


01536 [PDF p.52] verse Mapping Parameter Updating (IMPU) method is proposed as an alternative. For


01537 [PDF p.52] this method, first, an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is trained offline using features


01538 [PDF p.52] of simulated transient response data. Then, in the online phase, this ANN maps, with


01539 [PDF p.52] little computational cost, a set of measured output response features to parameter value


01540 [PDF p.52] estimates enabling real-time model updating. In this chapter, various types of transient


01541 [PDF p.52] response features are introduced to update parameter values of nonlinear dynamical sys-


01542 [PDF p.52] tems with increased computational efficiency and accuracy. To analyze the efficacy of


01543 [PDF p.52] these features, the IMPU method is applied to a (simulated) nonlinear multibody system.


01544 [PDF p.52] It is shown that a smart selection of features, based on, e.g., the frequency content of the
