01559 [PDF p.53]     2.1      Introduction


01560 [PDF p.53]     As part of the fourth industrial revolution, Digital Twins (DTs) hold the promise


01561 [PDF p.53]     of increasing the efficiency, and lowering costs and throughput times of, among


01562 [PDF p.53]     others, high-tech engineering systems and manufacturing processes [67], such as


01563 [PDF p.53]     wire bonder machines, lithography systems, or steel manufacturing plants. As


01564 [PDF p.53]     the name ‘digital twin’ suggests, this potential is achieved by having a digital


01565 [PDF p.53]     representation of a physical system.


01566 [PDF p.53]         Using this DT, the behavior of the ‘physical twin’ is predicted risk-free by


01567 [PDF p.53]     simulating and analyzing the digital copy of the system [65]. In the design pro-


01568 [PDF p.53]     cess of future generations of the system, this provides engineers with valuable


01569 [PDF p.53]     insight into the dynamics of the current system, enabling improved design of the


01570 [PDF p.53]     next generation. Additionally, measured behavior of the actual system can be


01571 [PDF p.53]     compared to behavior predicted by a DT of the healthy system for the benefit


01572 [PDF p.53]     of structural/machine health monitoring [60], enabling efficient maintenance man-


01573 [PDF p.53]     agement, minimizing maintenance cost, and leading to an increase of the lifetime of


01574 [PDF p.53]     the system. Furthermore, during the operation of a system, a DT is able to suggest


01575 [PDF p.53]     different operation modes or adapt mission planning if it senses that the current


01576 [PDF p.53]     state of the system is not suited for an originally planned operation mode or mis-


01577 [PDF p.53]     sion [94]. This application can also be extended to using a dedicated DT for each


01578 [PDF p.53]     machine in a fleet of akin machines, based on its most recent measured condition,


01579 [PDF p.53]     to account for machine-to-machine variations originating from, e.g., manufacturing


01580 [PDF p.53]     tolerances. The availability of such dedicated DTs allows to adapt model-based


01581 [PDF p.53]     (feedforward) controllers to enhance the performance of each individual machine.


01582 [PDF p.53]         Coined in 2014 by Grieves [64], the concept of digital twins is relatively novel


01583 [PDF p.53]     and still faces multiple broad challenges, such as managing heterogeneous models


01584 [PDF p.53]     across varying disciplines and combining models and big-data for, among others,


01585 [PDF p.53]     fault-detection and performance optimization [21]. In this chapter, these chal-


01586 [PDF p.53]     lenges are regarded as out of scope, however, and the assumption is made that


01587 [PDF p.53]     a DT is given by a parametric (dynamical) model, derived using either: 1) ana-


01588 [PDF p.53]     lytical approaches based on First Principles (FP) such as Lagrange’s equations of


01589 [PDF p.53]     motion or Hamilton’s principle, 2) (multiphysical) modeling and analysis software


01590 [PDF p.53]     packages, such as finite element or multibody dynamics packages, and 3) software


01591 [PDF p.53]     tools that combine techniques from multiple engineering disciplines, e.g., dynamic


01592 [PDF p.53]     modeling and motion control, such as the Matlab-based Simulink or Simscape


01593 [PDF p.53] 


01594 [PDF p.54] 2.1. Introduction                                                                   27


01595 [PDF p.54] 


01596 [PDF p.54] 


01597 [PDF p.54] packages. Note that, although these three modeling approaches are all based on


01598 [PDF p.54] FPs, only the first approach provides direct access to the closed-form dynamical


01599 [PDF p.54] equations for the user. Models from the second and third approach are therefore


01600 [PDF p.54] also referred to as simulation models, where it is noted that, also for these ap-         2


01601 [PDF p.54] proaches, the user has access to the parameter values. Another challenge that is


01602 [PDF p.54] faced by digital twins is related to the ever-present mismatch between measure-


01603 [PDF p.54] ments of a physical system and the corresponding predictions of its DT. For the


01604 [PDF p.54] DT to reach its full potential, this mismatch should be minimal throughout the


01605 [PDF p.54] system’s operational life [67, 94, 224]. This challenge of giving DTs life-long learn-


01606 [PDF p.54] ing capabilities is referred to as autonomous model updating and is considered in


01607 [PDF p.54] this chapter.


01608 [PDF p.54]     In Mottershead et al. [151, 152], the mismatch between the measurement and


01609 [PDF p.54] the model predictions is contributed to three distinct model error sources; incorrect


01610 [PDF p.54] model structure, i.e., incorrectly or unmodeled dynamical effects and unmodeled


01611 [PDF p.54] states [100, 216], discretization errors [42], and/or errors due to incorrect parameter


01612 [PDF p.54] values. This chapter focuses on model parameter updating as to minimize the last


01613 [PDF p.54] error source. Consequently, model structure and discretization errors are assumed


01614 [PDF p.54] negligible. Furthermore, in this work, measurement/experimental errors caused


01615 [PDF p.54] by, e.g., sensing or calibration errors, are assumed to be corrected, negligible, or at


01616 [PDF p.54] least much smaller than the modeling errors, which is the case in many practical


01617 [PDF p.54] situations.


01618 [PDF p.54]     Given the intended application in a general digital twin context, key require-


01619 [PDF p.54] ments for an autonomous model updating procedure are defined as follows: 1)


01620 [PDF p.54] although control optimization and structural/machine health monitoring are not


01621 [PDF p.54] considered in this thesis, the aim is to develop a model updating methodology ap-


01622 [PDF p.54] plicable in the context of model-based control and/or health monitoring; therefore,


01623 [PDF p.54] updating should be performed in real-time, 2) updated parameter values should


01624 [PDF p.54] be physically interpretable to enable insightful health monitoring, 3) the updating


01625 [PDF p.54] method should be applicable to (complex) nonlinear dynamical models, and 4)


01626 [PDF p.54] the updating method should be suitable for parametric models (not necessarily of


01627 [PDF p.54] dynamical systems) derived using FPs, finite element/multibody software, or mul-


01628 [PDF p.54] tidisciplinary software tools. The presentation of an autonomous model updating


01629 [PDF p.54] method simultaneously fulfilling these four requirements, is the main contribution


01630 [PDF p.54] of the current chapter. The corresponding technical contributions will be discussed


01631 [PDF p.54] in more detail later in this section.


01632 [PDF p.54]     Approaches for model parameter updating found in literature are divided in


01633 [PDF p.54] four types. The first type concerns updating methods originating from the field of


01634 [PDF p.54] structural dynamics, see, e.g., [152, 188] for an overview. Although some excep-


01635 [PDF p.54] tions exist, see [72, 73, 128, 214], these updating methods are typically limited to


01636 [PDF p.54] linear(ized) systems [9, 151]. Furthermore, these methods are based on expensive


01637 [PDF p.54] iterative sensitivity methods [6, 50, 56, 109, 128, 133, 149, 214, 220] or physically


01638 [PDF p.54] 


01639 [PDF p.55]     28        Chapter 2. Model parameter updating using inverse mapping models


01640 [PDF p.55] 


01641 [PDF p.55] 


01642 [PDF p.55]     non-interpretable direct methods [16, 37, 56, 193]. Consequently, these techniques


01643 [PDF p.55]     do not meet all four requirements for model updating for DTs as mentioned above,


01644 [PDF p.55]     and are thus not regarded as a viable solution to the problem considered here.


01645 [PDF p.55] 2       Alternatively, system identification techniques are used to find a model that


01646 [PDF p.55]     describes measured data. For an overview of system identification techniques see,


01647 [PDF p.55]     for example, [8, 134, 165]. Note that, in contrast to model updating in the field


01648 [PDF p.55]     of, typically linear(ized), structural dynamics, system identification methods have


01649 [PDF p.55]     also been developed for nonlinear systems [103, 187]. However, due to the fact that


01650 [PDF p.55]     in system identification generic model structures are fitted to data, the identified


01651 [PDF p.55]     models are difficult to interpret from a physical perspective [15], and thus do not


01652 [PDF p.55]     satisfy all of the above requirements.


01653 [PDF p.55]         A third type of parameter updating techniques concerns filter-based methods


01654 [PDF p.55]     (also referred to as observer-based methods). Examples are the vanilla [222], ex-


01655 [PDF p.55]     tended [24, 132], and unscented Kalman filter [41, 88, 210], Gaussian filters [2, 111],


01656 [PDF p.55]     and particle filters [5]. Although these approaches are often used for DTs, for com-


01657 [PDF p.55]     plex systems, i.e., systems with many states and/or parameters, filter methods


01658 [PDF p.55]     might suffer from relatively high (online) computational costs, prohibiting online


01659 [PDF p.55]     updating (especially if the required sampling frequency is relatively high) [5]. Fur-


01660 [PDF p.55]     thermore, filter-based methods require an initial guess for the parameter estimates.


01661 [PDF p.55]     If this information is not available or sudden changes to the parameter values oc-


01662 [PDF p.55]     cur, filter methods might end up in local minima. To avoid this, initial parameter


01663 [PDF p.55]     values may be estimated using a coarse global parameter estimation method [41]


01664 [PDF p.55]     at a significant cost of computation time. Finally, filter-based updating methods


01665 [PDF p.55]     typically require direct accessibility of the closed-form dynamical equations of the


01666 [PDF p.55]     model. Consequently, filter-based methods can not be directly applied to simula-


01667 [PDF p.55]     tion models (as obtained from, e.g., finite element/multibody software packages,


01668 [PDF p.55]     or Matlab-based packages such as Simulink or Simscape), that may be used to


01669 [PDF p.55]     constitute a digital twin.


01670 [PDF p.55]         The fourth approach to model updating employs Machine Learning (ML). Here,


01671 [PDF p.55]     again, we can distinguish between, firstly, identification, i.e., identifying a system


01672 [PDF p.55]     without using an FP reference model, and, secondly, updating (parameters of) a


01673 [PDF p.55]     predefined reference model. An example of the former is the work of Li on identify-


01674 [PDF p.55]     ing nonlinear normal modes using physics-integrated deep learning [127]. An other


01675 [PDF p.55]     example of ML-based identification is the work by Karniadakis et al. [139, 176, 233]


01676 [PDF p.55]     on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) that is also adopted by other re-


01677 [PDF p.55]     searchers [226]. In this method, a neural network is trained to approximate the


01678 [PDF p.55]     solution to (partial) differential equations governing a physical system by incor-


01679 [PDF p.55]     porating physical laws, expressed as differential equations, into its loss function.


01680 [PDF p.55]     Consequently, PINNs can learn solutions that satisfy these physical laws equations


01681 [PDF p.55]     while fitting the given data. The trained neural network itself does, however, not


01682 [PDF p.55]     provide physical insight. Additionally, training the neural network can take signifi-

01685 [PDF p.56] 


01686 [PDF p.56] 


01687 [PDF p.56] cant computation time and hence impede real-time updating. This holds especially


01688 [PDF p.56] for models consisting of a large number of states and/or parameters. An other


01689 [PDF p.56] ML-based identification methodology is the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dy-


01690 [PDF p.56] namics (SINDy) algorithm developed by Brunton et al. [34, 39, 90, 173, 201]. This      2


01691 [PDF p.56] method finds (a sparse set of) coefficients of differential equations, which may not


01692 [PDF p.56] correspond to physical quantities, again hindering physical interpretation. Note


01693 [PDF p.56] that this argument holds for most system identification methods (based on ML


01694 [PDF p.56] or not). An ML-based method more closely related to (physically interpretable)


01695 [PDF p.56] model updating is found in the work of Willcox et al. [91–93, 123, 196]. Here, a


01696 [PDF p.56] model is selected from a predefined library of models, representing systems with


01697 [PDF p.56] various fault types, using an optimal decision tree. Due to a prerequisite library


01698 [PDF p.56] of models, the ‘updated’ model is, however, limited to a discrete set of models


01699 [PDF p.56] that are manually defined by the user, and consequently is of limited accuracy.


01700 [PDF p.56] Other methodologies, based on AI, aim at finding, online, the (global) parameter


01701 [PDF p.56] values corresponding to a measured signal (in a continuous domain) using, for ex-


01702 [PDF p.56] ample, iterative genetic algorithms [174, 217, 238] and particle swarm algorithms


01703 [PDF p.56] [63, 174]. In this case, however, the (genetic) search over the parameter space


01704 [PDF p.56] takes considerable computational effort, rendering real-time updating impossible


01705 [PDF p.56] [41].


01706 [PDF p.56]     As an alternative, the inverse problem of estimating physically interpretable


01707 [PDF p.56] parameter values in a continuous domain using measurement data can be solved


01708 [PDF p.56] using an Inverse Mapping Model (IMM). Here, the IMM directly maps, with neg-


01709 [PDF p.56] ligible computational cost, a set of measured features, describing the (dynamical)


01710 [PDF p.56] behavior of a system, to a set of corresponding physically-interpretable parameter


01711 [PDF p.56] values of the reference model. In literature, (trained) Artificial Neural Networks


01712 [PDF p.56] (ANNs) have been found suitable to constitute these IMMs due to their generic


01713 [PDF p.56] function approximation characteristics [9, 125, 147, 159, 229]. Consequently, this


01714 [PDF p.56] methodology was coined the neural network updating method by Atalla [9]. Note


01715 [PDF p.56] that, since other generic function approximation algorithms may also be used to


01716 [PDF p.56] constitute IMMs, this methodology is referred to as the Inverse Mapping Param-


01717 [PDF p.56] eter Updating (IMPU) method in this thesis. For example, in other work of the


01718 [PDF p.56] author, Gaussian processes are used as IMMs [107]. The main qualitative ad-


01719 [PDF p.56] vantage of this method with respect to previously discussed parameter updating


01720 [PDF p.56] methods is that online parameter updating is enabled even for large-scale systems


01721 [PDF p.56] with high sampling frequencies. This is achieved by shifting a significant major-


01722 [PDF p.56] ity of the computation time to an offline (training) phase, whereas the required


01723 [PDF p.56] online (inference) computations are extremely efficient and scale marginally with


01724 [PDF p.56] the complexity of the system or model. Although this IMPU methodology thus


01725 [PDF p.56] satisfies requirements 1 (real-time updating), 2 (physically interpretable updat-


01726 [PDF p.56] ing), and 4 (suitable for parametric models derived using various methods), it has,


01727 [PDF p.56] however, only been applied to linear(ized) dynamical systems.

01732 [PDF p.57]          Therefore, the three main contributions of this work are:


01733 [PDF p.57]          1. extension of the IMPU method towards nonlinear dynamical systems. Hereto,


01734 [PDF p.57]             the use of transient-based output signal features is proposed to update non-


01735 [PDF p.57] 2           linear dynamical systems online by inferring (physically interpretable) pa-


01736 [PDF p.57]             rameter values using IMMs with little (online) computational cost. Here,


01737 [PDF p.57]             multiple types of transient-based features are introduced that use engineer-


01738 [PDF p.57]             ing knowledge to increase accuracy and computational efficiency of the IMPU


01739 [PDF p.57]             methodology,


01740 [PDF p.57]          2. an application and evaluation of the introduced methodology and feature


01741 [PDF p.57]             types to two simulated nonlinear multibody systems,


01742 [PDF p.57]          3. an extensive evaluation of the generalization capabilities of the introduced


01743 [PDF p.57]             feature types by varying the number of training samples and using incomplete


01744 [PDF p.57]             training data.


01745 [PDF p.57]         The outline of this chapter is as follows. In Section 2.2, a formal definition


01746 [PDF p.57]     of the model parameter updating problem is given. Moreover, the employment


01747 [PDF p.57]     of transient-based output features to update, online, interpretable parameter val-


01748 [PDF p.57]     ues of nonlinear models with low computational costs is proposed. Subsequently,


01749 [PDF p.57]     in Section 2.3, different transient-based output features are introduced. In Sec-


01750 [PDF p.57]     tion 2.4, the introduced technique is applied on a (simulated) rigid double beam


01751 [PDF p.57]     model and results are analyzed. Additionally, this section analyzes the gener-


01752 [PDF p.57]     alization capabilities of the aforementioned transient-based features. Then, in


01753 [PDF p.57]     Section 2.5, the IMPU method is applied on a roll plane model, and a brief (quan-


01754 [PDF p.57]     titative) comparison is made with the application of an extended Kalman filter to


01755 [PDF p.57]     update parameter values. Finally, conclusions are discussed and recommendations


01756 [PDF p.57]     for future work are given in Section 2.6.

01759 [PDF p.57]     2.2       Model updating using inverse mapping models


01760 [PDF p.57]     2.2.1      Problem definition


01761 [PDF p.57]     It is assumed that a DT of a dynamical system is available in the form of a


01762 [PDF p.57]     (nonlinear) reference model of which the dynamics may be given in first-order

01861 [PDF p.59]     To solve the minimization problem in (2.5) with low computational effort, inverse


01862 [PDF p.59]     mapping models are employed, as proposed in [125]. In contrast to forward models,

01868 [PDF p.60] output features and its output is the set of corresponding inferred (or estimated)


01869 [PDF p.60] parameter values θ̂. Mathematically, the IMM is represented by the function


01870 [PDF p.60] I : Rnψ → Rnup :                                                                                   2


01871 [PDF p.60]

01875 [PDF p.60] the approximate nature of the IMM. To constitute the function I, a feedforward


01876 [PDF p.60] Artificial Neural Network (abbreviated as ANN and also known as the multilayer


01877 [PDF p.60] perceptron) is trained in an offline phase. These ANNs are renowned for their


01878 [PDF p.60] universal function approximation capabilities [23]. Moreover, in the online phase,


01879 [PDF p.60] inferring parameter values using ANNs is computationally efficient, as is also dis-


01880 [PDF p.60] cussed in [238], where ANNs are used as surrogates for forward FP models. Note


01881 [PDF p.60] that, in contrast to parameter updating methods such as PINNs or filter-based


01882 [PDF p.60] techniques (see Section 2.1), known physics are not explicitly used in the ANN.


01883 [PDF p.60] However, since training data is generated using the FP model, the physics-based


01884 [PDF p.60] relations that govern this model are implicitly incorporated in and learned by the


01885 [PDF p.60] ANN.


01886 [PDF p.60] Remark 2.2 In the case that the model structure is incorrect, the IMM method will


01887 [PDF p.60] try to find suitable parameter values such that the measured features are mimicked as


01888 [PDF p.60] closely as possible using the model parameterized with the updated parameter values,


01889 [PDF p.60] i.e., the updated model. Note that in this case, the identified parameter values do not


01890 [PDF p.60] fully represent their physical counterparts as intended in the reference model, and should,


01891 [PDF p.60] therefore, be handled with care for, e.g., health monitoring.

01895 [PDF p.60] tions 2.2.2.2 and 2.2.2.3, respectively.

02037 [PDF p.64]     Having generated the normalized training data, the weights of the ANN with


02038 [PDF p.64] a user-defined structure, i.e., hyperparameters such as activation functions and


02039 [PDF p.64] number of layers and neurons, are tuned. First, the associated weights are ini-


02040 [PDF p.64] tialized with random values. Subsequently, during the iterative application of ne        2


02041 [PDF p.64] epochs these weights are tuned, where in one epoch all training data is used once.


02042 [PDF p.64] At the start of each epoch, all training data is randomly divided over nb batches


02043 [PDF p.64] (subsets of training data containing multiple training samples). Then, for each


02044 [PDF p.64] sample s in a batch, the following sequence of steps is performed:


02045 [PDF p.64]   1. The ANN (parameterized using the momentary values for the weights) is


02046 [PDF p.64]      used to estimate the parameter values given the features of sample s, i.e.,


02047 [PDF p.64]      Ĭk ψ(θ s )), where the breve indicates that the ANN weights are still being


02048 [PDF p.64]      tuned.


02049 [PDF p.64] 


02050 [PDF p.64]   2. The cost function value is calculated using θ s and its momentary estimate


02051 [PDF p.64]      Ĭk ψ(θ s )). In this chapter, the squared error is used as the cost function:


02052 [PDF p.64] 


02053 [PDF p.64]               ϵ = (Ĭ ψ(θ s ) − θs )⊤ (Ĭ ψ(θ s ) − θs ).                       (2.9)


02054 [PDF p.64]                                                 


02055 [PDF p.64] 


02056 [PDF p.64]       Note that, in contrast to (2.5), (2.9) minimizes the difference between the


02057 [PDF p.64]       estimated and known training parameter values instead of features, due to


02058 [PDF p.64]       the inverse nature of the mapping.


02059 [PDF p.64] 


02060 [PDF p.64]   3. Using backpropagation, the gradients of ϵ with respect to all weights are


02061 [PDF p.64]      calculated.


02062 [PDF p.64] Using the gradients obtained in step 3 for all samples in the batch, ANN weights


02063 [PDF p.64] are updated such that the mean squared error in the parameter values over all


02064 [PDF p.64] samples in the batch is minimized. After this update, steps 1-3 are repeated for


02065 [PDF p.64] a new batch, until all batches have been processed. Then, the validation data is


02066 [PDF p.64] used to calculate the validation loss (mean squared error) in the parameter values.


02067 [PDF p.64] Here, the validation data is obtained in an equivalent manner as the training data


02068 [PDF p.64] (with distinctively sampled parameter values), see Figure 2.2, and used to evaluate


02069 [PDF p.64] the performance of the ANN without being biased towards the training data. If


02070 [PDF p.64] the validation loss has not decreased for nes consecutive epochs or all ne epochs


02071 [PDF p.64] have been processed, training is stopped and the ANN with the lowest validation


02072 [PDF p.64] loss is saved, otherwise a new epoch is started. This is referred to as patience-based


02073 [PDF p.64] early stopping and is employed to prevent overfitting [168]. For more information


02074 [PDF p.64] about backpropagation and ANN training in general, the reader is referred to [23].

02077 [PDF p.64] After having trained the ANN offline with simulated data, leading to the trained


02078 [PDF p.64] inverse mapping in (2.7), in the online phase, this trained ANN is used to infer

02081 [PDF p.65] 


02082 [PDF p.65] 


02083 [PDF p.65]     parameter values θ̂ from measured data using (2.7), where the hat ( ˆ· ) indicates


02084 [PDF p.65]     that these are inferred parameter values. As shown in Figure 2.3, this is achieved


02085 [PDF p.65]     by feeding normalized output features ψ̃  ¯ to the ANN see (2.7). Here, ψ̃ ¯ is ob-


02086 [PDF p.65] 2   tained by normalizing (similar to normalization of the training data) features that


02087 [PDF p.65]     are extracted from a measurement of a true/physical system, see Appendix A.1.


02088 [PDF p.65]     Recall that an overbar ( ¯· ) is used to indicate that these features relate to the


02089 [PDF p.65]     true/physical system. Since the ANN has been trained using normalized features


02090 [PDF p.65]     and parameter values to increase robustness, in the online phase, again normalized


02091 [PDF p.65]     features and parameter values are utilized. To maintain consistency, normaliza-


02092 [PDF p.65]     tion in the online phase is performed using bounds ψ min and ψ max as obtained


02093 [PDF p.65]     during training, see Appendix A.1. The inferred (or updated) normalized param-


02094 [PDF p.65]     eter values are then denormalized and substituted in the parameterized reference


02095 [PDF p.65]     model (2.1) resulting in the updated model such that the DT better mimics the


02096 [PDF p.65]     true system. Furthermore, although the model that constitutes a DT should in


02097 [PDF p.65]     general be computationally efficient, e.g., for control purposes, the IMPU method


02098 [PDF p.65]     does not require online evaluation of the parameterized model (2.1), since in the


02099 [PDF p.65]     online phase only measurements are used and the ANN is evaluated for the mea-


02100 [PDF p.65]     sured features to generate a parameter estimate. Defining parametric models with


02101 [PDF p.65]     low online model evaluation time, i.e., real-time simulation, which can be achieved


02102 [PDF p.65]     using, e.g., parametric model order reduction techniques is therefore regarded as


02103 [PDF p.65]     out of scope for this chapter.


02104 [PDF p.65]         Due to the use of transient data to accommodate for nonlinear systems, in


02105 [PDF p.65]     contrast to (modal) characteristics of linear systems as previously used in [125,


02106 [PDF p.65]     147, 159], the measured experiment in the online phase should be identical to


02107 [PDF p.65]     the experiments simulated in the offline phase. Therefore, the initial conditions


02108 [PDF p.65]     and excitation signals used in both phases are required to be equal and known in


02109 [PDF p.65]     advance. Consequently, this updating method is only suited for applications with


02110 [PDF p.65]     known forcing as is the case in, e.g., high-performance motion stage systems with


02111 [PDF p.65]     known reference trajectory inputs.


02112 [PDF p.65]     Remark 2.4 In a practical setting, a homing procedure should be used to achieve the


02113 [PDF p.65]     desired initial conditions. In applications where, during operation of the physical system,


02114 [PDF p.65]     a certain action needs to be performed repetitively, the corresponding initial conditions


02115 [PDF p.65]     and excitation signals can be used to constitute the aforementioned experiment, enabling


02116 [PDF p.65]     on-the-fly parameter updating.

02161 [PDF p.67] 


02162 [PDF p.67]     obtained from a simulated (for a model parameterized with θ) or measured exper-


02163 [PDF p.67]     iment. In other words, different definitions for function L in (2.4) are introduced.


02164 [PDF p.67]     Here, the aim is to define highly informative features, i.e., features that are sensi-


02165 [PDF p.67] 2   tive to variations in output signals resulting from variations in updating parameter


02166 [PDF p.67]     values. We aim to do so by exploiting engineering knowledge such that the ac-


02167 [PDF p.67]     curacy and the computational efficiency of the IMPU method are improved. For


02168 [PDF p.67]     the remainder of this section, the notation for the offline simulated training data


02169 [PDF p.67]     (without overbar) will be used. The discussed feature extraction methodologies


02170 [PDF p.67]     are applied identically for the validation/test and online measured data.


02171 [PDF p.67]         The introduced feature types are divided in time- and frequency-domain fea-


02172 [PDF p.67]     tures, which will be discussed in Sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2, respectively.


02173 [PDF p.67] 


02174 [PDF p.67]     2.3.1    Time-domain features


02175 [PDF p.67]     Here, feature types are introduced that directly use the sampled transient data y.


02176 [PDF p.67]     In Figures 2.2 and 2.3, these feature types are indicated in the two left ’extract


02177 [PDF p.67]     features’ blocks in the feature extraction part (marked in yellow).


02178 [PDF p.67] 


02179 [PDF p.67]     Time sample


02180 [PDF p.67]     Time Sample (TS) features simply refer to the case in which a selection of nTS


02181 [PDF p.67]     entries of the sampled output signal are used as features:


02182 [PDF p.67] 


02183 [PDF p.67]             ψ TS = y[v TS ],                                                       (2.10)


02184 [PDF p.67] 


02185 [PDF p.67]     with v TS ∈ NnTS denoting a vector containing the indices of the selected entries in


02186 [PDF p.67]     y. In this work, v TS is chosen such that the feature vector consists of time samples


02187 [PDF p.67]     measured at equidistant moments in time. Note that, as the initial conditions are


02188 [PDF p.67]     identical for all simulations and experiments, the measurements at initial time


02189 [PDF p.67]     t = 0 should not be included in the feature vector. Using TS features, the ANN is


02190 [PDF p.67]     provided with the raw time series data as directly obtained from the measurements.


02191 [PDF p.67]     Therefore, without exploiting engineering knowledge, the ANN has to implicitly


02192 [PDF p.67]     extract ‘hidden features of the underlying system’ from the time series data in its


02193 [PDF p.67]     hidden layer(s). In contrast, feature extraction methods that exploit engineering


02194 [PDF p.67]     knowledge to aid the ANN by directly providing more informative data about the


02195 [PDF p.67]     system will be introduced later. Specifically, the goal is to extract (smaller) sets


02196 [PDF p.67]     of features that have higher information density, thereby improving accuracy and


02197 [PDF p.67]     computational efficiency of the offline training of the ANN and the online inference


02198 [PDF p.67]     of parameter estimates using the ANN.


02199 [PDF p.67] 


02200 [PDF p.68] 2.3. Definition of transient-based output features                                   41


02201 [PDF p.68] 


02202 [PDF p.68] 


02203 [PDF p.68] Time extremum


02204 [PDF p.68] For Time Extremum (TE) features, the magnitude at and temporal location of a


02205 [PDF p.68] selection of nTE local extrema in the time-domain signal are used:


02206 [PDF p.68]                                                                                            2


02207 [PDF p.68]                                     ⊤


02208 [PDF p.68]         ψ TE = y[v TE ]⊤ , t[v TE ]⊤ .                                           (2.11)


02209 [PDF p.68]               


02210 [PDF p.68] 


02211 [PDF p.68] 


02212 [PDF p.68] Here, t = [t1 , . . . , tN ] consists of all time instances at which the measured signal


02213 [PDF p.68] is sampled, and v TE ∈ NnTE contains the (ascending) indices of the first nTE ex-


02214 [PDF p.68] trema that are identified using some extrema-finding algorithm. Note here that


02215 [PDF p.68] local extrema, i.e., local minima and local maxima, are defined as the local max-


02216 [PDF p.68] ima/minima near the peaks and/or troughs of the signals, such that, despite the


02217 [PDF p.68] influence of noise, only one extremum is found per peak/trough. In practice, this


02218 [PDF p.68] can be achieved by using various options of the findpeaks algorithm in Matlab such


02219 [PDF p.68] as the minimum peak prominence (a user-specified minimum change in signal value


02220 [PDF p.68] required on either side of the peak/trough before the signal attains a value beyond


02221 [PDF p.68] the peak/trough itself [141]). As, the measured signals may not have the same


02222 [PDF p.68] number of extrema for different (training) samples obtained for distinct sets of


02223 [PDF p.68] parameter values, nTE should be equal to or smaller than the lowest number of


02224 [PDF p.68] extrema encountered in the output signal across all training samples.


02225 [PDF p.68]     An advantage of TE features is that, especially if the transient signal is similar


02226 [PDF p.68] to a free response, the height and temporal location of extrema in the transient


02227 [PDF p.68] signal are related to dynamic characteristics such as amplitude decay of eigen-


02228 [PDF p.68] modes and eigenfrequencies, respectively. For example, the heights of consecutive


02229 [PDF p.68] peaks in an impulse response (which decrease in magnitude) are indicative about


02230 [PDF p.68] the amount of damping in a system. Consequently, only few of these features can


02231 [PDF p.68] already contain a lot of information about the transient response that is closely


02232 [PDF p.68] related to physical parameters such as mass, damping, and stiffness parameters.


02233 [PDF p.68] Therefore, compared to, e.g., TS features, the ANN only needs to learn a rela-


02234 [PDF p.68] tively simple IMM, potentially boosting its accuracy and simultaneously lowering


02235 [PDF p.68] training and inference times due to the smaller set of features. A disadvantage,


02236 [PDF p.68] however, is that the temporal location of an extremum is relatively sensitive to


02237 [PDF p.68] noise, potentially causing the true location of the extremum to be identified at one


02238 [PDF p.68] of the neighboring entries in t. Due to the discrete nature of t, this may cause


02239 [PDF p.68] relatively large variations in the resulting feature values.


02240 [PDF p.68] 


02241 [PDF p.68] 2.3.2     Frequency-domain features


02242 [PDF p.68] Alternatively, features can be extracted from frequency-domain data Y ∈ CN/2+1 ,


02243 [PDF p.68] where N is an even integer such that we obtain N/2 − 1 complex numbers and


02244 [PDF p.68] 2 real numbers (for f = 0 and half of the Nyquist frequency). For this, as is


02245 [PDF p.68] indicated in Figures 2.2 and 2.3, first, the measured/simulated time-domain data


02246 [PDF p.68] 


02247 [PDF p.69]     42        Chapter 2. Model parameter updating using inverse mapping models


02248 [PDF p.69] 


02249 [PDF p.69] 


02250 [PDF p.69]     y is transformed to the frequency domain:


02251 [PDF p.69] 


02252 [PDF p.69]             Y = F(y),                                                               (2.12)


02253 [PDF p.69] 2


02254 [PDF p.69]     where F represents the discrete Fourier transform. In practice, usually the Fast


02255 [PDF p.69]     Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm is used for computational efficiency.


02256 [PDF p.69]         Since the discrete frequency-domain data is represented in a set of complex


02257 [PDF p.69]     numbers, there are two options to pass this Fourier Transform (FT) data to the


02258 [PDF p.69]     ANN (which requires real valued data): 1) using the Magnitude and Phase infor-


02259 [PDF p.69]     mation (MP); see (2.13), or 2) using the Real and Imaginary components of the


02260 [PDF p.69]     frequency-domain data (RI); see (2.14):


02261 [PDF p.69]                    h                          i⊤


02262 [PDF p.69]                              ⊤              ⊤


02263 [PDF p.69]             ψ MP = |Y[v FT ]| , ∠ (Y[v FT ])     ,                                  (2.13)


02264 [PDF p.69]                    h                             i⊤


02265 [PDF p.69]                                 ⊤              ⊤


02266 [PDF p.69]              ψ RI = ℜ (Y[v FT ]) , ℑ (Y[v FT ])     ,                               (2.14)


02267 [PDF p.69] 


02268 [PDF p.69]     where | · |, ∠( · ), ℜ( · ), and ℑ( · ), represent the magnitude, phase, real part, and


02269 [PDF p.69]     imaginary part of a complex number, respectively. Since the phase and imaginary


02270 [PDF p.69]     part at f1 = 0 and at the folding frequency (half of the sample frequency) of real


02271 [PDF p.69]     valued time signals are always zero, these numbers do not convey any information


02272 [PDF p.69]     and are therefore excluded from the feature vector.


02273 [PDF p.69]         Although the discrete frequency-domain signal contains, by definition, exactly


02274 [PDF p.69]     the same information as the discrete time-domain signal, the relevant information


02275 [PDF p.69]     may be more condensed in the frequency-domain signal. For example, frequencies


02276 [PDF p.69]     at which the measured signal has only small magnitudes, are likely less informative


02277 [PDF p.69]     about the system’s dynamics and response than frequencies with high magnitudes.


02278 [PDF p.69]     Indices of the frequency bins that are deemed informative, e.g., located near eigen-


02279 [PDF p.69]     frequencies of the linearized system or as encountered in exploratory experiments,


02280 [PDF p.69]     are therefore collected in the index set v FT ∈ NnFT . Only using the features


02281 [PDF p.69]     belonging to these more relevant frequencies bins, which are referred to as the Fre-


02282 [PDF p.69]     quency Bins of Interest (FBoIs), leads to a more compact set of features, raising


02283 [PDF p.69]     potential for improved performance of the ANN. For example, at bins correspond-


02284 [PDF p.69]     ing to high frequencies, the signals may be dominated by noise. Excluding these


02285 [PDF p.69]     bins from v FT , can improve the quality of the inverse mapping learned by the


02286 [PDF p.69]     ANN. In this chapter, FT-based features that are limited to the information in


02287 [PDF p.69]     some FBoIs are indicated by the suffix (FBoI).

02326 [PDF p.70] about its Center of Mass (CoM). The position of beam 1 is indicated by y1 (t) [m]

02330 [PDF p.70] (lCoM,1 sin(y2 ) + lCoM,2 cos(y2 )) e2 , where e1 and e2 represent unit vectors of a


02331 [PDF p.70] (global) fixed reference frame as indicated in Figure 2.4.

02335 [PDF p.70] with gravitational acceleration constant g. For reference, the Equations of Motion

02485 [PDF p.74] 2.4.1.2    Output features for exploratory simulations


02486 [PDF p.74] In this section, exploratory simulation results are shown for the five updating pa-


02487 [PDF p.74] rameter cases defined in Table 2.3. These simulations are performed according to


02488 [PDF p.74]                                                                                        2


02489 [PDF p.74] the simulated experiment design (excitation signals and initial conditions) intro-


02490 [PDF p.74] duced in Section 2.4.1.1. Furthermore, features are extracted conform the theory


02491 [PDF p.74] in Section 2.3, and plotted for additional insight.


02492 [PDF p.74]     Some settings to extract the features are as follows. For the time sample


02493 [PDF p.74] features, two variants are used: 1) dense with nψ = N = 256, and 2) sparse with


02494 [PDF p.74] nψ = 34. For the time extremum features, the minimum peak prominence mpp(y)


02495 [PDF p.74] is used for output signal y (as used in the timepeaks Matlab function [141]) and


02496 [PDF p.74] is defined as


02497 [PDF p.74]           mpp(y) = 0.15 (max(y) − min(y)) ,                                  (2.16)


02498 [PDF p.74] where y denotes a sampled output signal. As a result, a peak is only defined if the


02499 [PDF p.74] value of y between that peak and the closest peak with a higher magnitude drops


02500 [PDF p.74] by a minimal amount of mpp [141]. Note that the definition of mpp(y) should be


02501 [PDF p.74] tailored towards the encountered responses using engineering insight. Due to the


02502 [PDF p.74] different dominating frequencies of both output signals, the number of peaks in


02503 [PDF p.74] output signals y1 (t) and y2 (t) are nTE,1 = 1 and nTE,2 = 5, respectively. Further-


02504 [PDF p.74] more, the FBoIs are defined as the frequency bins within the frequency interval


02505 [PDF p.74] from 0 Hz to 4 Hz, such that the (damped) eigenfrequencies of the linearized


02506 [PDF p.74] models, as given in Table 2.3, lie within this range.


02507 [PDF p.74]     In Figures 2.5 and 2.6, time-domain responses, here referred to as TS (dense)


02508 [PDF p.74] features, are shown for the various parameter cases. In addition, TS (sparse)


02509 [PDF p.74] and TE features are indicated by color-coded squares in Figures 2.5 and 2.6,


02510 [PDF p.74] respectively. Furthermore, Figures 2.7 and 2.8 show the corresponding Fourier


02511 [PDF p.74] transforms of the TS (dense) response features using the MP representation, and


02512 [PDF p.74] the RI representation, respectively. Additionally, Figures 2.7 and 2.8 indicate the


02513 [PDF p.74] features corresponding to the FBoIs using color-coded squares.

02634 [PDF p.78] 2.4.2.1   Inferred parameter accuracy


02635 [PDF p.78] 


02636 [PDF p.78] To analyze the accuracy of the inferred parameter values, θ̂, the reference model


02637 [PDF p.78] is simulated for ns̄ = 1000 test samples. These test samples are obtained simi-


02638 [PDF p.78]                                                                                          2


02639 [PDF p.78] larly to the training and validation samples, see Figure 2.2. Note that, since, for


02640 [PDF p.78] testing, measurements are mimicked, the overbar notation ( ¯· ) is used to indicate


02641 [PDF p.78] (the number of) test samples. To ensure an unbiased evaluation of the ANN per-


02642 [PDF p.78] formance, the test samples should be distinct from the training and validation


02643 [PDF p.78] samples. Therefore, for each test sample s̄, the model is parameterized with a set


02644 [PDF p.78] of true parameters θ̄ s̄ that are randomly selected in P, using a uniform probability


02645 [PDF p.78] distribution. To mimic actual measurements, artificial noise is added to the sim-


02646 [PDF p.78] ulated outputs (see (2.2)) with equal properties as used to generate the training


02647 [PDF p.78] data. The features extracted from these simulated measurements are denoted as


02648 [PDF p.78] ψ̄ s̄ and fed into the ANN, see (2.7), to obtain θ̂ s̄ .


02649 [PDF p.78]       The accuracy of the inferred parameter values of test sample s̄ is evaluated


02650 [PDF p.78] based on the relative error, εs̄ ∈ Rnup , of the parameter estimate θ̂ s̄ :

02658 [PDF p.78] the scenario in which only the RI (FBoI) features are used as inputs to the ANN.


02659 [PDF p.78] Figure 2.9 displays the distribution of these relative errors (in percentages) per


02660 [PDF p.78] updating parameter in a histogram. Indeed, the ANN is able to infer parameter


02661 [PDF p.78] values from the provided features. The accuracy of the estimates varies per updat-


02662 [PDF p.78] ing parameter, with d1 being estimated with the lowest accuracy and k2 with the


02663 [PDF p.78] highest accuracy. It is remarked that, despite a relatively larger contribution of


02664 [PDF p.78] noise in y2 compared to y1 (as mentioned in Section 2.4.1.1), the parameters most


02665 [PDF p.78] closely related to this signal, i.e., k2 and d2 , are estimated with slightly higher


02666 [PDF p.78] accuracy than k1 and d1 . Here, please note that, as is explained in Appendix A.3,


02667 [PDF p.78] the responses of the system are largely uncoupled. The observation that k2 and d2


02668 [PDF p.78] are estimated more accurately, is most likely a result of the relatively low amount


02669 [PDF p.78] of oscillations in signal y1 compared to y2 , as seen in Figures 2.5 and 2.8. Nev-


02670 [PDF p.78] ertheless, even for d1 , the worst encountered relative error is only approximately


02671 [PDF p.78] 10%, whereas the majority lies below 5%. Therefore, it can be concluded that the


02672 [PDF p.78] parameter values are inferred with good accuracy.

02829 [PDF p.82] 3 and 5. For example, the normalized features for parameter combinations 2 and


02830 [PDF p.82] 4 are both approximately 1. Therefore, the ANN has difficulty in distinguishing


02831 [PDF p.82] between each of these similar parameter cases. In contrast, this is only the case


02832 [PDF p.82] to a lesser extent for normalized features originating from ℑ(Y1 ) in Figure 2.12.


02833 [PDF p.82] Consequently, distinguishing between these parameter cases when using MP fea-


02834 [PDF p.82] tures is mostly done based on the |Y1 | features, whereas for the RI features, both


02835 [PDF p.82] ℜ(Y1 ) and ℑ(Y1 ) can be employed to distinguish between these cases.


02836 [PDF p.82]      Finally, comparing the performance of the TS features with the RI (FBoI)


02837 [PDF p.82] features in Table 2.5, it is observed that the RI (FBoI) features yield better per-


02838 [PDF p.82] formance than the sparse set of TS features (with an identical number of features).


02839 [PDF p.82] Alternatively, the dense TS features yield comparable performance at the cost of


02840 [PDF p.82] 15 times as many features. However, it is worth noting that the RI (FBoI) fea-


02841 [PDF p.82] tures still perform slightly better. This, again, leads to the conclusion that, the


02842 [PDF p.82] individual RI (FBoI) features are relatively informative.


02843 [PDF p.82]      It should be remarked that the conclusions drawn here are found for a spe-


02844 [PDF p.82] cific system and (simulated) experiment design. Different systems or designs, e.g.,


02845 [PDF p.82] systems with higher modal density, (highly) coupled DoFs, and insufficient actu-


02846 [PDF p.82] ation will influence accuracy of the individual features types. For example, TE


02847 [PDF p.82] features are expected to be less profitable to estimate damping properties related


02848 [PDF p.82] to higher-order (or less dominant) modes. Therefore, automated feature selec-


02849 [PDF p.82] tion techniques have high potential to select the most informative features for any


02850 [PDF p.82] system and experiment design [77] and are discussed in Chapter 3.


02851 [PDF p.82]      Nevertheless, some general conclusions are drawn. Firstly, by using transient-


02852 [PDF p.82] based output response features as input to an IMM, physically interpretable pa-


02853 [PDF p.82] rameter values of nonlinear dynamical models can be updated online with little


02854 [PDF p.82] computational effort while achieving acceptable levels of accuracy. Furthermore,


02855 [PDF p.82] it is shown that, at least for mechanical systems, defining features using engineer-


02856 [PDF p.82] ing knowledge can improve the performance of the ANN. For example, only using


02857 [PDF p.82] frequency-domain based features in the relevant frequency ranges can result in a


02858 [PDF p.82] higher accuracy of the inferred updating parameter values.

02977 [PDF p.86] 2.4.3     Generalization capabilities


02978 [PDF p.86] Since the IMM is trained using training data, it is important to obtain insight


02979 [PDF p.86] in how accurate the IMM is for data that it has not yet seen before. Note that


02980 [PDF p.86]                                                                                           2


02981 [PDF p.86] the analysis in Section 2.4.2.1, which is similar to the analysis in [9], gives limited


02982 [PDF p.86] insight in the generalization capabilities of the ANN. Therefore, in this section, a


02983 [PDF p.86] more extensive analysis of the generalization capabilities is provided by 1) varying


02984 [PDF p.86] the number of training samples (Section 2.4.3.1), and 2) excluding parts of the


02985 [PDF p.86] training samples (Section 2.4.3.2).


02986 [PDF p.86] 


02987 [PDF p.86] 2.4.3.1   Number of training samples


02988 [PDF p.86] The impact of the number of training samples, ns , on the accuracy of the inferred


02989 [PDF p.86] parameter values is analyzed, such that insight in the generalization capabilities


02990 [PDF p.86] of the discussed output features is obtained. Here, the (training and testing)


02991 [PDF p.86] parameter space are equivalent and as defined in Table 2.1. In Figure 2.15, the


02992 [PDF p.86] mean absolute relative error for each updating parameter has been plotted versus


02993 [PDF p.86] ns for the different output feature types.


02994 [PDF p.86]     In general, for ns < 100, the accuracy of the parameter estimates is observed to


02995 [PDF p.86] be relatively low, showing that these low amounts of training samples do not suf-


02996 [PDF p.86] fice to properly learn the inverse relation between output features and parameter


02997 [PDF p.86] values. Please note that the updating parameter space is, in this use case, four-


02998 [PDF p.86] dimensional. Consequently, such few training samples do not sufficiently cover


02999 [PDF p.86] P in all its dimensions and hence performance of the IMPU method is relatively


03000 [PDF p.86] poor. Overall, it seems that, for almost all analyzed values of ns , the RI (FBoI)


03001 [PDF p.86] features perform best or approximately equally as well as the next best alterna-


03002 [PDF p.86] tive(s). Furthermore, when using all frequency bins for the MP and RI features,


03003 [PDF p.86] significantly more training samples are required to achieve the same accuracy as


03004 [PDF p.86] when only information in the FBoIs is used. Again, this is caused by the large


03005 [PDF p.86] amount of redundant and noisy high frequency information, making these features


03006 [PDF p.86] generalize relatively poorly. Since all TS features in both the dense and sparse


03007 [PDF p.86] variant carry useful information about the system, we do not see this behavior for


03008 [PDF p.86] the time-series-based features. Finally, the accuracy of the TE features is rela-


03009 [PDF p.86] tively consistent, although comparatively low for some parameters, when varying


03010 [PDF p.86] ns (especially for d1 and d2 ). This agrees with the fact that the difference in


03011 [PDF p.86] magnitude between subsequent minima/maxima is closely related to the damping


03012 [PDF p.86] values. This thus shows that the IMM between the damping parameter values


03013 [PDF p.86] and the TE features is relatively easy to learn for the ANN as was hypothesized


03014 [PDF p.86] in Section 2.3.1, i.e., TE features generalize well for different values of ns .

03032 [PDF p.87]     2.4.3.2   Excluded training zones


03033 [PDF p.87]     In practice, the true parameter values of the DT may lie (far) outside the expected


03034 [PDF p.87]     parameter space, for example, when the system is (suddenly) badly damaged. In


03035 [PDF p.87]     this case, the IMPU method should recognize this to, at least, some extent for the


03036 [PDF p.87]     benefit of health monitoring.


03037 [PDF p.87]         Therefore, in this section, generalization (and extrapolation capabilities) is


03038 [PDF p.87]     analyzed by deliberately omitting parts of the training space and testing how


03039 [PDF p.87]     accurate test samples are in distinct ‘test-zones’. In the following, changes are


03040 [PDF p.87]     only made to the training/testing ranges of d1 and d2 . Specifically, for both d1


03041 [PDF p.87]     and d2 , the range of testing values is extended on both sides of the training range


03042 [PDF p.87]     with 50% of its width. Furthermore, for both damping parameters, a central band


03043 [PDF p.87]     (20% of the width of their training range) is excluded from the training data.


03044 [PDF p.87]     In Figure 2.16, all test samples are allocated to six test-zones, indicated by a


03045 [PDF p.87]     color-coded box, where all retained training samples are located in test-zone 1. A


03046 [PDF p.87]     higher index-number of a test-zone indicates decreasing number and proximity of


03047 [PDF p.87]     adjacent boxes that contain training data (or zone 1 boxes). For example, each


03048 [PDF p.87]     box in zone 2 shares two edges with adjacent zone 1 boxes and for zone 6 only one


03049 [PDF p.87]     of the corners of each box coincides with the corner of a zone 1 box.


03050 [PDF p.87]         To acquire the training data, the Latin hypercube sampled training data used

03225 [PDF p.91]     values, one can, however, often recognize that the true system’s parameter values

03369 [PDF p.95]     2.6     Conclusions and recommendations


03370 [PDF p.95]     To minimize the mismatch between a physical system and its Digital Twin (DT,


03371 [PDF p.95] 2   which is constituted by a model), this chapter proposes to update physically inter-


03372 [PDF p.95]     pretable parameter values of nonlinear dynamical models in real-time by using the


03373 [PDF p.95]     Inverse Mapping Parameter Updating (IMPU) approach. This approach consists


03374 [PDF p.95]     of an offline and an online phase. In the offline phase, an Artificial Neural Network


03375 [PDF p.95]     (ANN) is trained using training samples consisting of output response features, as


03376 [PDF p.95]     obtained from a simulated user-defined experiment (with known excitations and


03377 [PDF p.95]     initial conditions), and corresponding (known) parameter values. The resulting


03378 [PDF p.95]     trained ANN then constitutes a direct inverse mapping between response features


03379 [PDF p.95]     and parameter values. In the online phase, this experiment is performed on a real


03380 [PDF p.95]     system. Then, the trained ANN is used to map the measured transient-based re-


03381 [PDF p.95]     sponse features to inferred parameter values. These inferred values are then used


03382 [PDF p.95]     to update the DT. Although data generation and training can take significant


03383 [PDF p.95]     time in the offline phase, computation times in the online phase are negligible,


03384 [PDF p.95]     allowing for (near) real-time parameter updating. To characterize time-domain


03385 [PDF p.95]     data, novel transient-based feature types have been introduced and evaluated on


03386 [PDF p.95]     a (simulated) 2-DoFs dynamical multibody system. Engineering knowledge about


03387 [PDF p.95]     this system is used to define informative output features resulting in improved


03388 [PDF p.95]     accuracy and computational efficiency (the latter both in the learning and in the


03389 [PDF p.95]     inferring phase) of the IMPU approach. Additionally, generalization capabilities


03390 [PDF p.95]     are demonstrated and improved by properly choosing output features such that rel-


03391 [PDF p.95]     atively few training samples already achieve satisfactory accuracy, and parameter


03392 [PDF p.95]     values outside the training space are estimated with reduced but still acceptable


03393 [PDF p.95]     accuracy. Furthermore, for a 4-DoFs roll plane model, parameter updating using


03394 [PDF p.95]     the IMPU method is compared to parameter updating using an Extended Kalman


03395 [PDF p.95]     Filter (EKF), where it is observed that, in quantitative sense, the IMPU method


03396 [PDF p.95]     is competitive with or even outperforms the EKF.


03397 [PDF p.95]         As estimates of true parameter values that lie beyond the training range become


03398 [PDF p.95]     less accurate, quantifying the uncertainty in the estimated parameter values will


03399 [PDF p.95]     be discussed in Chapter 4. Additionally, the choice of ANN structure and training


03400 [PDF p.95]     settings is far from trivial. Therefore, systematically optimizing the ANN hyper-


03401 [PDF p.95]     parameters will be discussed in Chapter 3. Furthermore, as the IMPU method


03402 [PDF p.95]     requires a highly accurate model structure, Chapter 5 focuses on simultaneous


03403 [PDF p.95]     updating of model parameter values and the model structure, i.e., its governing


03404 [PDF p.95]     dynamical equations. Finally, instead of discussing simulated use cases as done in


03405 [PDF p.95]     this chapter, the IMPU method will be applied to physical systems in Chapters 3


03406 [PDF p.95]     and 4.

03413 [PDF p.96] Abstract - A digital twin should be and remain an accurate model representation of


03414 [PDF p.96] a physical system throughout its operational life. To this end, the goal is to update


03415 [PDF p.96] (physically interpretable) parameter values of such a model in an online fashion. Hereto,


03416 [PDF p.96] the Inverse Mapping Parameter Updating (IMPU) method is employed which uses an


03417 [PDF p.96] Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to map features, extracted from measurement data, to


03418 [PDF p.96] parameter estimates. This is achieved by training the ANN offline on simulated data,


03419 [PDF p.96] i.e., pairs of sets of known parameter values sets of features extracted from corresponding


03420 [PDF p.96] simulations. Since a plethora of features (and feature types) can be extracted from


03421 [PDF p.96] simulated time-domain data, Feature Selection (FS) strategies are investigated. These


03422 [PDF p.96] strategies employ the mutual information between features and parameters to select a


03423 [PDF p.96] subset of features that are informative about the parameter values. Hereby, accuracy


03424 [PDF p.96] of the parameter values estimated by the ANN is increased and, at the same time,


03425 [PDF p.96] ANN training and inference computation times are decreased. Additionally, Bayesian


03426 [PDF p.96] search-based hyperparameter tuning is employed to enhance performance of the ANNs


03427 [PDF p.96] and optimize the ANN topology for various FS strategies. Finally, the IMPU method

03436 [PDF p.97]     is applied to a high-tech industrial use case involving a machine used in semi-conductor


03437 [PDF p.97]     manufacturing, for which measurements are performed in closed-loop on the controlled


03438 [PDF p.97]     physical system. This system is modeled as a nonlinear multibody model in the Simscape

03442 [PDF p.97] 3


03443 [PDF p.97]     3.1      Introduction


03444 [PDF p.97]     As part of the fourth industrial revolution, digital twins have the potential to


03445 [PDF p.97]     monitor the structural/machine health and improve the performance of a physical


03446 [PDF p.97]     system, e.g., via model-based control. To achieve this, the digital twin, e.g., a


03447 [PDF p.97]     dynamical multibody model, should accurately represent the true physical system.


03448 [PDF p.97]     In practice, however, it may be difficult to accurately and efficiently tune the model


03449 [PDF p.97]     parameter values for a fleet of systems due to manufacturing tolerances. Moreover,


03450 [PDF p.97]     due to, e.g., wear, the system dynamics may change over time. Consequently, there


03451 [PDF p.97]     is a need for updating methods that update physically interpretable parameter


03452 [PDF p.97]     values and are applicable in an online setting. Furthermore, to allow for fast fault


03453 [PDF p.97]     detection (which is important in the scope of diagnostics), the updating procedure


03454 [PDF p.97]     should be computationally efficient. Finally, the method should be able to update


03455 [PDF p.97]     a broad range of nonlinear dynamics models.


03456 [PDF p.97]          As a solution to the problem posed here, the Inverse Mapping Parameter Up-


03457 [PDF p.97]     dating (IMPU) method was proposed in Chapter 2. This method employs an Ar-


03458 [PDF p.97]     tificial Neural Network (ANN) that infers (online) a set of parameter values from


03459 [PDF p.97]     a set of features extracted from measured data. Here, the ANN is trained in an


03460 [PDF p.97]     offline phase using supervised learning on simulated training data, where the fea-


03461 [PDF p.97]     tures and parameter values serve as inputs and outputs to the ANN, respectively.


03462 [PDF p.97]     By using simulated training data, direct access to the (physically interpretable)


03463 [PDF p.97]     updating parameter values is obtained, which are typically not measurable on a


03464 [PDF p.97]     physical system. Furthermore, by shifting the majority of the computation time


03465 [PDF p.97]     to the offline phase, parameter values can be inferred in the order of microseconds


03466 [PDF p.97]     in the online (or parameter estimation) phase. Due to the use of input (features)


03467 [PDF p.97]     and output (parameter values) data only, this methodology is applicable to a large


03468 [PDF p.97]     variety of (dynamic) models, i.e., models in closed form derived from first princi-


03469 [PDF p.97]     ples or opaque simulation models, such as those constructed in software, e.g., in


03470 [PDF p.97]     Simscape Multibody [142].


03471 [PDF p.97]          In contrast, other popular model (parameter) updating methods, e.g., the Ex-


03472 [PDF p.97]     tended Kalman Filter (EKF) [24, 41, 88, 132, 222], typically require the explicit


03473 [PDF p.97]     dynamical equations of a model. The main advantages of the IMPU method


03474 [PDF p.97]     over the EKF are mostly of a qualitative nature. A quantitative comparison


03475 [PDF p.97]     (using simulated measurements, polluted with artificial noise) was provided in


03476 [PDF p.97] 


03477 [PDF p.98] 3.1. Introduction                                                                  71


03478 [PDF p.98] 


03479 [PDF p.98] 


03480 [PDF p.98] Chapter 2. Other conventional (sensitivity-based) parameter updating techniques


03481 [PDF p.98] [56, 128, 133] require costly iterative computations, which are undesirable for on-


03482 [PDF p.98] line application. Moreover, these sensitivity-based updating techniques (as well as


03483 [PDF p.98] EKF) require initial guesses for the parameter values, where an incorrect guess may


03484 [PDF p.98] result in sub-optimal parameter estimates. Furthermore, traditional system iden-


03485 [PDF p.98] tification methods typically yield models in a generic form. Consequently, (some)


03486 [PDF p.98] physical interpretability, which is valuable for intelligible health monitoring and


03487 [PDF p.98]                                                                                          3


03488 [PDF p.98] digital twins, is lost [134].


03489 [PDF p.98]      As discussed in Chapter 2, a wide range of response features can be used in


03490 [PDF p.98] the IMPU method: multiple (combinations of) transient-based types, i.e., sampled


03491 [PDF p.98] values of a time-signal, the extrema thereof, and (complex) values of the Fourier-


03492 [PDF p.98] transformed signal. In practice, however, some features might be irrelevant as


03493 [PDF p.98] they are barely influenced by the updated parameters. As a result, the ANN


03494 [PDF p.98] may become unnecessarily large which causes slower (offline) training and (online)


03495 [PDF p.98] inference. Additionally, the accuracy of the inferred parameter values might suffer


03496 [PDF p.98] from these irrelevant (noisy) features as they can make training more challenging


03497 [PDF p.98] [146, 215].


03498 [PDF p.98]      Therefore, Feature Selection (FS) techniques can be employed [236] that de-


03499 [PDF p.98] termine which features should be retained and which features should be omitted.


03500 [PDF p.98] Within FS, methods are available for supervised, semi-supervised, and unsuper-


03501 [PDF p.98] vised learning [129, 234]. Since the IMPU method is based on supervised learning,


03502 [PDF p.98] only supervised FS methods will be considered. Furthermore, a distinction is made


03503 [PDF p.98] between embedded, wrapper, and filter FS methods [40]. Since only filter meth-


03504 [PDF p.98] ods allow for feature selection prior to training an ANN, and are consequently


03505 [PDF p.98] computationally less demanding, this type of methods is used in this work. To


03506 [PDF p.98] determine if a feature is relevant for the accurate updating of a particular param-


03507 [PDF p.98] eter, the Mutual Information (MI) [33] score between a feature and parameter is


03508 [PDF p.98] calculated using the training data. Then, a user-defined number of features with


03509 [PDF p.98] the highest MI scores is selected. An advantage of MI is that this metric can deal


03510 [PDF p.98] with non-monotonic and nonlinear relations between the assessed variables. This


03511 [PDF p.98] is in contrast to other filter methods, such as the Pearson’s correlation coefficient,


03512 [PDF p.98] Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, and Kendall’s tau coefficient [53].


03513 [PDF p.98]      Additionally, manual tuning of training- and topology-related settings of an


03514 [PDF p.98] ANN is both difficult and time consuming. Therefore, ANN HyperParameter


03515 [PDF p.98] Tuning (HPT) is employed to automatically tune these hyperparameters such that


03516 [PDF p.98] performance is improved and online inference time is decreased.


03517 [PDF p.98]      Finally, the IMPU method is applied to an industrial use case. Specifically,


03518 [PDF p.98] parameters of the closed-loop controlled motion stages of a high-tech wire bonder


03519 [PDF p.98] system [7] are updated. In contrast to previous work in which measurements were


03520 [PDF p.98] simulated, in this chapter, model updating is also performed based on data that


03521 [PDF p.98] is measured on a physical wire bonder machine.

03526 [PDF p.99]          To summarize, the main contributions of this work are:


03527 [PDF p.99] 


03528 [PDF p.99]          1. extension of the Inverse Mapping Parameter Updating method with mutual-


03529 [PDF p.99]             information-based Feature Selection, thereby improving efficiency and ac-


03530 [PDF p.99]             curacy of the parameter updating approach. Herein, the effectiveness of


03531 [PDF p.99]             different FS approaches is investigated,


03532 [PDF p.99] 


03533 [PDF p.99] 3        2. the use of Hyperparameter Tuning for the Inverse Mapping Parameter Up-


03534 [PDF p.99]             dating method. Hyperparameter tuning is, for example, used to optimize


03535 [PDF p.99]             the Artificial Neural Network topology for different sets of selected features,


03536 [PDF p.99] 


03537 [PDF p.99]          3. the application and analysis of the proposed method on a multibody model


03538 [PDF p.99]             of an industrial system that is measured in closed-loop with feedback and


03539 [PDF p.99]             feedforward control.


03540 [PDF p.99] 


03541 [PDF p.99]         The outline of this chapter is as follows. In Section 3.2, a summary of the IMPU


03542 [PDF p.99]     method and preliminaries for HPT are provided. Section 3.3 discusses feature


03543 [PDF p.99]     selection by introducing the concept of MI, and introducing various MI-based FS


03544 [PDF p.99]     strategies. Subsequently, Section 3.4 demonstrates the industrial application of


03545 [PDF p.99]     the discussed methodologies. Results are shown based on both simulated and


03546 [PDF p.99]     real-world measurements of the wire bonder machine. Finally, conclusions and


03547 [PDF p.99]     recommendations for future work are discussed in Section 3.5.

03552 [PDF p.99]     In the IMPU method, the goal is to update parameter values, stored in θ ∈ Rnup

03558 [PDF p.99]

03562 [PDF p.99]     the state and input vector, respectively. Here, the inputs are known as they are


03563 [PDF p.99]     defined by the user (hence the overbar ( ¯· )). Furthermore, g is the nonlinear vector


03564 [PDF p.99]     field, h is the output function, and ν is zero-mean additive measurement noise.


03565 [PDF p.99]     The number of states, outputs, inputs, and updating parameters is given by nx ,


03566 [PDF p.99]     ny , nu , and nup , respectively.

03655 [PDF p.101]     3.2.2     ANN Hyperparameter tuning


03656 [PDF p.101]     The training parameter settings (e.g., learning rate, and batch size) and topology


03657 [PDF p.101]     (e.g., number of layers, and number of neurons in each layer) of an ANN directly


03658 [PDF p.101]     influence its training time and, more importantly, its inference accuracy. There-


03659 [PDF p.101]     fore, these so-called hyperparameter values can be tuned such that some metric,


03660 [PDF p.101]     e.g., the validation loss, is minimized. Since the (validation) loss varies in each


03661 [PDF p.101]     epoch during training, the instance of the ANN with the lowest validation loss


03662 [PDF p.101]     over all epochs is saved and evaluated.


03663 [PDF p.101]     Remark 3.1 The validation loss is the loss (in our case defined as the mean squared error


03664 [PDF p.101]     between parameter values inferred based on sets of features and the true known parameter

03670 [PDF p.102] and actual parameter values are normalized (between 0 and 1) as this improves the


03671 [PDF p.102] conditioning for the training of the ANN [82]. This type of ‘normalization for training’


03672 [PDF p.102] (indicated by a tilde ( ˜· )) is not to be confused with ‘normalization for confidentiality’


03673 [PDF p.102] (indicated by a superscript nor ) as will be used in Section 3.4. Hence, the validation loss


03674 [PDF p.102] is measured on a distinct scale. Validation data is similar to, yet independent from, the


03675 [PDF p.102] training data such that an unbiased evaluation of the ANN’s performance is achieved.


03676 [PDF p.102]                                                                                                3


03677 [PDF p.102]      Although some directions can be found in [3], manually tuning hyperparameter


03678 [PDF p.102] values can prove both difficult and time consuming. Therefore, different automated


03679 [PDF p.102] HPT search methods have been developed [170]. In such searches, ANNs are


03680 [PDF p.102] trained and evaluated for different configurations of hyperparameter values. The


03681 [PDF p.102] most popular search methods are grid, random, and Bayesian searches [191]. Since


03682 [PDF p.102] in a grid search all possible configurations of hyperparameter values are evaluated


03683 [PDF p.102] for a predefined discretized set of values for each hyperparameter, this is typically


03684 [PDF p.102] a computationally intensive search. In contrast, random and Bayesian searches do


03685 [PDF p.102] not use a predefined discretized set of hyperparameter values. Random searches


03686 [PDF p.102] tend to be less costly but suffer significantly from uncertainty. In a Bayesian search,


03687 [PDF p.102] a Gaussian process is used that models the relationship between hyperparameter


03688 [PDF p.102] values and the validation loss such that the probability of improvement is optimized


03689 [PDF p.102] [192]. Since Bayesian searches compromise well between accuracy, efficiency, and


03690 [PDF p.102] reliability, this search type is employed for this research. As is the case for any


03691 [PDF p.102] Bayesian method, a prior on the hyperparameter values is required. In this work,


03692 [PDF p.102] it is assumed that all hyperparameter values are equally likely. Therefore, uniform


03693 [PDF p.102] priors are employed.

03784 [PDF p.104] 3.3.2     MI-based FS strategies


03785 [PDF p.104] To select features based on their MI, they are ranked based on a relevance score


03786 [PDF p.104] J. This score is calculated for each feature (indexed by i) to quantify the impor-


03787 [PDF p.104] tance of that feature with respect to the k th parameter. Although a large variety


03788 [PDF p.104] of definitions for this relevance score exist, here, this discussion will be limited


03789 [PDF p.104] to three strategies: (1) Mutual Information Maximization (MIM) [52, 126], (2)


03790 [PDF p.104] Max-Relevance Min-Redundancy (MRMR) [68], and (3) Joint Mutual Informa-                    3


03791 [PDF p.104] tion (JMI) [227]. For these strategies, the relevance score for candidate feature i


03792 [PDF p.104] with respect to parameter k are given by

03797 [PDF p.104] for γ1 = γ2 = 1 JMI is obtained. Furthermore,

03811 [PDF p.104]     All three strategies employ JREL,ik which quantifies the relevance of feature i to


03812 [PDF p.104] parameter k using their MI score. The second term, JRED,i , penalizes redundancy


03813 [PDF p.104] between features, i.e., feature i is penalized if it contains information similar to the


03814 [PDF p.104] information carried by features that have already been selected. The third term,


03815 [PDF p.104] JCRED,ik (conditional redundancy), can partly mitigate the second term. This


03816 [PDF p.104] term recognizes that the correlation between two similar features, i.e., between


03817 [PDF p.104] feature i and any of the already selected features, can be useful. To illustrate,


03818 [PDF p.104] suppose that, for some combination of features, this correlation is stronger given


03819 [PDF p.104] some knowledge about the parameter k than the correlation when this knowledge


03820 [PDF p.104] is absent. Then, if we indeed see strong correlation, we still obtain some informa-


03821 [PDF p.104] tion about the parameter and it is therefore valuable to select both features [33].


03822 [PDF p.104] In other words, JMI, which is the only strategy discussed here that employs con-


03823 [PDF p.104] ditional redundancy, promotes the complementary information between features


03824 [PDF p.104] and acknowledges that “correlation between features does not imply redundancy”


03825 [PDF p.104] [66].


03826 [PDF p.104]     For MIM, only JREL contributes to J. Consequently, the relevance score J


03827 [PDF p.104] does not depend on the set of (already) selected features. As a result, MIM is, in


03828 [PDF p.104] contrast to MRMR and JMI, a non-iterative strategy and, hence, computationally

04073 [PDF p.110] 3.4.2.1   Data generation


04074 [PDF p.110] The dataset used to train the ANNs in Section 3.4.2.3 consists of ns = 10000


04075 [PDF p.110] training samples. For each training sample, a set of parameter values θ s is sam-


04076 [PDF p.110] pled from P using Latin Hyper Cube sampling. By employing Latin Hyper Cube


04077 [PDF p.110] sampling, the training parameters are sampled with sufficient uniformity across


04078 [PDF p.110] P (see [145] for a detailed explanation). Then, the Simscape Multibody model is


04079 [PDF p.110] parameterized and simulated for each training sample for a simulated experiment


04080 [PDF p.110] defined by reference profiles r̄X (t), r̄Y (t), and r̄Z (t) over some period of time.


04081 [PDF p.110] Furthermore, as initial conditions x̄0 , the system is at rest at the origin (achieved


04082 [PDF p.110] using a homing procedure on the physical system in Section 3.4.4). The simulated


04083 [PDF p.110] signals are sampled with a sampling frequency identical to the sampling frequency


04084 [PDF p.110] of the encoders on the physical setup. The reference profiles, together with the


04085 [PDF p.110] feedback and feedforward controllers, take over the role of ū(t) in Figures 3.1 and


04086 [PDF p.110] 3.3 and (3.1), where g and h in (3.1) now represent the closed-loop dynamics. The


04087 [PDF p.110] experiment that is used to train the IMM in the offline phase and used to infer


04088 [PDF p.110] parameter values from in the online phase, is referred to as ‘experiment 1’. Alter-


04089 [PDF p.110] nating smoothed step-up and step-down profiles (closely resembling the steps in


04090 [PDF p.110] the reference profiles used during operation of the system) are employed to excite


04091 [PDF p.110] all stages, see the blue lines in Figure 3.4.


04092 [PDF p.110]     The set of potential features (from which specific features can be selected) is


04093 [PDF p.110] extracted from the discretized true/measured tracking errors ēX , ēY , and ēZ of

04126 [PDF p.111]     Feature selection is performed using the training data that is generated as de-


04127 [PDF p.111]     scribed in Section 3.4.2.1, where for each parameter k (k = 1, . . . , 10) nψ,sel,k = 30


04128 [PDF p.111]     features are selected. In Table 3.2, several FS results are listed per FS strategy.


04129 [PDF p.111]         When using MIM, there is overlap between the features selected for different


04130 [PDF p.111]     parameters, resulting in the total number of selected features being smaller than


04131 [PDF p.111]     300, i.e., nψ,sel,MIM < nψ,sel,MRMR = nψ,sel,JMI = 300. Furthermore, we observe

04166 [PDF p.112] 3.4.2.3    ANN training and HPT


04167 [PDF p.112] Selected sets of features, together with their corresponding training parameter


04168 [PDF p.112] values are employed to train various ANNs. In this work, the ANNs are constructed


04169 [PDF p.112] using the Keras application programming interface for the Tensorflow library in


04170 [PDF p.112] the Python programming language [102]. Furthermore, the Adam optimizer is


04171 [PDF p.112] used to train the ANNs. All ANNs employed in this work are fully connected


04172 [PDF p.112] feedforward networks [23] and have Sigmoid activation functions in their output


04173 [PDF p.112] layers. Furthermore, early stopping with a patience of 40 epochs is employed,


04174 [PDF p.112] i.e., if the validation loss does not decrease for 40 consecutive epochs, the training


04175 [PDF p.112] process is terminated [168]. After training, the ANN that achieved the lowest


04176 [PDF p.112] validation loss over all epochs is saved.


04177 [PDF p.112]      As a benchmark, one ANN is trained on the training data without FS, i.e.,


04178 [PDF p.112] nψ = 4553 features are used, with manually tuned hyperparameter values. Here,


04179 [PDF p.112] manual HPT is mostly based on general experience in neural network training, i.e.,


04180 [PDF p.112] understanding the effects of hyperparameters on, among others, training/inference


04181 [PDF p.112] time and inference accuracy (see [3] for some general insights). The hyperparame-


04182 [PDF p.112] ter values used for this ‘manual’ ANN related to the training settings are listed in

04216 [PDF p.113]     ANN are optimized in phase 2. In both phases, Bayesian searches are applied.

04463 [PDF p.119]         In the last six columns of Table 3.5, the average (over all test samples) RMSE


04464 [PDF p.119]     and emax are listed per motion direction for the evaluated ANNs. In general, it is


04465 [PDF p.119]     observed that all ANNs yield small prediction errors compared to the magnitude
