04468 [PDF p.119] 3


04469 [PDF p.119]     HPT yields slightly better results compared to the benchmark ANN.


04470 [PDF p.119]         Choosing different FS strategies, however, has a less pronounced effect on the


04471 [PDF p.119]     prediction error. Some ANNs perform relatively well for specific output signals,


04472 [PDF p.119]     whereas they perform comparatively poorly for other output signals. This is at-


04473 [PDF p.119]     tributed to the fact that the ANN is trained to minimize the parameter error


04474 [PDF p.119]     rather than the prediction error, where each updating parameter influences the


04475 [PDF p.119]     output signals to a different extent due to the dynamic coupling. Furthermore,


04476 [PDF p.119]     due to the black-box nature of the ANN, it is non-trivial to predict which features


04477 [PDF p.119]     yield accurate updating parameter estimates. Finally, the employed FS strategies


04478 [PDF p.119]     aim to find the optimal set of features, whereas, in reality, this optimal set is only


04479 [PDF p.119]     approximated. Combining these uncertainties, the effect of the FS strategy on the


04480 [PDF p.119]     accuracy of the individual output signals would require a practically infeasible sen-


04481 [PDF p.119]     sitivity analysis that spans the nonlinear time-domain simulation, ANN mapping,


04482 [PDF p.119]     and MI-based FS.


04483 [PDF p.119]         If the user would like to be more accurate for a specific output signal (or sig-


04484 [PDF p.119]     nals), a parameter sensitivity study can be performed to identify the most relevant


04485 [PDF p.119]     updating parameters for that signal. Then, the user may select more features that


04486 [PDF p.119]     are informative about these parameters (by varying nψ,sel,k for each parameter


04487 [PDF p.119]     indexed by k). Additionally or alternatively, the ANN training/validation loss can


04488 [PDF p.119]     be weighted such that these parameters are estimated with a comparatively high


04489 [PDF p.119]     accuracy.

04768 [PDF p.127]     3.5       Conclusions and recommendations


04769 [PDF p.127]     The IMPU method is used to update, within microseconds, (nonlinear) multi-body


04770 [PDF p.127]     dynamics models by inferring parameter values from features that are extracted


04771 [PDF p.127]     from measured response data. To this end, an Inverse Mapping Model (IMM)


04772 [PDF p.127]     is utilized that is constituted by an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) which is


04773 [PDF p.127]     trained on simulated data using supervised learning. In the current chapter, the


04774 [PDF p.127]     IMPU method, introduced in Chapter 2, is extended to incorporate three mutual


04775 [PDF p.127]     information-based Feature Selection (FS) strategies: Mutual Information Maxi-


04776 [PDF p.127]     mization (MIM), Max-Relevance-Min-Redundancy (MRMR), and Joint Mutual


04777 [PDF p.127]     Information (JMI). These FS strategies leverage training data to determine which


04778 [PDF p.127]     response features are informative with respect to the updating parameters.


04779 [PDF p.127]         In this chapter, the IMPU method is applied to an industrial use case (a wire


04780 [PDF p.127]     bonder machine). An analysis based on simulated data has demonstrated that the


04781 [PDF p.127]     IMPU method results in accurately inferred parameter values. This also results in


04782 [PDF p.127]     accurate updated models that are capable to generate responses that closely resem-


04783 [PDF p.127]     ble the response of the true (simulated) system. It is demonstrated that employing


04784 [PDF p.127]     FS increases the accuracy of the inferred parameter values since uninformative, yet


04785 [PDF p.127]     noisy, features are omitted. Moreover, training and inference times are reduced,


04786 [PDF p.127]     as fewer trainable weights are required due to the smaller input space. Compar-


04787 [PDF p.127]     ing the different FS strategies, approximately equivalent offline training times and


04788 [PDF p.127]     online inference times are observed. The resulting validation losses and parameter


04789 [PDF p.127]     errors are also comparable, although taking the redundancy between features into


04790 [PDF p.127]     account (using the JMI strategy) results in a slight decrease in validation loss and

04836 [PDF p.130] Abstract - For a digital twin to reach its full predictive potential, it must accurately


04837 [PDF p.130] reflect its physical counterpart throughout its operational lifetime. To this end, the


04838 [PDF p.130] inverse mapping parameter updating method enables physically interpretable parameter


04839 [PDF p.130] values to be updated, in real-time, for a wide range of (nonlinear) dynamical models


04840 [PDF p.130] using features extracted from measured response data. This chapter proposes to extend


04841 [PDF p.130] this method by employing a probabilistic Bayesian neural network, which is trained


04842 [PDF p.130] offline using simulated data, to infer, again in real-time, probability distributions for


04843 [PDF p.130] the updating parameter values instead of (traditionally obtained) point estimates. As a


04844 [PDF p.130] result, the user obtains a quantification of the (un)certainty, providing insight into the


04845 [PDF p.130] degree of trust to be placed in the updated parameter values, which supports the decision-


04846 [PDF p.130] making process for which the digital twin is employed. Additionally, it is proposed to


04847 [PDF p.130] include so-called ‘input parameters’, that characterize the specific settings on the physical


04848 [PDF p.130] setup, as inputs to the (probabilistic Bayesian) neural network to allow for a broader


04849 [PDF p.130] applicability of the parameter updating method. To validate the proposed methodology,


04850 [PDF p.130] it is applied, using both simulated and real-world measurements, to a medical mechanical

04864 [PDF p.131]     4.1      Introduction


04865 [PDF p.131]     In this chapter, a parameter updating method is proposed that allows real-time


04866 [PDF p.131]     updating of digital twins, while simultaneously providing a quantification of the


04867 [PDF p.131]     uncertainty in the updated parameter values. Here, a digital twin [64] is a virtual


04868 [PDF p.131] 4   representation of a physical system, which is assumed to be represented by a


04869 [PDF p.131]     parameterized (nonlinear dynamical) model. By updating a digital twin online,


04870 [PDF p.131]     e.g., in real-time, we can assure that it is and remains an accurate representation


04871 [PDF p.131]     of the physical system throughout its operational life. Since this chapter concerns


04872 [PDF p.131]     parameter updating, the structure of the model for the system dynamics, e.g., its


04873 [PDF p.131]     governing (dynamical) equations, is assumed to be sufficiently representative to


04874 [PDF p.131]     capture the relevant dynamics of the physical system.


04875 [PDF p.131]         Updating model parameter values can be beneficial for adapted trajectory de-


04876 [PDF p.131]     sign [94], model-based control, and structural health monitoring [60]. However, if


04877 [PDF p.131]     an incorrectly estimated model parameter value is carelessly used to base decisions


04878 [PDF p.131]     or operations on, this could have severe negative impacts on costs and/or safety.


04879 [PDF p.131]     Therefore, the quantification of the (un)certainty in the updated model (parame-


04880 [PDF p.131]     ters) has gathered increasing interest [1, 78, 194, 219]. Examples of methodologies


04881 [PDF p.131]     that incorporate Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) for model parameter updating


04882 [PDF p.131]     are: (extended) Kalman filters [24, 132, 222], particle filters [5], Bayesian inference


04883 [PDF p.131]     [154, 162], rejection sampling [131, 167], and (transitional) Markov chain Monte


04884 [PDF p.131]     Carlo-based updating [18, 190].


04885 [PDF p.131]         In the context of digital twins, model (parameter) updating methods should,


04886 [PDF p.131]     however, 1) be computationally efficient for online application, 2) update phys-


04887 [PDF p.131]     ically interpretable parameters, and 3) be applicable to a broad range of (non-


04888 [PDF p.131]     linear) models that are derived analytically from first principles or are obtained


04889 [PDF p.131]     using (opaque) modeling software packages. The aforementioned parameter up-


04890 [PDF p.131]     dating methods that enable UQ, e.g., Kalman filters and Bayesian inference do,


04891 [PDF p.131]     however, not satisfy these joint requirements. For example, Bayesian inference re-


04892 [PDF p.131]     quires several computational iterations to update parameter values, thereby lim-


04893 [PDF p.131]     iting real-time application. Furthermore, Kalman filters typically require direct


04894 [PDF p.131]     access to the model’s governing equations, limiting their applicability to models


04895 [PDF p.131]     constructed using commercial software. Therefore, in Chapters 2 and 3, the au-


04896 [PDF p.131]     thors have proposed the Inverse Mapping Parameter Updating (IMPU) method


04897 [PDF p.131]     to satisfy the above requirements. This method uses a machine-learning based


04898 [PDF p.131]     Inverse Mapping Model (IMM), that is trained in an offline phase using super-


04899 [PDF p.131]     vised learning on simulated data. In the subsequent online phase, this IMM infers


04900 [PDF p.131] 


04901 [PDF p.132] 4.1. Introduction                                                                105


04902 [PDF p.132] 


04903 [PDF p.132] 


04904 [PDF p.132] updating parameter values from measured output features with negligible com-


04905 [PDF p.132] putational costs. Note that, in Chapter 2, a quantitative comparison between


04906 [PDF p.132] the IMPU method and extended Kalman filter (without UQ) is provided, where


04907 [PDF p.132] the IMPU method is demonstrated to be competitive with or even outperform


04908 [PDF p.132] extended Kalman filter in terms of accuracy.


04909 [PDF p.132]     The deterministic Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) that have been used as


04910 [PDF p.132] IMMs in the IMPU method so far, i.e., in Chapters 2 and 3, do, however, only


04911 [PDF p.132] provide point estimates for the parameter values. This may lead to critical situ-


04912 [PDF p.132] ations in which parameter values are updated without knowing that the ANN is


04913 [PDF p.132] operating outside its training space where it is (significantly) less accurate. For


04914 [PDF p.132] example, for medical applications, e.g., the mechanical ventilation for lung pa-        4


04915 [PDF p.132] tients use case considered in this chapter, decisions based on inaccurate parameter


04916 [PDF p.132] values can have severe consequences. To this end, this chapter proposes the novel


04917 [PDF p.132] use of Probabilistic Bayesian Neural Networks (PBNNs). These PBNNs can si-


04918 [PDF p.132] multaneously infer parameter values and their associated uncertainties, resulting


04919 [PDF p.132] in a significant advancement over the use of deterministic ANNs.


04920 [PDF p.132]     Alternatively, in other work of the author, noisy output Gaussian Processes


04921 [PDF p.132] (GPs) have been used as IMM to quantify the uncertainty in the inferred parameter


04922 [PDF p.132] values [107]. However, when using GPs, real-time online inference is hampered if a


04923 [PDF p.132] large number of training samples is required. Moreover, due to the inverse nature


04924 [PDF p.132] of the problem at hand, actually, noisy input Gaussian [19, 144] processes should


04925 [PDF p.132] be used (traditional GPs only assume the outputs, i.e., the parameter values,


04926 [PDF p.132] to be noisy). This type of GP, however, requires tuning of significantly more


04927 [PDF p.132] hyperparameters, which makes training more difficult, e.g., in terms of convergence


04928 [PDF p.132] [144]. PBNNs do not suffer from these qualitative disadvantages.


04929 [PDF p.132]     Since the PBNN is trained offline for a specific experiment, an identical ex-


04930 [PDF p.132] periment needs to be performed online on the physical system, see Chapter 2. To


04931 [PDF p.132] alleviate this requirement, it is proposed to define additional input parameters that


04932 [PDF p.132] parametrically define the experiment. By varying these input parameters during


04933 [PDF p.132] training, i.e., sample them along with the updating parameters, the trained PBNN


04934 [PDF p.132] is applicable for a broader range of experiments.


04935 [PDF p.132]     Summarizing, the main contributions of this chapter are:


04936 [PDF p.132]   1. the addition of Uncertainty Quantification to the Inverse Mapping Parameter


04937 [PDF p.132]      Updating method by employing Probabilistic Bayesian Neural Networks to


04938 [PDF p.132]      satisfy the aforementioned requirements for model parameter updating in a


04939 [PDF p.132]      digital twin context,


04940 [PDF p.132]   2. the inclusion of variable user-defined settings as input parameters to the


04941 [PDF p.132]      Inverse Mapping Model to promote broad (online) applicability,


04942 [PDF p.132]   3. the application of the developed methodology to a (medical) use case, i.e., a


04943 [PDF p.132]      mechanical ventilation system, with real-world data.

04959 [PDF p.133]     The Inverse Mapping Parameter Updating (IMPU) method is used to update


04960 [PDF p.133]     model parameter values θ up ∈ Rnup of a generic nonlinear dynamical model (see


04961 [PDF p.133]     Chapters 2 and 3) of which the continuous-time state-space model is described by:

04968 [PDF p.133]     with states x(t), (parametric) inputs u(t) = ū(t; θ in )4.1 , and outputs y(t) ∈ Rny .


04969 [PDF p.133]     Here, the overbar ( ¯· ) denotes that the user-defined function ū(t; θ in ) is known.


04970 [PDF p.133]     To simulate the model, the states are initialized with (parametric) initial state


04971 [PDF p.133]     values x(t = 0) = x0 = x̄0 (θ in ). Note that it is assumed that the user is able


04972 [PDF p.133]     to control both u(t) and x0 on the physical system. The goal is to update the


04973 [PDF p.133]     values for θ up such that y(t) as obtained from the model parameterized with


04974 [PDF p.133]     the updated parameter values closely resembles the data measured on the phys-


04975 [PDF p.133]     ical system. Note that the initial state values, the time-dependent inputs, the


04976 [PDF p.133]     nonlinear vector field g, and the output function h are functions of so-called in-


04977 [PDF p.133]     put parameters θ in ∈ Rnin . These (known) input parameters enable the user to

05109 [PDF p.136] Remark 4.1 Due to the use of the inverse mapping, the accuracy and the training time


05110 [PDF p.136] of the IMPU method are dictated by the complexity of the inverse mapping between


05111 [PDF p.136] features and parameter values. For example, a large number of parameters will increase


05112 [PDF p.136] data generation and training time due to the curse of dimensionality. Moreover, the


05113 [PDF p.136] informativeness of the extracted and selected features affects this complexity, see Chap-


05114 [PDF p.136] ters 2 and 3. As a result, however, the efficacy of the method is only marginally affected    4


05115 [PDF p.136] by the complexity of the to-be-updated model, i.e., its governing (dynamical) equations.


05116 [PDF p.136] Furthermore, the online computation/inference time is affected by the size of the Neural


05117 [PDF p.136] Network (NN), which is dictated by the number of features, input parameters, updat-


05118 [PDF p.136] ing parameters, and the neural network topology (that reflects the complexity of the


05119 [PDF p.136] inverse mapping). Nevertheless, inference using a direct feedforward neural network is,


05120 [PDF p.136] in general, considered computationally efficient due to the relatively simple nature of the


05121 [PDF p.136] involved mathematical operations. The complexity of the function to extract features


05122 [PDF p.136] (i.e., L in (4.2)), may, however, increase online computation times more significantly.


05123 [PDF p.136] 


05124 [PDF p.136]     In Chapters 2 and 3, deterministic Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have


05125 [PDF p.136] been used to constitute the IMM I. These, however, lack a quantification of the


05126 [PDF p.136] uncertainty in the inferred parameter values. Therefore, in the following section,


05127 [PDF p.136] Probabilistic Bayesian Neural Networks (PBNNs) will be employed instead. In-


05128 [PDF p.136] deed, as shown in the bottom right of Figure 4.1, a PBNN infers a probability


05129 [PDF p.136] distribution (quantified by means µ̂θ and covariances ĉθ ) for each updating pa-


05130 [PDF p.136] rameter, thereby providing a quantification of the uncertainty.


05131 [PDF p.136]     Summarizing, the IMPU method infers updating parameter values from a set of


05132 [PDF p.136] input parameter values and from a set of selected features that are extracted from


05133 [PDF p.136] output responses by using an inverse mapping model. This IMM is constituted by


05134 [PDF p.136] a PBNN to enable uncertainty quantification and is trained based on simulated


05135 [PDF p.136] data. In Section 4.3, a comprehensive introduction to PBNNs will be given and


05136 [PDF p.136] their envisioned role as IMM will be introduced.

05520 [PDF p.144] inference time of a PBNN (and BNN) is higher than for an ANN or PNN (which, for the

05522 [PDF p.144] weights, e.g., during the measurement performed to obtain the inputs to the (P)BNN,

05528 [PDF p.144] 4.4      Mechanical ventilation use case


05529 [PDF p.144] In this section, the previously discussed methodology is applied to a medical use


05530 [PDF p.144] case of a mechanical ventilation system. In Section 4.4.1, the medical use case


05531 [PDF p.144] and the ventilator system are introduced. Section 4.4.2 discusses the (training)


05532 [PDF p.144] data generation and introduces the employed PBNN and its (training) settings.


05533 [PDF p.144] Finally, Sections 4.4.3 and 4.4.4 discuss results based on simulated and measured


05534 [PDF p.144] data, respectively.


05535 [PDF p.144] 


05536 [PDF p.144] 4.4.1     Use case and system description


05537 [PDF p.144] Mechanical ventilation is employed in intensive-care units to aid or stimulate res-


05538 [PDF p.144] piration for patients that are incapable of autonomously breathing. For optimal


05539 [PDF p.144] treatment, it is essential to tailor a breathing pressure profile to the patient [4, 120].


05540 [PDF p.144] In this regard, medical personnel can use the patient’s lung characteristics and the


05541 [PDF p.144] uncertainty on their estimates to change their mechanical ventilation treatment.


05542 [PDF p.144] Moreover, the ventilator should be controlled to accurately track this pressure


05543 [PDF p.144] profile during treatment, for which various pressure control strategies have been


05544 [PDF p.144] suggested [29, 79, 179, 180]. To prevent (potentially fatal) lung damage, these


05545 [PDF p.144] control strategies require accurate information on the patient’s lung character-


05546 [PDF p.144] istics [58, 199]. Here, it is proposed to use the IMPU method to retrieve this


05547 [PDF p.144] information. Among others, lung parameters of a dynamical model of the me-


05548 [PDF p.144] chanical ventilation system and their associated uncertainties are inferred. For


05549 [PDF p.144] demonstration purposes, a lung emulator [81] is used instead of an actual patient.


05550 [PDF p.144]

05743 [PDF p.148] can not be influenced. Without going into further detail, it is expected that the


05744 [PDF p.148] inference accuracy of the IMPU method (inferred parameter values and their stan-


05745 [PDF p.148] dard deviations) decreases for increased noise levels. The PBNN should, however,


05746 [PDF p.148] recognize the increased aleatoric uncertainty and infer larger standard deviations.


05747 [PDF p.148] By using realistic characterizations of the true measurement noise to generate the


05748 [PDF p.148] training data, it is expected that the deterioration in inference accuracy is limited


05749 [PDF p.148] to some extent. This accuracy may be improved further by selecting more features


05750 [PDF p.148] (as long as they are comparatively informative about the updating parameter val-


05751 [PDF p.148] ues) to lessen the overall influence of the noise on each individual feature. Compare


05752 [PDF p.148] this, for instance, to a hypothetical case where only a single feature is affected by


05753 [PDF p.148] noise, making it impossible to mitigate the noise’s impact effectively. Note that


05754 [PDF p.148] adding features increases training and inference times, see Chapter 3. A detailed


05755 [PDF p.148] investigation on this topic, however, requires further research.

05886 [PDF p.151]     4.4.2.1     Manual feature selection


05887 [PDF p.151]     Since, typically, there is a mismatch between a physical system and its model,


05888 [PDF p.151]     automated FS as described in Chapter 3 may perform sub-optimally, see, e.g.,


05889 [PDF p.151]     Section 4.4.4. Namely, due to these mismatches, the mapping learned in the of-


05890 [PDF p.151]     fline phase (based on the simulated model) is not the same as the (ideal) mapping


05891 [PDF p.151]     required for (a perfect model of) the physical system, resulting in (slightly) flawed


05892 [PDF p.151]     inferred parameter values. To alleviate this issue, manual feature selection is em-


05893 [PDF p.151]     ployed to only select features where the simulated and measured signals are known


05894 [PDF p.151]     to correspond reasonably well4.6 . In Figure 4.10, measured signals are compared


05895 [PDF p.151]     to simulated signals that are obtained with a reference model parameterized with


05896 [PDF p.151]                                  all

05898 [PDF p.151]     in dedicated experiments. Here, the simulated and measured signals correspond


05899 [PDF p.151]     relatively well for some time samples, but less so at others. For example, in


05900 [PDF p.151]     Figure 4.10, it is observed that values for Qout near 0 mL/s and values at time


05901 [PDF p.151]     instances where the time derivative of the signal is high are clearly different for the


05902 [PDF p.151]     reference and measured signals (as is evident from the black and green triangles

05904 [PDF p.151]     explanations for these mismatches are:

06219 [PDF p.160] As already shown in Section 4.4.2, JMI selects features at time samples where the


06220 [PDF p.160] model does not fully capture the behavior of the physical system. As a result,


06221 [PDF p.160] the majority of the inferred updating parameter values is inaccurate when using


06222 [PDF p.160] measured data, see Table 4.6.


06223 [PDF p.160]     In contrast, using manual FS, the updating parameters are inferred significantly


06224 [PDF p.160] more accurately, see Table 4.7. This holds especially for Rlung and Clung . These


06225 [PDF p.160] inferred lung parameter values comfortably fall within the 15% margin of error that


06226 [PDF p.160] is sufficient for medical personnel to guide the patient treatment decision process.


06227 [PDF p.160] Nevertheless, Rlin and Rquad are still inferred less accurately as is observed in


06228 [PDF p.160] Table 4.7. This can be partly attributed to the assumption of a static instead


06229 [PDF p.160] of a dynamic hose model [189]. From Table 4.7, we also observe that the errors


06230 [PDF p.160] for experiments 3 and 4 are, on average, larger than those for experiments 1


06231 [PDF p.160] and 2. This is explained by the relatively low density of training samples in the


06232 [PDF p.160] (half-)cosine regions where Rlung (and Clung ) are located for experiments 3 and 4.


06233 [PDF p.160] Moreover, from (4.21), (4.22), and (4.26), it is apparent that the influence of Rlin


06234 [PDF p.160] and Rquad on the output signals is similar in the linear region and therefore might


06235 [PDF p.160] compensate each other. Comparing the two last columns in Table 4.7, this does


06236 [PDF p.160] indeed seem to be the case.

06238 [PDF p.160] used deterministic ANNs, PBNNs provide a quantification of the uncertainty (in

06240 [PDF p.160] FS yields inaccurate µ̂up θ,pr , the analysis of these inferred standard deviations is


06241 [PDF p.160] limited to those obtained using manual FS, see Table 4.8. Additionally, Figure 4.15

06243 [PDF p.160] values lie inside the tolerances on the reference lung parameter values (10% and 5%


06244 [PDF p.160] for Rlung and Clung , respectively [81]). Furthermore, it is observed from Figure 4.15


06245 [PDF p.160] that the inferred probability distributions lie predominantly inside these tolerance

06426 [PDF p.166] 4.5     Conclusions and recommendations


06427 [PDF p.166] In conclusion, this chapter presents a scalable and efficient method for real-time


06428 [PDF p.166] parameter updating with uncertainty quantification for digital twins, demonstrat-


06429 [PDF p.166] ing significant potential for critical applications such medical ventilation systems.


06430 [PDF p.166]     To achieve this, the Inverse Mapping Parameter Updating (IMPU) method that


06431 [PDF p.166] infers physically-interpretable parameters for a wide range of nonlinear dynamical      4


06432 [PDF p.166] models with negligible online computational effort, has been extended to provide a


06433 [PDF p.166] quantification of the uncertainty. This is achieved by training, in an offline phase,


06434 [PDF p.166] a Probabilistic Bayesian Neural Network (PBNN), that captures both aleatoric


06435 [PDF p.166] and epistemic uncertainty, on simulated data. This methodology is applied on a


06436 [PDF p.166] mechanical ventilation unit for lung patients.


06437 [PDF p.166]     Simulated experiments have shown that the updating parameter values are


06438 [PDF p.166] inferred accurately. The resulting PBNN is, however, found to be slightly un-


06439 [PDF p.166] derconfident in quantifying their corresponding uncertainties when analyzing on


06440 [PDF p.166] simulated data.


06441 [PDF p.166]     For measured experiments, the inferred distributions for the updating parame-


06442 [PDF p.166] ters lie within the tolerance regions (when available) of the true parameter values.


06443 [PDF p.166] Additionally, the magnitude of the inferred uncertainties increases when evalu-


06444 [PDF p.166] ating measurements for which less training samples were employed, highlighting


06445 [PDF p.166] that the PBNN does indeed indicate when it is less certain about its inferred pa-


06446 [PDF p.166] rameter values. Furthermore, it is shown that the inclusion of input parameters


06447 [PDF p.166] (which parameterize the experiment) allows different experiments to be conducted


06448 [PDF p.166] to update parameter values. The updated model is shown to have comparable


06449 [PDF p.166] accuracy as the model parameterized with the known true parameter values of


06450 [PDF p.166] the physical system. The measured signal, however, tends to protrude beyond the


06451 [PDF p.166] inferred 95% signal CI, which is likely related to the fact that the real system is


06452 [PDF p.166] not completely in the model class.


06453 [PDF p.166]     In future research, more attention should be devoted to a quantitative anal-


06454 [PDF p.166] ysis of the inferred uncertainties for measurement data, because this has proven


06455 [PDF p.166] difficult for the current use case. Hence, the methodology should be applied to a


06456 [PDF p.166] use case where the (probability distributions of the) true parameters are known


06457 [PDF p.166] more accurately. Also the influence of (measurement) noise on the inferred param-


06458 [PDF p.166] eter values and corresponding standard deviations requires further investigation.


06459 [PDF p.166] Furthermore, also on simulated data, the accuracy of the inferred (predictive) un-


06460 [PDF p.166] certainties when employing PBNNs can be improved. This is, however, regarded


06461 [PDF p.166] as fundamental research on PBNNs, as this problem is encountered in other liter-


06462 [PDF p.166] ature as well [69, 87, 98]. Finally, the dynamic model, e.g., the structure and/or

06488 [PDF p.170] Abstract - Nonlinear dynamics models derived using First Principles (FPs) often have


06489 [PDF p.170] limited accuracy when compared to the complex physical systems they represent. There-


06490 [PDF p.170] fore, model updating may be employed to improve the accuracy of the FP model. In this


06491 [PDF p.170] work, a machine learning-based updating methodology is proposed where an existing FP


06492 [PDF p.170] model is extended by introducing new states using a subspace encoder (to capture, e.g.,


06493 [PDF p.170] unmodeled modes or parasitic degrees of freedom), and capture their governing dynam-


06494 [PDF p.170] ical equations using a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). Additionally, the retained FP


06495 [PDF p.170] equations of motion are augmented by additional RNNs to capture unmodeled dynamics


06496 [PDF p.170] (e.g. nonlinearities) and account for improper model parameter values. Simultaneously


06497 [PDF p.170] training all neural networks such that an output prediction error-based loss is minimized


06498 [PDF p.170] yields an Extension and Augmentation-based (EA) model that significantly decreases the


06499 [PDF p.170] prediction error with respect to the FP model. This methodology is applied on two use


06500 [PDF p.170] cases, one of which uses measurements performed on an industrial wire bonder. These


06501 [PDF p.170] use cases demonstrate that, also when changes are made to the model/plant parameter


06502 [PDF p.170] values, excitation signals, and controllers, the EA model still shows significant improve-

06522 [PDF p.171]     5.1      Introduction


06523 [PDF p.171]     To achieve the high demands on accuracy and throughput of (high-tech) engineer-


06524 [PDF p.171] 5


06525 [PDF p.171]     ing systems, precise, nonlinear (dynamical) models for accurate response predic-


06526 [PDF p.171]     tion are required. Moreover, for digital twins [64], having an accurate model of a


06527 [PDF p.171]     physical system is of high importance to enable, among others, structural health


06528 [PDF p.171]     monitoring [60], model-based/predictive control, and path planning [94]. Typi-


06529 [PDF p.171]     cally, to model an engineering system, First Principles (FPs, e.g., physical laws)


06530 [PDF p.171]     are utilized. Since the resulting FP models (a type of white-box model) explicitly


06531 [PDF p.171]     contain the underlying physics, they benefit from high interpretability. However,


06532 [PDF p.171]     due to the difficulty in accurately modeling complex (dynamical) systems using


06533 [PDF p.171]     FPs exclusively, often, if not always, mismatches exist between the model and the


06534 [PDF p.171]     physical system. In other words, when the FP model is simulated, the obtained


06535 [PDF p.171]     (dynamical) response behavior is (in the best case slightly) different from the be-


06536 [PDF p.171]     havior measured on the physical system, resulting in a non-zero prediction error,


06537 [PDF p.171]     i.e., the mismatch between measured and simulated output signals.


06538 [PDF p.171]          Consequently, alternative ways to ‘model’ a system have been researched. A


06539 [PDF p.171]     popular type of modeling methods is System Identification (SI), where parameter


06540 [PDF p.171]     values of generic model structures are tuned such that the resulting model best


06541 [PDF p.171]     reproduces data measured on the physical system (for a general introduction on


06542 [PDF p.171]     SI see, e.g., [8, 95, 134]). Since the model is identified directly from measured


06543 [PDF p.171]     data, the resulting models typically have a smaller mismatch with respect to the


06544 [PDF p.171]     measured system. Such SI methods can be divided in methods to identify linear


06545 [PDF p.171]     and nonlinear models. Since the complex (dynamical) effects that cause the afore-


06546 [PDF p.171]     mentioned mismatches are generally nonlinear, we limit our focus to nonlinear


06547 [PDF p.171]     identification/modeling methods.


06548 [PDF p.171]          As mentioned by Ljung [135, 136], the (nonlinear) models obtained via SI are


06549 [PDF p.171]     either Black Box (BB) or Grey Box (GB). Some examples of BB model structures


06550 [PDF p.171]     for SI are, among many others, fuzzy models [116] and neural networks [14, 155,


06551 [PDF p.171]     182] (for an extensive overview, see [198]). These methodologies benefit from an


06552 [PDF p.171] 


06553 [PDF p.172] 5.1. Introduction                                                                145


06554 [PDF p.172] 


06555 [PDF p.172] 


06556 [PDF p.172] elaborate model structure which allows complex (dynamical) relations between


06557 [PDF p.172] variables to be captured. However, this elaborate structure also makes this type


06558 [PDF p.172] of models difficult to interpret.


06559 [PDF p.172]     In contrast, in the case of GB models, prior physical information about the


06560 [PDF p.172] system is embedded in the model structure as much as possible, making them


06561 [PDF p.172] (at least partly) interpretable [136]. Examples of GB identification methods are,


06562 [PDF p.172] among others, Nonlinear Autoregressive (Moving Average) with Exogenous inputs


06563 [PDF p.172] (NAR(MA)X) model structures [20], Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics


06564 [PDF p.172] (SINDy) [34, 35, 89, 90, 184], Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) [176,


06565 [PDF p.172] 216], and free-forming governing differential equations [10, 202]. Some of these GB


06566 [PDF p.172] methodologies, such as the SINDy and free-forming governing equation methods


06567 [PDF p.172] require a full-state measurement, which is unavailable in many practical situations.


06568 [PDF p.172] Moreover, it is emphasized that the interpretability of these GB models is often


06569 [PDF p.172] of a mathematical kind. However, for digital twins, it is preferred to have models      5


06570 [PDF p.172] that are physically interpretable, i.e., the relations between physical properties of


06571 [PDF p.172] the system, such as inertia properties and displacement variables, are of interest


06572 [PDF p.172] and should thus be understood.


06573 [PDF p.172]     To ensure physical interpretability, one can alternatively update an existing


06574 [PDF p.172] FP model. Note that model updating can be regarded as a subclass of GB sys-


06575 [PDF p.172] tem identification, where an initial model structure (in our case based on FPs) is


06576 [PDF p.172] updated using data-based (or machine learning) techniques. Model updating tech-


06577 [PDF p.172] niques begin with an FP model that is then enhanced to retain, at least partially,


06578 [PDF p.172] its physical interpretability. Here, the goal is to reduce the mismatch between


06579 [PDF p.172] the (FP) model and the physical system. Therefore, the methodology proposed


06580 [PDF p.172] here is a form of physics-encoded Machine Learning (ML) [44] (also referred to as


06581 [PDF p.172] data-based hybrid modeling). In general, the mismatches between a model and


06582 [PDF p.172] a physical system may originate from five sources: 1) incorrect model parameter


06583 [PDF p.172] values, e.g., incorrectly estimated stiffness/damping parameter values, 2) missing


06584 [PDF p.172] or incorrectly modeled dynamical effects, e.g., nonlinear behavior of springs or


06585 [PDF p.172] friction effects, 3) missing states and their governing dynamical equations, e.g.,


06586 [PDF p.172] related to unmodeled (flexible) modes, 4) discretization errors, e.g., the use of an


06587 [PDF p.172] overly coarse finite element mesh and excessively large time steps in a simulation,


06588 [PDF p.172] 5) measurement errors, e.g., errors due to incorrect sampling or faulty sensors.


06589 [PDF p.172] In this chapter, we will focus our attention on mismatches originating from the


06590 [PDF p.172] model, i.e., errors in its governing dynamical equations, thereby assuming that the


06591 [PDF p.172] influence of discretization and measurement errors is negligible.


06592 [PDF p.172]     Techniques exist to limit the effects of subsets of these former three mismatch


06593 [PDF p.172] sources. For example, in [28], neural networks are used to augment existing FP


06594 [PDF p.172] models in state-space form by simultaneously correcting for incorrect parameter


06595 [PDF p.172] values and missing/incorrectly modeled dynamical effects. However, this approach


06596 [PDF p.172] does not account for missing states. Alternatively, in Part II of this thesis, the


06597 [PDF p.172]

06601 [PDF p.173]     Inverse Mapping Parameter Updating (IMPU) method was proposed to update


06602 [PDF p.173]     model parameter values online. This method reduces the prediction error of an


06603 [PDF p.173]     FP model by updating the model with parameter values inferred from measured


06604 [PDF p.173]     data. However, as discussed in Chapters 3 and 4, the updated parameter val-


06605 [PDF p.173]     ues (e.g., representing inertial, damping, elastic, and geometrical properties) may


06606 [PDF p.173]     sometimes not represent their true values on a physical system anymore. This


06607 [PDF p.173]     is explained by the observation that these updated parameter values reduce the


06608 [PDF p.173]     mismatches between the model and the physical system not only by correcting


06609 [PDF p.173]     initially incorrect parameter values, but also by addressing errors in the model


06610 [PDF p.173]     structure (e.g., the second and third of the aforementioned mismatch sources). As


06611 [PDF p.173]     a consequence, the physical interpretability of the updated parameters is partially


06612 [PDF p.173]     lost.


06613 [PDF p.173]         Since, in practice, multiple mismatch sources can not be distinguished based


06614 [PDF p.173] 5   on output measurements alone, a methodology that aims at resolving these first


06615 [PDF p.173]     three types of mismatches at the same time is required. To this end, the Extension


06616 [PDF p.173]     and Augmentation-based model updating method (or, in short, EA model updat-


06617 [PDF p.173]     ing) is proposed. Here, extension refers to extending the number of states of the


06618 [PDF p.173]     FP model. Augmentation refers to augmenting the existing state equations with


06619 [PDF p.173]     terms that simultaneously: 1) compensate for incorrect parameter values in the


06620 [PDF p.173]     FP model, and 2) add or correct dynamical effects that are present in the physical


06621 [PDF p.173]     system but are not, or incorrectly, modeled in the FP model.


06622 [PDF p.173]         The proposed EA model updating method is inspired by the Subspace-Encoder


06623 [PDF p.173]     Network (SUBNET) method [12, 14], which uses Recurrent Neural Networks


06624 [PDF p.173]     (RNNs) to identify discrete-time state-space equations for a latent state-space.


06625 [PDF p.173]     Additionally, an encoder (constituted by a feedforward neural network) is used


06626 [PDF p.173]     to define this latent state space. In the training phase, the combination of all


06627 [PDF p.173]     Neural Networks (NNs, i.e., RNNs and encoder) is trained simultaneously to min-


06628 [PDF p.173]     imize the prediction error. Note that, during training, intermediate instances of


06629 [PDF p.173]     the SUBNET model are simulated to minimize this prediction error. The result-


06630 [PDF p.173]     ing SUBNET model in [12, 14], however, is completely BB since the latent state


06631 [PDF p.173]     space does not bear any physical meaning. In contrast, the proposed approach


06632 [PDF p.173]     completely retains the FP model. Consequently, its physical interpretability is


06633 [PDF p.173]     retained as well. By taking the FP model as the basis for model updating, the


06634 [PDF p.173]     to-be-trained NN weights of the EA model can be initialized in such a way that the


06635 [PDF p.173]     dynamics of the FP model are dominant at the start of the training phase. Since


06636 [PDF p.173]     the FP model is retained, this methodology is referred to as a model updating


06637 [PDF p.173]     method. By extending and augmenting the difference equations of the white-box


06638 [PDF p.173]     FP model, a (partly) physically interpretable GB model is obtained with improved


06639 [PDF p.173]     accuracy compared to the FP model.


06640 [PDF p.173]         Furthermore, the proposed model updating method allows models of both sta-


06641 [PDF p.173]     ble and unstable systems to be updated based on data obtained from closed-loop

06676 [PDF p.174] 5.2      Model updating using extension and augmen-


06677 [PDF p.174]          tation


06678 [PDF p.174] As already mentioned, the proposed model updating approach starts from a dy-


06679 [PDF p.174] namical model that has been constructed using first principles. For example, we


06680 [PDF p.174] know from Newton’s second law that, if a mass is excited by some internal or


06681 [PDF p.174] external forces, this directly affects its acceleration. In turn, acceleration induces


06682 [PDF p.174] a change in velocity, and a velocity induces a change in position. This principle


06683 [PDF p.174] is referred to as second-order dynamics, which can be encoded directly in the FP


06684 [PDF p.174] model. In Section 5.2.1, an FP model will be represented in State-Space (SS) form,


06685 [PDF p.174] where the states either represent the position or velocity of system components at


06686 [PDF p.174] some instant of time. By calculating the time derivative of these states for a given


06687 [PDF p.174] dynamical force at some time instant, resulting in velocities and accelerations, and


06688 [PDF p.174] 


06689 [PDF p.175]     148   Chapter 5. Extension and augmentation-based model structure updating


06690 [PDF p.175] 


06691 [PDF p.175] 


06692 [PDF p.175]     integrating these state-derivatives over a small time step, we obtain the state at


06693 [PDF p.175]     the succeeding time instant5.1 . Furthermore, at each instant of time, the predicted


06694 [PDF p.175]     model output, e.g., some positions or velocities of the system that are of interest


06695 [PDF p.175]     to the engineer (and which are, for that reason, typically also measured), is com-


06696 [PDF p.175]     puted from the state values at that time instant. Given some initial conditions


06697 [PDF p.175]     to initialize the states, and repeating this process, the dynamical behavior of the


06698 [PDF p.175]     model is obtained for a time interval consisting of multiple consecutive time steps.


06699 [PDF p.175]         In practice, however, the predicted output may not resemble the output mea-


06700 [PDF p.175]     sured on a physical system with sufficient accuracy due to the presence of model


06701 [PDF p.175]     mismatches (see, e.g., Section 1.3). Therefore, we propose to enhance the existing


06702 [PDF p.175]     FP model using artificial NNs that aim to mitigate these model mismatches. For


06703 [PDF p.175]     example, incorrect parameter values may be compensated for by the added NNs.


06704 [PDF p.175]     Moreover, unmodeled dynamical effects (e.g., the nonlinear behavior of a spring


06705 [PDF p.175] 5   or a missing viscous damper) can be captured using neural networks. In these two


06706 [PDF p.175]     examples, the outputs of the NNs represent a type of internal forcing in the FP


06707 [PDF p.175]     model and can hence be used to augment the existing state derivative equations of


06708 [PDF p.175]     the FP model, i.e., state augmentation is applied. A third type of model mismatch


06709 [PDF p.175]     is missing states. In this case, the physical system exhibits dynamical behavior


06710 [PDF p.175]     that operates on additional, different timescales (or for linear systems; eigenfre-


06711 [PDF p.175]     quencies) than those already present in the FP model. These may be caused by,


06712 [PDF p.175]     among others, flexible dynamics and parasitic degrees of freedom. To account


06713 [PDF p.175]     for this type of model mismatch, completely new states are required, which also


06714 [PDF p.175]     require their own governing dynamical state equations, i.e., state extension is ap-


06715 [PDF p.175]     plied. To this end, again, NNs are employed. Specifically, an encoder NN is used


06716 [PDF p.175]     to find the initial conditions of the extended states, which are required to simulate


06717 [PDF p.175]     the EA model. The governing dynamical state equations are captured by separate


06718 [PDF p.175]     NNs. Here, we have the choice to use physical knowledge and assume that these


06719 [PDF p.175]     equations take on a second-order structure to limit the workload of the neural


06720 [PDF p.175]     network. In this chapter, we indeed will assume a second-order structure for the


06721 [PDF p.175]     extended states. The mathematical structure of the resulting EA model will be


06722 [PDF p.175]     introduced in more detail in Section 5.2.2.


06723 [PDF p.175]         Training the weights and biases of the NNs is achieved my minimizing a cost


06724 [PDF p.175]     function based on the output prediction error, i.e., the error between the output


06725 [PDF p.175]     predicted by the model and the output measured on the physical system. There-


06726 [PDF p.175]     fore, the EA model (with not yet fully-trained weights and biases) is simulated


06727 [PDF p.175]     during training to obtain the predicted output signal for the simulated time in-


06728 [PDF p.175]     terval. Then, gradients are computed and the weights and biases of all NNs are


06729 [PDF p.175]     updated simultaneously using conventional optimization strategies for NNs. In

06756 [PDF p.176]     Finally, in the explanation above, the input to the (open-loop) system was


06757 [PDF p.176] considered to be a force. For controlled (closed-loop) systems, see Figure 5.1, the


06758 [PDF p.176] user-defined reference profile can, however, be regarded as the input. Namely, for a


06759 [PDF p.176] controlled system, the force, which is exerted on the (model of the) actual machine


06760 [PDF p.176] (represented by the EA model in the green box in Figure 5.1), is determined by


06761 [PDF p.176] the reference profile in combination with FeedBack (FB) and/or FeedForward (FF)


06762 [PDF p.176] controllers. The goal of these controllers is to determine the force applied to the


06763 [PDF p.176] model such that the output tracks the reference profile as closely as possible. Here,


06764 [PDF p.176] the FF controller predicts a (model-based) force required on the system to follow


06765 [PDF p.176] the reference profile. Since the FF controller may lack in accuracy and does not


06766 [PDF p.176] account for unknown disturbance forces, the FB controller controls the system


06767 [PDF p.176] in closed-loop to further minimize the tracking error, i.e., the difference between


06768 [PDF p.176] the reference profile and the output. In the following, the proposed methodology


06769 [PDF p.176] is explained in detail, and without loss of generality, for closed-loop controlled


06770 [PDF p.176] systems.

07072 [PDF p.181]     5.2.3     EA model training


07073 [PDF p.181]     To train the weights w1 , w2 , and w3 , standard optimizers for NN training can be


07074 [PDF p.181]     used to minimize a loss (or cost function). This loss is defined as the (weighted)


07075 [PDF p.181]     squared L2 -norm of the output prediction error, i.e., the error between outputs


07076 [PDF p.181]     ȳ measured on the physical system (the overbar ( ¯· ) is used to denote measured


07077 [PDF p.181]     variables) and outputs ŷ obtained by simulating the EA model. In this work, and


07078 [PDF p.181]     inspired by [14, 54, 55], a truncated loss VT is used to improve training stability


07079 [PDF p.181]     [181]. To this end, the training signals of length N ∈ N are divided in to nTW


07080 [PDF p.181]     (overlapping) Truncated Windows (TWs) of length T ∈ N (indicating the number


07081 [PDF p.181]     of time instants within TW). The first time instant of each TW, indicated by


07082 [PDF p.181]     τ ∈ {no + 1, . . . , N − T + 1} (no will be defined a few lines further), is used

07319 [PDF p.185]         When training the EA model, i.e., tuning the weights of the NNs, typically,


07320 [PDF p.185]     batched training is used. This means that, instead of calculating VT for all TWs


07321 [PDF p.185]     (as is done in (5.12)), only a batch containing a random selection of TWs is used.


07322 [PDF p.185]     Then, using standard backpropagation (see [23] for a general introduction on back-


07323 [PDF p.185]     propagation for NNs), the gradients of VT with respect to w0 , w1 , w2 , and w3


07324 [PDF p.185]     are calculated and used to update the weights using an optimizer of choice. Due


07325 [PDF p.185]                            (1) (2)        (3)


07326 [PDF p.185]     to the recurrence of lw1 , lw2 , and lw3 in (5.12), this backpropagation step has to


07327 [PDF p.185]     pass multiple times through these NNs, which are stacked for all time instants


07328 [PDF p.185]     in a TW, as illustrated in Figure 5.4. Consequently, the backpropagation step


07329 [PDF p.185]     involves many consecutive applications of the product/chain differentiation rule.


07330 [PDF p.185]     As a result, gradients may vanish/explode which, if this is the case, causes the


07331 [PDF p.185]     convergence of the training to become slow or even impossible [80] (as mentioned,


07332 [PDF p.185]     the use of TWs already alleviates this issue to some extent). Also note that the


07333 [PDF p.185]     gradients of the FP model and FB controller equations (in (5.1) and (5.3)) should


07334 [PDF p.185]     be available. Hence, the retained FP model and FB controller must be differen-


07335 [PDF p.185]     tiable with respect to the variables, e.g., in our case, (5.1) should be differentiable


07336 [PDF p.185]     with respect to xk and uk , and (5.3) should be differentiable with respect to xFB  k


07337 [PDF p.185]     and y k .

07366 [PDF p.186] 5.3      Application to use cases


07367 [PDF p.186] In this section, the proposed methodology is applied to two use cases. The first


07368 [PDF p.186] use case, discussed in Section 5.3.1, involves a linear academic demonstrator where


07369 [PDF p.186] measurements are obtained by simulating a known plant model. At first glance,


07370 [PDF p.186] using an NN-based methodology to update such a simple system might appear


07371 [PDF p.186] unnecessarily complex, especially when the plant dynamics are known to be lin-


07372 [PDF p.186] ear. However, the linear use case allows us to evaluate the extrapolation capa-


07373 [PDF p.186] bilities of the updated model (outside the training data/frequencies) in terms of


07374 [PDF p.186] Frequency Response Functions (FRFs). Here, the extrapolation capabilities of


07375 [PDF p.186] the EA model benefit from the presence of the retained FP terms, in contrast to


07376 [PDF p.186] black-box methodologies. The second use case, discussed in Section 5.3.2, involves


07377 [PDF p.186] a (nonlinear) industrial wire bonder system which is updated based on closed-


07378 [PDF p.186] loop measurements obtained from a physical wire bonder. A comparison of the


07379 [PDF p.186] differences in key characteristics of these two use cases is provided in Table 5.1.


07380 [PDF p.186]     Note that, in Sections 5.3.1 and 5.3.2, the definition of the losses used to evalu-


07381 [PDF p.186] ate the accuracy of the updated/identified models (for the training, validation, and


07382 [PDF p.186] testing signals) will be different from the definition used in the training process of


07383 [PDF p.186] the EA model (for training and cross-validation), i.e., VT in (5.12). The primary


07384 [PDF p.186] reason for this is that summing over all nTW TWs and hence simulating the EA


07385 [PDF p.186] model as many times during training and validation (just to calculate the train-


07386 [PDF p.186] ing/validation losses) is expensive and significantly increases the training time.


07387 [PDF p.186] Please note that the training time includes the validation step since validation is

07521 [PDF p.189]     5.3.1.2    Training process


07522 [PDF p.189]     In this section, EA model updating is employed to update the FP model. To this


07523 [PDF p.189]     end, the plant model is excited using a multisine signal of length N = 5000 as


07524 [PDF p.189]     input ū. This multisine consists of seven frequencies (all with random phases)


07525 [PDF p.189]     among which are the resonance and anti-resonance frequencies of the (known)


07526 [PDF p.189]     plant, see Table 5.35.5 . Then, EA models are trained by updating the FP model


07527 [PDF p.189]     using the EA model updating theory in Section 5.2.3, with next = {0, 2, 6}. For


07528 [PDF p.189]     comparison, a SUBNET model (which is fully black-box) is trained following the


07529 [PDF p.189]     SUBNET approach [14], i.e., without the initial FP model and without an imposed


07530 [PDF p.189]     second-order structure. For the SUBNET model we choose next = 4, such that


07531 [PDF p.189]     the total number of states equals 4, i.e., the same total number of states as the


07532 [PDF p.189]     true plant and as the EA model with next = 2. Hyperparameter values, e.g., the


07533 [PDF p.189]     learning rate, NN topology, and weight initialization, used to train the EA and


07534 [PDF p.189]     SUBNET models are manually tuned (individually for each method) and provided


07535 [PDF p.189]     in Appendix D.3.

07537 [PDF p.189]     calculating the validation loss. Here, the validation loss is calculated using (5.14),


07538 [PDF p.189]     where the EA/SUBNET models are excited with a new multisine signal of length

07686 [PDF p.193]         Finally, it is remarked that, in theory, the extension and augmentation terms of


07687 [PDF p.193]     the EA model are completely independent from the FP terms. However, since the


07688 [PDF p.193]     model is trained while retaining the terms from a specific FP model, the trained


07689 [PDF p.193]     NNs may potentially depend on these FP terms. As a result, the extension and


07690 [PDF p.193]     augmentation terms might (partially) negate the FP terms, which is a phenomenon


07691 [PDF p.193]     referred to as ‘negation’. Negation is undesirable, because the RNN-related terms


07692 [PDF p.193]     should only take account of missing dynamics and/or (small) corrections to the FP


07693 [PDF p.193]     model instead of canceling (parts of) the FP model and reconstructing the canceled


07694 [PDF p.193]     (parts of the) FP model. Consequently, it is advised to, in future work, get a better


07695 [PDF p.193]     understanding of this concept and investigate approaches to mitigate its effects.

07717 [PDF p.194] 5.3.2     Nonlinear industrial use case


07718 [PDF p.194] In this section, the EA model updating method is applied to the three-dimensional


07719 [PDF p.194] motion stage of a high-tech industrial wire bonder developed and manufactured


07720 [PDF p.194] by ASMPT [7]. In Section 5.3.2.1, the (physical) system and its FP model are


07721 [PDF p.194] introduced. Then, in Section 5.3.2.2, the training procedure for the EA model


07722 [PDF p.194] is discussed. Finally, Section 5.3.2.3, discusses the obtained results, including a


07723 [PDF p.194] qualitative comparison with an attempt to obtain a purely data-based model via


07724 [PDF p.194] the SUBNET method [14].


07725 [PDF p.194]

07728 [PDF p.194] other electronic components using thin golden wires. This process is achieved

07749 [PDF p.195]     the wire bonder consists of four stacked bodies: a base frame, and an X-, Y-,


07750 [PDF p.195]     and Z-stage. Each stage allows for the motion of the point of interest (indicated


07751 [PDF p.195]     in Figure 5.9) along one specific axis. The motion in each direction is measured


07752 [PDF p.195]     using encoders at the interfaces between the stages and controlled using FB and


07753 [PDF p.195]     FF control to (accurately) follow a position reference profile. Note that the vertical


07754 [PDF p.195]     motion of the point of interest is achieved by rotation of the Z-stage around a pivot


07755 [PDF p.195]     point instead of translation.


07756 [PDF p.195]         As the FP model of this system, a 3-DoFs multibody model is employed, where


07757 [PDF p.195]     each body represents one stage, and the base frame is assumed to be the fixed


07758 [PDF p.195]     world. A schematic overview of this system is provided in Figure 5.10. The


07759 [PDF p.195]     discrete-time EoMs of the FP model are given in Appendix D.2.2. Since sensor time


07760 [PDF p.195]     delays (which are fractional in terms of ∆t) are encountered on the physical setup,


07761 [PDF p.195]     for the FP model, these time delays are approximated using linear interpolation

07977 [PDF p.201]     random initialization of the SUBNET model at the start of training, which, in


07978 [PDF p.201]     closed-loop, is prone to instability. Even if the initial model is stable by chance,


07979 [PDF p.201]     the closed-loop system may easily become unstable during training. Due to the


07980 [PDF p.201]     instability, output values can become (virtually) infinite, which makes gradient


07981 [PDF p.201]     computation in the backpropagation step impossible, thereby making it futile to


07982 [PDF p.201]     update the NN weights. In contrast, the EA model updating procedure is initial-


07983 [PDF p.201]     ized with an FP model that is typically stable in closed loop. Furthermore, if the


07984 [PDF p.201]     discrepancy between the FP model and the true plant is comparatively small, it


07985 [PDF p.201]     is generally valid to assume that the EA model is unlikely to become unstable in


07986 [PDF p.201]     closed-loop during training for the current use case.


07987 [PDF p.201]     Remark 5.6 Instead of identifying the SUBNET model by simulating the closed-loop


07988 [PDF p.201]     system, one might try to identify the open-loop system, as is done in [13] for the electro-


07989 [PDF p.201]     mechanical positioning system benchmark (see [83] for a detailed description of this


07990 [PDF p.201]     benchmark). To this end, input-output data are measured in a closed-loop experiment


07991 [PDF p.201]     and used to identify the open-loop system, i.e., without embedding the controller in the


07992 [PDF p.201]     training process. This open-loop approach has also been attempted for the wire bonder


07993 [PDF p.201]     use case, but was unsuccessful. As discussed in [208], this issue may be explained by the


07994 [PDF p.201]     fact that identification of systems based on input-output data measured in closed-loop


07995 [PDF p.201]     is prone to suffer from noise-induced biases caused by correlation between the input and


07996 [PDF p.201]     the output measurement noise and the integration action in the FB controller.

08001 [PDF p.202] 5.3.2.3     Test results


08002 [PDF p.202] In this section, we assess the accuracy of the trained EA model(s) on test data.


08003 [PDF p.202] Here, we will primarily focus on the EA model with next = 14, which performs


08004 [PDF p.202] best among the trained EA models.


08005 [PDF p.202]     We begin by evaluating the simulation behavior using a reference profile that


08006 [PDF p.202] consists of a concatenation of the training and validation reference signals. In


08007 [PDF p.202] Figure 5.12, the signals obtained by simulating the FP model and the EA model


08008 [PDF p.202] (with next = 14) are compared to each other and to the measured system response.


08009 [PDF p.202] Here, it is clearly visible that the EA model resembles the measured system sig-


08010 [PDF p.202] nificantly better than the FP model for all output signals. In addition, in the


08011 [PDF p.202] bottom row of plots in Figure 5.12 (which contain zoomed-in parts of the top row


08012 [PDF p.202] of plots), the (scaled) settling error bounds used by the industrial company are


08013 [PDF p.202] plotted. These bounds indicate the maximum allowed deviation (after some set-


08014 [PDF p.202]                                                                                             5


08015 [PDF p.202] tling time) from the reference signal for proper operation of the wire bonder, and


08016 [PDF p.202] thus provide insight into the required accuracy of the model of the physical system.


08017 [PDF p.202] For certain instants of time, the FP model incorrectly predicts that the system


08018 [PDF p.202] is outside the settling bounds, while the measured system and the EA model are


08019 [PDF p.202] within these bounds (and vice versa). In other words, the FP model can not be


08020 [PDF p.202] used to accurately assess the real settling behavior of the physical system, while


08021 [PDF p.202] the EA model is (much better) suited to serve this purpose. Consequently, the FP


08022 [PDF p.202] model may lead to incorrect decisions, e.g., on controller tuning, highlighting one


08023 [PDF p.202] of the advantages of the EA model. Please note that, for the Z-signal, the settling


08024 [PDF p.202] bounds are not provided since the requirements of the Z-stage are more complex


08025 [PDF p.202] due to the specifics of the actual wire bonding.

08192 [PDF p.207]     5.4      Conclusions and recommendations


08193 [PDF p.207]     To decrease the mismatch between a physical system and its digital twin (or


08194 [PDF p.207]     model), the Extension and Augmentation-based (EA) model updating method is


08195 [PDF p.207]     proposed. This method extends the number of states in the dynamical equations


08196 [PDF p.207]     of a First Principles (FP) model and augments the already existing dynamical


08197 [PDF p.207]     equations by employing (recurrent) neural networks, while retaining the original


08198 [PDF p.207]     FP model terms. The neural networks are trained by minimizing a truncated


08199 [PDF p.207]     output prediction error loss, inspired by the black-box subspace-encoder network


08200 [PDF p.207]     (SUBNET) approach [14].

08253 [PDF p.209]     combinations of reference trajectories and controllers, of which three test scenarios

08255 [PDF p.209]     continued to exhibit significant improvement over the FP model in terms of predic-


08256 [PDF p.209]     tion error, indicating good generalization capabilities of the EA model. Unlike the


08257 [PDF p.209]     SUBNET approach, the EA model facilitates model updating based on closed-loop


08258 [PDF p.209]     data through stabilizing closed-loop simulations by (approximately) initializing the


08259 [PDF p.209]     model as the FP model. For the SUBNET approach, such smart initialization is


08260 [PDF p.209]     not possible and random initialization has to be used instead. This random initial-


08261 [PDF p.209]     ization, however, causes the initialized SUBNET model to be unstable in closed


08262 [PDF p.209]     loop, which hinders the SUBNET model to be trained properly.

08264 [PDF p.209]     states without the imposed second-order structure could be added to better accom-

08272 [PDF p.210] it is expected that results can be improved further by optimizing the experiment

08277 [PDF p.210] systems that are controlled using sampled data that necessitate zero-order hold

08281 [PDF p.210] using the encoder, limiting the EA model’s use in simulations where the initial


08282 [PDF p.210] values of extended states, representing non-physical or non-measurable variables,


08283 [PDF p.210] are unknown. Studies to find a solution to this issue or to investigate the im-


08284 [PDF p.210] pact of incorrect initial values for the extended states are therefore encouraged.


08285 [PDF p.210] Furthermore, instead of compensating for incorrect FP model parameter values           5


08286 [PDF p.210] via the augmented RNNs, the parameter values in the FP model can be made


08287 [PDF p.210] variable and tuned directly (possibly with regularization) within the optimization


08288 [PDF p.210] problem as is done in, e.g., [28]. Moreover, as mentioned in Remark 5.2, investigat-


08289 [PDF p.210] ing methodologies to enforce orthogonality between the extended and augmented


08290 [PDF p.210] terms on the one hand, and the FP terms on the other hand, i.e., dynamical terms


08291 [PDF p.210] already captured in the FP model should not be (partially) covered again by the


08292 [PDF p.210] extended and augmented model terms, could enhance physical interpretability.


08293 [PDF p.210] Additionally, enforcing this orthogonality may aid in preventing negation, which


08294 [PDF p.210] in itself is a concept that requires attention in future research. Recall from Sec-


08295 [PDF p.210] tion 5.3.1.3 that negation is the phenomenon where the trained NNs may depend


08296 [PDF p.210] on the FP terms used to train those NNs and (partly) negate those FP terms.


08297 [PDF p.210] This dependency makes it less ideal to update parameter values of the FP terms


08298 [PDF p.210] online (using, e.g., the inverse mapping parameter updating method introduced in


08299 [PDF p.210] Part II) without potential consequences. Finally, future research may be devoted


08300 [PDF p.210] to obtaining sparse mathematical representations of the trained RNNs to obtain


08301 [PDF p.210] improved mathematical (or even physical) insight. This could allow to update,


08302 [PDF p.210] in addition to parameter values of the FP terms, a relatively small set of model


08303 [PDF p.210] parameter values related to the extended and augmented terms, using online pa-

08316 [PDF p.214] 6.1     Conclusions


08317 [PDF p.214] In this thesis, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based model updating techniques for non-


08318 [PDF p.214] linear dynamical systems are developed. Updating models is especially relevant for


08319 [PDF p.214] digital twins of contemporary engineering systems, as it enables the use of accu-


08320 [PDF p.214] rate models for, among others, model-based control and structural/machine health


08321 [PDF p.214] monitoring, without the risk of damaging expensive real-world systems. Special


08322 [PDF p.214] focus has been directed towards employing physics-enhanced Machine Learning


08323 [PDF p.214] (ML) techniques for model updating to combine the benefits of (physics-based)


08324 [PDF p.214] FP modeling and data-driven ML techniques. Challenges for model updating were


08325 [PDF p.214] discussed in Chapter 1, where its application to digital twins was emphasized. In


08326 [PDF p.214] this thesis, a distinction is made between updating model parameter values (on-


08327 [PDF p.214] line) and updating the structure of models that have been constructed using first


08328 [PDF p.214] principles.


08329 [PDF p.214]     In model parameter updating for digital twins, parameter values should be


08330 [PDF p.214] updated online with minimal computational effort such that up-to-date param-


08331 [PDF p.214] eter values are available and can be used as a basis for, e.g., (machine) health


08332 [PDF p.214] monitoring. When a model that is based on First Principles (FPs) is updated, the


08333 [PDF p.214] parameter values are physically interpretable, greatly aiding the operator/engineer


08334 [PDF p.214] in understanding the condition of the physical system, which benefits the decision-


08335 [PDF p.214] 


08336 [PDF p.215]     188                                  Chapter 6. Conclusions and recommendations


08337 [PDF p.215] 


08338 [PDF p.215] 


08339 [PDF p.215]     making process. To allow parameter values of nonlinear dynamical models to be


08340 [PDF p.215]     updated, features that are highly informative about the condition of the system


08341 [PDF p.215]     need to be extracted from measured output responses. Furthermore, as (physics-


08342 [PDF p.215]     guided) ML-based methods are exploited to update model parameter values, it


08343 [PDF p.215]     is especially relevant to include quantifications of the uncertainty in the updated


08344 [PDF p.215]     parameter values such that the operator can assess the level of trust to have in


08345 [PDF p.215]     these parameter values. The presence of other sources of mismatches (between


08346 [PDF p.215]     a physical system and its model) than incorrect parameter values, may, however,


08347 [PDF p.215]     limit the efficacy of the parameter updating method when applied to real-world


08348 [PDF p.215]     systems.


08349 [PDF p.215]         To address mismatches arising from both incorrect parameter values and an


08350 [PDF p.215]     incorrect or incomplete model structure, which are common in engineering systems,


08351 [PDF p.215]     model structure updating methods need to be developed. Such model updating


08352 [PDF p.215]     methods should be able to simultaneously mitigate model errors originating from


08353 [PDF p.215]     incorrect parameter values, incorrectly modeled or unmodeled dynamical effects,


08354 [PDF p.215]     and unmodeled states. Again, one of the main challenges in such methods is to


08355 [PDF p.215] 6   ensure physical interpretability of (parts of) the updated model as this greatly


08356 [PDF p.215]     benefits the model’s applicability as a digital twin. To this end, physics-encoded


08357 [PDF p.215]     ML can be used, in which an FP model is retained and enhanced using ML-


08358 [PDF p.215]     techniques that are fed by data measured on the physical system. Furthermore,


08359 [PDF p.215]     to enable applicability of the model structure updating method to a broad class


08360 [PDF p.215]     of engineering systems, it should be applicable to both open-loop and closed-loop


08361 [PDF p.215]     systems.


08362 [PDF p.215]         Based on these challenges, the general research objective of this thesis was


08363 [PDF p.215]     formulated in Chapter 1:


08364 [PDF p.215] 


08365 [PDF p.215] 


08366 [PDF p.215]           Develop model updating techniques for digital twins for (nonlinear) dynam-


08367 [PDF p.215]           ical systems that maintain physical interpretability of the original first prin-


08368 [PDF p.215]           ciples model and increase its accuracy with respect to a physical system.


08369 [PDF p.215] 


08370 [PDF p.215]         To address this general research objective, the contributions of this thesis has


08371 [PDF p.215]     been divided into two parts: online model parameter updating and model structure


08372 [PDF p.215]     updating.


08373 [PDF p.215]         In Chapter 2 in Part II of this thesis, the core methodology for online model


08374 [PDF p.215]     parameter updating proposed in this thesis is presented. This methodology is


08375 [PDF p.215]     based on an Inverse Mapping Model (IMM) that infers a set of updating param-


08376 [PDF p.215]     eter values from a set of features that is extracted from output response data.


08377 [PDF p.215]     Consequently, this methodology is referred to as the Inverse Mapping Parameter


08378 [PDF p.215]     Updating (IMPU) method. The IMM employed in this method is constituted by


08379 [PDF p.215]     a (deterministic) Artificial Neural Network (ANN). This ANN is trained in an

08382 [PDF p.216] 


08383 [PDF p.216] 


08384 [PDF p.216] offline phase using simulated data consisting of known parameter values and their


08385 [PDF p.216] corresponding features that are extracted from the simulated output responses.


08386 [PDF p.216] Afterwards, in the online phase, similar features are extracted from measured out-


08387 [PDF p.216] put responses to infer, with negligible online computational cost, parameter val-


08388 [PDF p.216] ues corresponding to the momentary physical system’s condition. Different types


08389 [PDF p.216] of features can be extracted, where physical knowledge, such as known relevant


08390 [PDF p.216] frequency ranges, can be leveraged to increase the information density of these


08391 [PDF p.216] features. This increased informativeness improves the accuracy of the inferred


08392 [PDF p.216] parameter values and the computational efficiency in both the offline and online


08393 [PDF p.216] phase. One of the key advantages of this updating method is that it shifts the


08394 [PDF p.216] vast majority of the computation time from the online phase to the offline phase,


08395 [PDF p.216] allowing for (near) real-time parameter updating in the former. Furthermore, due


08396 [PDF p.216] to the sole use of the mapping between output response features and parameter


08397 [PDF p.216] values, the method is highly versatile, allowing for application on systems mod-


08398 [PDF p.216] eled using commercial software without direct access to the explicit (differential)


08399 [PDF p.216] equations representing the model. Additionally, a wide range of parameters can


08400 [PDF p.216] be updated, among which are physically interpretable parameters that, when up-         6


08401 [PDF p.216] dated, provide valuable insight about the system’s condition to the engineer. In


08402 [PDF p.216] Chapter 2, the IMPU method is applied on two simulated nonlinear use cases,


08403 [PDF p.216] where accurate parameter values are inferred with online computation times in


08404 [PDF p.216] the order of milliseconds. The IMM is also shown to generalize well and infer pa-


08405 [PDF p.216] rameter values with reasonable (yet reduced) accuracy (moderately) outside the


08406 [PDF p.216] space for which the ANN was trained.


08407 [PDF p.216]      In Chapter 3, the IMPU method is enhanced by selecting a small set of rela-


08408 [PDF p.216] tively informative (with respect to the updating parameter values) features from a


08409 [PDF p.216] large set of extracted features. Advantages of using Feature Selection (FS) are that


08410 [PDF p.216] it improves the accuracy of the inferred parameter values (by omitting, e.g., noise-


08411 [PDF p.216] dominated) features, and that it decreases offline and online computation times


08412 [PDF p.216] since the input layer of the employed ANN is smaller. Additionally, Bayesian


08413 [PDF p.216] optimization-based hyperparameter tuning is employed, where, among others, it


08414 [PDF p.216] is shown that also the number of neurons in the hidden layers of the ANN may


08415 [PDF p.216] be reduced when only a small set of informative features is selected. The pro-


08416 [PDF p.216] posed approach is employed to update parameter values of a (nonlinear) model


08417 [PDF p.216] of a wire bonder used in the back-end semiconductor manufacturing industry us-


08418 [PDF p.216] ing data measured on a real-world wire bonder. The updated model is compared


08419 [PDF p.216] to a reference model of which the parameter values are either determined based


08420 [PDF p.216] on engineering knowledge or manually tuned using frequency response functions.


08421 [PDF p.216] The updated model is shown to outperform the reference model in terms of output


08422 [PDF p.216] prediction errors with respect to the measured system. Also for reference trajecto-


08423 [PDF p.216] ries that are distinct from the training experiment, significant improvement of the


08424 [PDF p.216] updated model over the reference model is observed, showing good generalization

08429 [PDF p.217]     capabilities of the updated model. Although the signals simulated using the up-


08430 [PDF p.217]     dated model resemble the signals measured on the physical system relatively well,


08431 [PDF p.217]     some of the updated parameter values do not seem to agree with their (expected)
