08436 [PDF p.217]          Chapter 4 extends the IMPU method by including Uncertainty Quantification


08437 [PDF p.217]     (UQ). It does so by employing a Probabilistic Bayesian Neural Network (PBNN)


08438 [PDF p.217]     instead of the originally used deterministic ANN to infer, for each updating pa-


08439 [PDF p.217]     rameter, a probability distribution instead of a deterministic value. By employing


08440 [PDF p.217]     a PBNN, both the uncertainty in the training/measurement data (aleatoric uncer-


08441 [PDF p.217]     tainty) and in the trained model (epistemic uncertainty) are taken into account.


08442 [PDF p.217]     Having a quantification of the uncertainty is highly valuable in model parameter


08443 [PDF p.217]     updating since it gives an indication of the level of trust a user of the model should


08444 [PDF p.217]     have in the updated parameter values. This is especially valuable when machine


08445 [PDF p.217] 6   learning-based methods are employed as is the case in the IMPU method. Further-


08446 [PDF p.217]     more, this chapter proposes to include so-called input parameters, that represent


08447 [PDF p.217]     user-controlled adjustable system or experiment settings, as additional inputs to


08448 [PDF p.217]     the PBNN. As such, the trained IMM can be utilized in applications where sys-


08449 [PDF p.217]     tem or experiment settings may change during operation, thereby broadening the


08450 [PDF p.217]     method’s applicability in an online context. An application to a real-world medical


08451 [PDF p.217]     mechanical ventilation setup is used to demonstrate the quantification of the un-


08452 [PDF p.217]     certainty in the updated parameter values obtained using the IMPU method. Here,


08453 [PDF p.217]     the inferred updating parameter value distributions are demonstrated to lie within


08454 [PDF p.217]     the tolerance regions (when available) of the true parameter values. Furthermore,


08455 [PDF p.217]     the simulated responses obtained with the updated model are comparable to sim-


08456 [PDF p.217]     ulated responses obtained with the model parameterized using the true parameter


08457 [PDF p.217]     values (which, in practice, are not available but are, for this use case, known within


08458 [PDF p.217]     certain tolerances), and accurately resemble the measured responses.


08459 [PDF p.217]          In Chapter 5 in Part III of this thesis, a model structure updating method


08460 [PDF p.217]     has been proposed. This updating method aims at simultaneously mitigating mis-


08461 [PDF p.217]     matches between a physical system and its model that originate from incorrect


08462 [PDF p.217]     model parameter values, unmodeled or incorrectly modeled dynamical terms, and


08463 [PDF p.217]     missing states. To address this challenge, a physics-encoded approach is adopted


08464 [PDF p.217]     where a (white-box) model that was constructed using FPs is updated (and hence


08465 [PDF p.217]     retained) by augmenting it with additional dynamical terms and extending it


08466 [PDF p.217]     with additional states and their governing dynamical equations. These augmented


08467 [PDF p.217]     terms and the equations governing the extended states are modeled using (black-


08468 [PDF p.217]     box) feedforward Neural Networks (NNs) that are used recurrently when simulat-


08469 [PDF p.217]     ing a system, and are therefore referred to as recurrent neural networks. To find

08477 [PDF p.218] Augmentation-based (EA) model structure updating method is applied on two


08478 [PDF p.218] use cases. The first use case is a linear open-loop academic use case, where the


08479 [PDF p.218] (grey-box) EA model is demonstrated to outperform a similar black-box method


08480 [PDF p.218] in accuracy beyond the training range, which is a result of the robustness that


08481 [PDF p.218] is facilitated by the retained FP model terms. Moreover, the convergence during


08482 [PDF p.218] training of the grey-box model to the best performing configuration is much more


08483 [PDF p.218] robust compared to the black-box model, where the best performing configuration


08484 [PDF p.218] seems to be found (more or less) by coincidence. For the second use case, the


08485 [PDF p.218] EA-based model updating method is applied on a real-world industrial wire bon-


08486 [PDF p.218] der, that exhibits nonlinear dynamics. To this end, measurements are obtained in


08487 [PDF p.218] closed loop. The predictive capacity of the trained EA model to simulate, e.g., the


08488 [PDF p.218] settling behavior of the system, shows a significant improvement compared to the


08489 [PDF p.218] original FP model. Furthermore, in contrast to a similar black-box method, the


08490 [PDF p.218] proposed approach makes it possible to update an (unstable open-loop) system            6


08491 [PDF p.218] by simulating it in closed loop with a (stabilizing) feedback controller. The EA


08492 [PDF p.218] model is also utilized to predict the behavior of the physical wire bonder for mod-


08493 [PDF p.218] ified reference trajectories and controllers with respect to those used for training.


08494 [PDF p.218] Even in this case, the EA model exhibits a significant improvement in terms of


08495 [PDF p.218] prediction accuracy compared to the FP model. This highlights the suitability of


08496 [PDF p.218] the EA model to be used for controller design, allowing for enhancement of the


08497 [PDF p.218] performance of the physical system, e.g., in terms of throughput and positioning


08498 [PDF p.218] accuracy.


08499 [PDF p.218]     Summarizing, for a digital twin to fulfill its potential, the (FP) model that


08500 [PDF p.218] constitutes the digital twin should be an accurate representation of the physical


08501 [PDF p.218] system it represents. To reduce the ever-existing mismatches between the model


08502 [PDF p.218] and the physical system, the (FP) model can be updated, i.e., improved, based on


08503 [PDF p.218] data measured on the physical system. In this thesis, two methodologies are de-


08504 [PDF p.218] veloped to update nonlinear dynamical models, where both methodologies exploit


08505 [PDF p.218] physics-enhanced ML to retain physical interpretability of the original FP model.


08506 [PDF p.218] The first methodology focuses on updating model parameter values online to allow


08507 [PDF p.218] for, among others, (machine) health monitoring. The second methodology aims at


08508 [PDF p.218] updating the model structure by augmenting existing dynamical equations and,


08509 [PDF p.218] in addition, extending them by adding new states. As a result, a higher fidelity


08510 [PDF p.218] model is obtained which significantly improves the predictive capacity compared


08511 [PDF p.218] to the original FP model. To conclude, this thesis thus provides model updating


08512 [PDF p.218] tools that ensure that the model of a digital twin is an accurate representation of


08513 [PDF p.218] its physical counterpart and remains so throughout its operational life.


08514 [PDF p.218] 


08515 [PDF p.219]     192                              Chapter 6. Conclusions and recommendations


08516 [PDF p.219] 


08517 [PDF p.219] 


08518 [PDF p.219]     6.2     Recommendations


08519 [PDF p.219]     In this final section, recommendations for future research related to the proposed


08520 [PDF p.219]     model parameter and model structure updating methodologies are discussed.


08521 [PDF p.219]         Starting with the (online) IMPU method discussed in Part II, several oppor-


08522 [PDF p.219]     tunities for further improvement of the methodology are recognized:


08523 [PDF p.219] 


08524 [PDF p.219]       • Excitation design: In the applications shown in this thesis, only little


08525 [PDF p.219]         attention has been paid to excitation design, i.e., the design of the input


08526 [PDF p.219]         signals for open-loop systems or of the reference trajectories for closed-loop


08527 [PDF p.219]         systems. For the industrial use cases, rather the reference trajectories in-


08528 [PDF p.219]         tended for conventional operation of the machines were used. By exciting


08529 [PDF p.219]         the system in such a way that the system’s response is highly sensitive to


08530 [PDF p.219]         (changes in) the parameter values, it is expected that the accuracy of the


08531 [PDF p.219]         updated parameter values can be enhanced. In an online setting, care should


08532 [PDF p.219]         be taken, however, that the use of optimized excitations does not interfere


08533 [PDF p.219]         with the application of the methodology during operation of the system. For


08534 [PDF p.219] 6       example, periods in which the system is idle (if available) may be employed


08535 [PDF p.219]         to use some optimized excitations on the system to update the parameter


08536 [PDF p.219]         values with improved accuracy.


08537 [PDF p.219] 


08538 [PDF p.219]       • Accuracy of uncertainty quantification: As already discussed at the


08539 [PDF p.219]         end of Chapter 4, more research on the verification of the accuracy of the


08540 [PDF p.219]         uncertainties in the updated parameter values estimated by a PBNN is re-


08541 [PDF p.219]         quired. For example, the IMPU method may be employed to use cases with


08542 [PDF p.219]         a more regulated environment where (the probability distributions of) the


08543 [PDF p.219]         true parameter values are known more accurately. Also when applying the


08544 [PDF p.219]         PBNNs on simulated data, room for improvement for the accuracy of the un-


08545 [PDF p.219]         certainties estimated by the PBNN is observed. Note that this is considered


08546 [PDF p.219]         to be more fundamental research on PBNNs as this issue was also observed


08547 [PDF p.219]         in literature [69, 87, 98].


08548 [PDF p.219] 


08549 [PDF p.219]       • Semi-supervised learning: Semi-supervised learning [211, 228] may be


08550 [PDF p.219]         employed to train an IMM. In the IMPU context, semi-supervised learn-


08551 [PDF p.219]         ing could be a mix of supervised learning using labeled data, i.e., pairs of


08552 [PDF p.219]         parameter values and simulated features, and unsupervised learning with un-


08553 [PDF p.219]         labeled data, i.e., only measured features without their corresponding ‘true’


08554 [PDF p.219]         parameter values as these are generally not known on the physical system.


08555 [PDF p.219]         Here, the idea is that by feeding measured features (without corresponding


08556 [PDF p.219]         parameter values) to the IMM during training, the IMM can be made aware


08557 [PDF p.219]         of possible model structure errors or other errors that do not originate from


08558 [PDF p.219]         incorrect parameter values but do affect the measured features. This may


08559 [PDF p.219] 


08560 [PDF p.220] 6.2. Recommendations                                                              193


08561 [PDF p.220] 


08562 [PDF p.220] 


08563 [PDF p.220]      be especially valuable when a PBNN is used as IMM, as the PBNN may use


08564 [PDF p.220]      this awareness in its estimates for the uncertainty.


08565 [PDF p.220] 


08566 [PDF p.220]   • Application to other domains/disciplines: Although, in this thesis,


08567 [PDF p.220]     the IMPU method has only been applied to systems from a single physical


08568 [PDF p.220]     domain, in theory, the methodology is also applicable to multi-physical do-


08569 [PDF p.220]     mains and other disciplines where dynamic parametrized models are used.


08570 [PDF p.220]     Therefore, applications and potential limitations in other (multi-)physical


08571 [PDF p.220]     domains and disciplines may be explored. For example, the computational


08572 [PDF p.220]     cost of complex fluid dynamics models may make offline data generation too


08573 [PDF p.220]     expensive.


08574 [PDF p.220]    For the EA model structure updating method proposed in Part III of this


08575 [PDF p.220] thesis, also several opportunities to enhance the accuracy and applicability of the


08576 [PDF p.220] method are recognized:


08577 [PDF p.220]   • Excitation design: Similar to the IMPU method, excitation design for the


08578 [PDF p.220]     experiment used to update the model should be investigated. Especially since


08579 [PDF p.220]     the EA model updating method is not intended for online application, the             6


08580 [PDF p.220]     system’s excitation can be optimized with limited constraints. For example,


08581 [PDF p.220]     a broader range of frequencies could be excited by using (colored) noise to


08582 [PDF p.220]     train the model for a wider range of frequencies.


08583 [PDF p.220] 


08584 [PDF p.220]   • Tune FP parameters: In the current methodology, incorrect FP model


08585 [PDF p.220]     parameter values are compensated by the augmenting RNNs. However, it


08586 [PDF p.220]     might be easier and more insightful to directly tune these parameter values


08587 [PDF p.220]     within the optimization problem. Note that this approach is already used in


08588 [PDF p.220]     [28] (which, however, lacks state extension).


08589 [PDF p.220] 


08590 [PDF p.220]   • Inclusion of first-order dynamics: For the applications in Chapter 5, it


08591 [PDF p.220]     was assumed that all missing states are related to second-order dynamics.


08592 [PDF p.220]     Consequently, a second-order structure was imposed on the extended states.


08593 [PDF p.220]     In practice, various dynamical phenomena exist that are described by first-


08594 [PDF p.220]     order dynamics, e.g., elasto-plastic or viscoelastic effects that require internal


08595 [PDF p.220]     states, or thermoelastic effects. Therefore, implementations where not all


08596 [PDF p.220]     extended states have an imposed second-order form may be able to more


08597 [PDF p.220]     accurately capture such first-order effects.


08598 [PDF p.220] 


08599 [PDF p.220]   • Continuous time: To enhance applicability of the method and reduce the


08600 [PDF p.220]     effect of temporal discretization errors, the EA model updating method may


08601 [PDF p.220]     be extended to continuous-time models. For the similar (black-box) sub-


08602 [PDF p.220]     space encoder network (SUBNET) method, this has already been researched


08603 [PDF p.220]     successfully in [13]. In this case, however, attention should be paid to the


08604 [PDF p.220]     implementation of the excitation. Namely, in practice, due to finite sampling


08605 [PDF p.220] 


08606 [PDF p.221]     194                               Chapter 6. Conclusions and recommendations


08607 [PDF p.221] 


08608 [PDF p.221] 


08609 [PDF p.221]           times, zero-order hold sampling for the input should be integrated in the EA


08610 [PDF p.221]           model for optimal accuracy. The presence of (discontinuous) zero-order hold


08611 [PDF p.221]           operations in the FP model may, however, cause difficulties regarding the dif-


08612 [PDF p.221]           ferentiation of the FP model terms during backpropagation of the EA model.


08613 [PDF p.221]           Hence, the extension of the EA model updating methodology to continuous


08614 [PDF p.221]           time and the related potential issues require further research.


08615 [PDF p.221] 


08616 [PDF p.221]       • Initialization of extended states: In the simulations obtained with the


08617 [PDF p.221]         EA models in Chapter 5, the initial values for the extended states were initial-


08618 [PDF p.221]         ized using the encoder and measured outputs. In many practical situations,


08619 [PDF p.221]         however, the model will be simulated without using some measured (output)


08620 [PDF p.221]         signals to determine the initial values of the extended states. Therefore,


08621 [PDF p.221]         other methods to initialize the extended states and the impact of incorrectly


08622 [PDF p.221]         initializing them should be researched.


08623 [PDF p.221] 


08624 [PDF p.221]       • Orthogonality and negation: In the current methodology, the extension


08625 [PDF p.221]         and augmentation terms are unconstrained, which may limit their comple-


08626 [PDF p.221] 6       mentarity with the FP model terms. This limited complementarity may


08627 [PDF p.221]         negatively affect the (physical) interpretability of the retained FP terms. To


08628 [PDF p.221]         address this issue, future work could explore methods that enforce orthog-


08629 [PDF p.221]         onality between the extension and augmentation terms, and the FP terms.


08630 [PDF p.221]         While such methods have already been developed for linear-in-the-parameter


08631 [PDF p.221]         problems [112], they are not yet available for more complex problems, as en-


08632 [PDF p.221]         countered in this research. Enforcing orthogonality could also help mitigate


08633 [PDF p.221]         the issue of negation, i.e., ensure that the trained NNs do not (partly) negate


08634 [PDF p.221]         (or cancel out) the FP terms. Note that negation is, however, a concept that


08635 [PDF p.221]         requires more fundamental attention in future research.


08636 [PDF p.221] 


08637 [PDF p.221]       • Limitations: It should be investigated where limitations of the EA model


08638 [PDF p.221]         updating method lie. For example, if the number of FP states and required


08639 [PDF p.221]         extended states is relatively large compared to the number of measured out-


08640 [PDF p.221]         puts, it will be more difficult to learn the proper behavior. Furthermore,


08641 [PDF p.221]         the complexity of the (unmodeled) nonlinearities that are present on the


08642 [PDF p.221]         physical system obviously influences the efficacy of the EA model updating


08643 [PDF p.221]         method. Moreover, it would be interesting to explore the limitations of the


08644 [PDF p.221]         EA model updating method with respect to the complexity of the FP model.


08645 [PDF p.221]         In principle, one would like to add as much physics-related knowledge as pos-


08646 [PDF p.221]         sible. However, a large number of FP states is expected to cause excessive


08647 [PDF p.221]         computation times due to the complexity of computing the required gradi-


08648 [PDF p.221]         ents during backpropagation. Consequently, updating models with flexible


08649 [PDF p.221]         multibody dynamics, for example, may prove difficult and may hence require


08650 [PDF p.221]         (component-level) reduction methods as proposed in [84].


08651 [PDF p.221] 


08652 [PDF p.222] 6.2. Recommendations                                                           195


08653 [PDF p.222] 


08654 [PDF p.222] 


08655 [PDF p.222]    Having discussed some potential research directions for the proposed model


08656 [PDF p.222] parameter and model structure updating methods, next, some final suggestions on


08657 [PDF p.222] how to combine them for optimal implementation in digital twins are offered:


08658 [PDF p.222]   • Combination of model structure updating and online model pa-


08659 [PDF p.222]     rameter updating: As already discussed in detail, the applicability of the


08660 [PDF p.222]     IMPU method is limited due to the fact that, in practice, the dynamic be-


08661 [PDF p.222]     havior of a physical system can typically only in approximation be described


08662 [PDF p.222]     by the model class of the FP model. Therefore, it is advised to first up-


08663 [PDF p.222]     date the model structure of the FP model offline, as shown at the far left


08664 [PDF p.222]     of Figure 6.1. Subsequently, an IMM can be trained by simulating the EA


08665 [PDF p.222]     model (which now better resembles the physical system), such that in the


08666 [PDF p.222]     online phase, the parameter values of the FP terms of the EA model can be


08667 [PDF p.222]     updated in (near) real-time (right-hand side of Figure 6.1).


08668 [PDF p.222]   • Interpretability of FP parameter values: Since the EA model can also


08669 [PDF p.222]     compensate for incorrect parameter values using the augmentation terms,


08670 [PDF p.222]     physical interpretability of those parameters in the FP terms may be com-         6


08671 [PDF p.222]     promised. To mitigate this, as mentioned before, FP parameter values may


08672 [PDF p.222]     directly be tuned within the EA model updating process. Moreover, orthogo-


08673 [PDF p.222]     nality of the extension and augmentation terms with respect to the FP terms


08674 [PDF p.222]     is beneficial for this purpose, i.e., dynamical terms that are already captured


08675 [PDF p.222]     by the FP model should not be (partially) covered again by the extended


08676 [PDF p.222]     or augmented terms. Note that such orthogonality ensuring methods have


08677 [PDF p.222]     been developed for linear-in-the-parameter cases [112], but are missing for


08678 [PDF p.222]     more complex problems such as the one discussed here.


08679 [PDF p.222]   • Online updating of extended and augmented terms: Besides updat-


08680 [PDF p.222]     ing the FP part of the EA model online through updating its parameter


08681 [PDF p.222]     values using the IMPU method, there is also potential to update parameter


08682 [PDF p.222]     values related to the extended and augmented terms of the EA model. Since


08683 [PDF p.222]     these terms are captured using (recurrent) neural networks, this is however


08684 [PDF p.222]     not practical due to the large amount of weights (which can be regarded as


08685 [PDF p.222]     parameters) that would require to be updated. To solve this issue, these


08686 [PDF p.222]     neural networks may be sparsified, e.g., using the Sparse Identification of


08687 [PDF p.222]     Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method [34] such that a sparse set of (mathe-


08688 [PDF p.222]     matically) interpretable terms that describes the state dynamics is obtained


08689 [PDF p.222]     from a large library of terms (X ) with corresponding parameters ξ (contained


08690 [PDF p.222]     within a matrix Ξ for all state signals). Alternatively, other dedicated ANN


08691 [PDF p.222]     sparsification/compression methods [59, 148] may be employed to limit the


08692 [PDF p.222]     number of NN-related parameters. These EA-related parameters ξ may than


08693 [PDF p.222]     be used, alongside the FP-related parameters θ to train an IMM. In the on-


08694 [PDF p.222]     line phase, values for both types of parameters can then be inferred with

08739 [PDF p.223]            negligible online computational cost. With this envisioned approach, a wide


08740 [PDF p.223]            range of (partly physically interpretable) parameter values of an EA model


08741 [PDF p.223]            with an accurate model structure can be updated online such that a high


08742 [PDF p.223]            fidelity model of the physical system is available throughout the physical


08743 [PDF p.223]            system’s operational life.


08744 [PDF p.223] 


08745 [PDF p.223]        Finally, to truly benefit from the potential of accurate digital twins (as obtained


08746 [PDF p.223]     through model updating), only having an (online) model updating method does


08747 [PDF p.223]     not suffice. Updating methods should namely be incorporated in the digital twin


08748 [PDF p.223]     workflow, along with other methods that have been developed for digital twins in


08749 [PDF p.223]     various fields, e.g., model reduction, control, and fault detection. Merging these


08750 [PDF p.223]     various techniques into a cohesive workflow poses a significant challenge which


08751 [PDF p.223]     needs to be addressed in order to successfully utilize the concept of digital twins.

08994 [PDF p.233]     B.2      Loss curves


08995 [PDF p.233]     In Figure B.1, the training and validation losses for ANNs, trained with tuned


08996 [PDF p.233]     hyperparameters, without FS and with FS (JMI) are plotted. As shown in this


08997 [PDF p.233]     figure, typical ANN training behavior is observed for both cases. However, it is


08998 [PDF p.233]     observed that the ANN with FS is able to achieve lower validation losses than


08999 [PDF p.233]     when no FS is employed (as is also observed in Table 3.4). In contrast, a lower


09000 [PDF p.233] B   training loss is achieved for the ANN without FS. As a result, the gap between the


09001 [PDF p.233]     validation and training loss is larger without employing FS, hinting at a form of


09002 [PDF p.233]     overfitting. Consequently, we conclude that including FS may reduce the chance


09003 [PDF p.233]     on overfitting. Regularization of the weights of the ANN may prevent overfitting


09004 [PDF p.233]     as well. However, since the trend of the validation loss (towards the final epochs)


09005 [PDF p.233]     is non-increasing, the accuracy of the ANN might improve still. For that reason,


09006 [PDF p.233]     regularization has not been applied here. Note that, for the ANN without FS,


09007 [PDF p.233]     training is stopped prematurely due to early stopping.

09158 [PDF p.240]                                                                    D


09159 [PDF p.240] D.1      Normalization versus scaling


09160 [PDF p.240] As discussed in Section 5.2.2, linear scaling (see (5.5)-(5.10)) is used for numerical


09161 [PDF p.240] conditioning purposes. Alternatively, affine normalization is typically employed


09162 [PDF p.240] in the original (purely data-based) SUBNET approach [14] and in the machine


09163 [PDF p.240] learning literature in general. However, when augmenting an existing FP model,


09164 [PDF p.240] normalization can hinder convergence during training. In the following, this issue


09165 [PDF p.240] is explained for a simplified example of a dynamical system exhibiting a single


09166 [PDF p.240] state (of the FP model) x̄ ∈ R for which the discrete vector field function of the


09167 [PDF p.240] true system (or plant) is given by


09168 [PDF p.240] 


09169 [PDF p.240]         x̄k+1 = āx̄k + c̄x̄k .                                                 (D.1)


09170 [PDF p.240] 


09171 [PDF p.240] To model this plant it is assumed that the term āx̄k is known (exactly) as an


09172 [PDF p.240] FP model, i.e., xk+1 = axk with a = ā. Consequently, the term c̄x̄k has to be


09173 [PDF p.240] learned by the RNN which is assumed to be a ’neural network’ with a single input,


09174 [PDF p.240] a single output, and zero hidden layers (i.e., a single weight w and a single bias


09175 [PDF p.240] b). In contrast to the traditional SUBNET approach, the presence of the (non-


09176 [PDF p.240] normalized) FP term, requires us to normalize and denormalize the EA model’s


09177 [PDF p.240] state x̂ within the discrete vector field function as follows:


09178 [PDF p.240] 


09179 [PDF p.240]         x̂k+1 = ax̂k + P −1 (wP(x̂k ) + b) ,                                    (D.2)


09180 [PDF p.240] 


09181 [PDF p.241]     214                                          Appendix D. Appendix to Chapter 5


09182 [PDF p.241] 


09183 [PDF p.241] 


09184 [PDF p.241]     where P and P −1 represent the (affine) normalization and denormalization func-


09185 [PDF p.241]     tion, respectively, defined as


09186 [PDF p.241]                           xk − xmin


09187 [PDF p.241]                P(xk ) =             ,                                               (D.3)


09188 [PDF p.241]                                ∆x


09189 [PDF p.241]             P −1 (x̃k ) = x̃k ∆x + xmin ,                                           (D.4)


09190 [PDF p.241]     where ∆x and xmin may be defined as in (5.8) and (5.10), respectively. The


09191 [PDF p.241]     analysis provided here assumes min-max normalization is considered, but holds


09192 [PDF p.241]     for any affine normalization method. Note that the only difference between the


09193 [PDF p.241]     scaling as defined in (5.5)-(5.7) and the affine normalization presented here is the


09194 [PDF p.241]     addition of xmin which makes the functions in (D.3) and (D.4) affine.


09195 [PDF p.241]         Using (D.3) and (D.4) to expand (D.2), we obtain


09196 [PDF p.241]             x̂k+1 = (a + w)x̂k − wxmin + b∆x + xmin .                               (D.5)


09197 [PDF p.241]     Here, it is recognized that the term xmin (which is an artifact of the affine denor-


09198 [PDF p.241]     malization) strongly influences the steady-state behavior of the EA model. Since,


09199 [PDF p.241]     for min-max normalization, as defined in (5.10), xmin is the minimum of the state


09200 [PDF p.241]     signal as obtained by simulating the FP model, it is typically non-zero. Note


09201 [PDF p.241]     that, in general, affine normalization will introduce a non-zero xmin . The resulting


09202 [PDF p.241]     steady-state solution of the EA model is given by:


09203 [PDF p.241]                                   −wxmin + b∆x + xmin


09204 [PDF p.241]             x̂steady-state,EA =                       .                             (D.6)


09205 [PDF p.241]                                       1−a−w


09206 [PDF p.241]                                                                    (1)


09207 [PDF p.241]     At the start of the training process, when w and b (for lw1 ) are initialized to


09208 [PDF p.241]     be small (see the second to last paragraph in Section 5.2.3), i.e., w ≈ b ≈ 0.


09209 [PDF p.241]     Consequently, the steady state solution of the EA model at the start of the training


09210 [PDF p.241]     process becomes:

09214 [PDF p.241] D   and will thus be non-zero for a non-zero xmin . In contrast, the steady-state solution


09215 [PDF p.241]     of the original FP model, which is assumed to be reasonably accurate, is zero for


09216 [PDF p.241]     this example. Evidently, this results in an inaccurate model at the start of the


09217 [PDF p.241]     training phase which may be relatively difficult to train such that it corrects for


09218 [PDF p.241]     this initial error (which, depending on the value of xmin may be significant).

09458 [PDF p.245]     D.3       Hyperparameter values


09459 [PDF p.245]     In this section, the NN topology, weight initialization, and other hyperparameter


09460 [PDF p.245]     values used to train the EA models in both use cases and the SUBNET model in


09461 [PDF p.245]     the linear academic use case are listed.


09462 [PDF p.245]          All NNs used in Chapter 5 consist of two hidden layers. The number of weights


09463 [PDF p.245]     in the first hidden layer of any NN equals 3 times the number of inputs to that


09464 [PDF p.245]     NN. Similarly, the number of weights in the second hidden layer of any NN equals


09465 [PDF p.245]     3 times the number of outputs of that NN. The only exception to this rule is for


09466 [PDF p.245]      (2)


09467 [PDF p.245]     lw2 (· · · ) of the SUBNET model for the academic use case. For this NN, 4 times


09468 [PDF p.245]     the number of inputs/outputs for the first/second hidden layer is used, to ensure


09469 [PDF p.245] D   that the total number of weights of the SUBNET model (13870) is comparable


09470 [PDF p.245]     to the number of weights for the EA model with next = 2 (13630). Furthermore,


09471 [PDF p.245]     for the industrial use case, fully connected linear bypasses (i.e., weighted connec-


09472 [PDF p.245]     tions directly going from the input layer to the output layer and thus bypassing


09473 [PDF p.245]                                                    (1)           (2)


09474 [PDF p.245]     the (nonlinear) hidden layers) are used in lw1 (· · · ) and lw2 (· · · ) to enhance the


09475 [PDF p.245]     numerical conditioning for the backpropagation step.


09476 [PDF p.245]          As activation functions for the hidden layers, linear activation functions are


09477 [PDF p.245]     used for the models trained for the academic use case (both the EA model and the


09478 [PDF p.245]     SUBNET model, see Section 5.3.1), and tanh activation functions for the industrial


09479 [PDF p.245]     use case (see Section 5.3.2). For the output layers, linear activation functions are


09480 [PDF p.245]     always used.

10682 [PDF p.274] Bas Mats Kessels was born in Sittard, The Nether-


10683 [PDF p.274] lands, in 1996. After finishing his secondary education

10685 [PDF p.274] ied Mechanical Engineering at Eindhoven University


10686 [PDF p.274] of Technology (TU/e), Eindhoven, The Netherlands.


10687 [PDF p.274] Here, he received his B.Sc.-degree (with great apprecia-


10688 [PDF p.274] tion) in Mechanical Engineering in August 2017. He re-


10689 [PDF p.274] ceived his M.Sc.-degree (cum laude) in Mechanical En-


10690 [PDF p.274] gineering from the TU/e in January 2020, graduating


10691 [PDF p.274] on improved assembly reduction by selection of compo-


10692 [PDF p.274] nent eigenmodes using frequency-based substructuring


10693 [PDF p.274] at the Dynamics and Control group under supervision of ir. Thijs Verhees (ASML),


10694 [PDF p.274] ir. Alexander Steenhoek (ASML), and prof.dr.ir. Nathan van de Wouw (TU/e).


10695 [PDF p.274]      In May 2020, he started as a Doctoral Candidate at the Dynamics and Control


10696 [PDF p.274] group of the Mechanical Engineering Department at the TU/e under the super-


10697 [PDF p.274] vision of prof.dr.ir. Nathan van de Wouw and prof.dr.ir. Rob Fey. For his PhD


10698 [PDF p.274] project, he focuses on model updating techniques for digital twins for which ar-


10699 [PDF p.274] tificial intelligence techniques are employed. This research is part of the Digital


10700 [PDF p.274] Twin perspective program, a Dutch research program funded by the Dutch Re-


10701 [PDF p.274] search Council (NWO). The main results of this research are presented in this


10702 [PDF p.274] dissertation.
